[1] (lifestyle-migraine-sleep)
## Why sleep gets its own note here

Sleep and migraine influence each other in both directions, which is unusual among the commonly
cited triggers. Disturbed sleep makes attacks more likely; attacks disturb sleep; and sleep is also
one of the more reliable ways an attack ends. A change in sleep pattern is among the most frequently
identified triggers people report, and it is one of the few that is straightforwardly modifiable.

## Regularity matters more than duration

The pattern most often described is that change, rather than any particular amount, is what provokes
attacks. Too little sleep triggers them; so does sleeping in. This is why weekend headaches are such
a recognizable pattern — a late Friday night followed by a long Saturday lie-in shifts sleep timing
in both directions across two days, and often takes a relaxation in caffeine intake with it.

The practical implication runs against instinct. Recovering lost sleep by extending the weekend
morning is the move most likely to produce an attack, and holding the wake time steady, then
catching up with a short early-afternoon nap if needed, is the alternative usually suggested.

## Sleep as an abortive

Many people find that sleep ends an attack, and that the attack lifts on waking. This is worth
knowing because it conflicts with the general advice about protecting night-time sleep pressure:
during an attack, lying down in a dark quiet room and sleeping is a reasonable response rather than
a habit to be resisted. The regularity advice applies to ordinary days, not to the day of an attack.

## Where the two conditions overlap

Insomnia and migraine occur together more often than either alone would predict, and so does
obstructive sleep apnea (apnoea). Two patterns are worth recognizing because they change what should
be looked at rather than what should be done at home: headache present on waking most mornings, and
loud snoring with witnessed pauses in breathing or heavy daytime sleepiness. Both are reasons for
assessment rather than for adjusting habits.

Frequent night waking with headache, or headache that repeatedly wakes someone from sleep, is
likewise a pattern to raise with a clinician rather than to manage with sleep habits.

## Caffeine sits inside the sleep question

Caffeine is a common component of acute headache treatment and also a determinant of sleep quality,
so the two cannot be adjusted independently. A steady daily intake, taken early in the day, avoids
both the withdrawal headache that follows an abrupt drop and the sleep fragmentation that follows a
late dose. Sudden changes in either direction are the part most often associated with attacks. The
migraine guideline note in this corpus covers acute and preventive treatment, including what happens
when acute treatment is used too often.

[2] (condition-migraine)
## What it is

Migraine is a recurrent neurological disorder whose most prominent feature is headache, but which
also involves sensory sensitivity, nausea and, in some people, transient neurological symptoms. It
is episodic in most people and chronic in a minority, where chronic migraine is defined as headache
on fifteen or more days per month, of which at least eight have migraine features, for more than
three months.

## The typical attack

A migraine headache is classically one-sided, pulsating, moderate to severe, and made worse by
routine physical activity; it is accompanied by nausea, vomiting, or sensitivity to light and sound.
Untreated attacks commonly last from several hours to three days. Not every attack has every
feature, and the headache is bilateral in a substantial proportion of people — which is one reason
migraine is frequently mislabeled as sinus or tension headache.

Attacks often have phases: a premonitory phase hours to a day beforehand with mood change, yawning,
food cravings or neck stiffness; in about a third of people an aura; the headache itself; and a
recovery phase with fatigue and difficulty concentrating. Recognizing the premonitory phase is
practically useful, because it is the point at which acute treatment works best.

## Aura

Aura is a set of fully reversible neurological symptoms that usually develop over five or more
minutes and last less than an hour. Most often visual — flickering lights, zigzag lines, or an area
of lost vision that expands across the visual field — and less often sensory, with spreading numbness
or tingling, or affecting speech. Aura most often precedes the headache but can accompany it or
occur without any headache at all, which is disconcerting the first time it happens.

Aura that begins abruptly at full intensity, that lasts longer than an hour, or that involves
weakness rather than sensory change is not typical and prompts assessment for another cause.

## Common triggers

Irregular sleep, missed meals, dehydration, stress and the let-down period after stress, hormonal
change around menstruation, alcohol, certain foods in susceptible individuals, weather change, bright
or flickering light, and overuse of acute headache medication. Triggers are individual and often
additive rather than absolute — a food that is tolerated when rested may not be after a poor night.
A headache diary is the usual way to identify them, since recall alone reliably produces false
associations by noticing the memorable and ignoring the times nothing happened.

## How it is generally managed

Three parts: treating attacks early when they occur, reducing frequency with preventive treatment
when attacks are frequent or disabling, and addressing contributing factors including sleep, meal
regularity, and overuse of acute medication. Treatment thresholds, drug classes and
medication-overuse limits are covered by the migraine guideline note in this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

A headache is not a migraine question when it is sudden and reaches maximum intensity within about a
minute, when it comes with fever and a stiff neck, when it follows a head injury, when it comes with
new weakness, numbness, confusion, visual loss or difficulty speaking that does not resolve, when it
begins after age 50 as a new headache type, or when it worsens progressively over days or weeks.
These require urgent medical assessment. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern them.

[3] (red-flag-sudden-severe-headache)
## Call emergency services immediately

- A headache that comes on abruptly and reaches maximum intensity within about a minute — often
  described as the worst headache of one's life, or as being hit on the head. This is a thunderclap
  headache.
- Headache with fever and a stiff neck, or with a rash that does not fade under pressure.
- Headache with new confusion, drowsiness, seizure, weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, or
  visual loss.
- Headache after a head injury, particularly with vomiting, drowsiness or worsening over hours.
- Headache with sudden severe eye pain, a red eye, and blurred vision or halos around lights.

## Seek same-day medical assessment

- A new type of headache beginning after age 50.
- Headache that steadily worsens over days or weeks, or that is consistently worse on waking, on
  lying flat, or on coughing, straining or bending.
- New headache in someone with cancer, HIV, immunosuppression, or on anticoagulation.
- New headache in pregnancy or the postpartum period, particularly with visual changes, swelling or
  upper abdominal pain.
- Headache with scalp tenderness or jaw pain on chewing in someone over 50.

## Why thunderclap headache is treated as an emergency

The pattern is the concern, not the severity. A headache that reaches peak intensity almost
instantly can indicate bleeding around the brain from a ruptured aneurysm, and several other serious
causes present the same way. The mortality is high and depends on how quickly it is treated.

The critical point is that a thunderclap headache warrants emergency assessment **even if it then
settles completely**, including where simple painkillers appear to have relieved it. Resolution does
not exclude the diagnosis, and a warning bleed can precede a much larger one by days.

## Why the others are on the list

Fever with a stiff neck raises meningitis; a non-blanching rash raises meningococcal infection.
Headache worse on waking or on straining raises raised pressure inside the skull. Scalp tenderness
and jaw claudication over 50 raise giant cell arteritis, which can cause irreversible blindness
within days and is one of the few headache causes where hours of delay change the outcome
permanently. Eye pain with a red eye and halos raises acute angle-closure glaucoma, also
sight-threatening.

## What this note is not for

Most headaches are not dangerous. Migraine and tension-type headache are common, recurrent, and
recognizable by pattern, and they are covered by the migraine notes in this corpus. The purpose here
is to identify the minority of presentations where the pattern itself — sudden onset, new type,
progressive course, or accompanying neurological or systemic features — is the warning, independent
of how severe the pain feels.

This system does not diagnose. Any presentation matching this note is escalated, and no answer it
produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

[4] (condition-insomnia)
## What it is

Insomnia is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking earlier than intended, despite
adequate opportunity to sleep, together with daytime consequences. Both halves are required. Sleeping
six hours and functioning well is not insomnia; sleeping six hours and being impaired by it may be.
The condition is defined by the mismatch between sleep obtained and sleep needed, not by a clock
value.

Short-term insomnia lasting days to weeks, usually with an identifiable precipitant, is common and
often self-limiting. Chronic insomnia disorder — at least three nights per week for at least three
months — is a distinct condition that persists after the original precipitant has resolved.

## Why it persists after the trigger goes

This is the part that explains the treatment. An episode is typically precipitated by stress,
illness or a schedule change. What perpetuates it are the responses: going to bed earlier to
"catch up", staying in bed awake, daytime napping, and increasing effort to fall asleep. Time in bed
rises while sleep does not, so the bed becomes associated with wakefulness, and the effort itself
increases arousal. The condition then maintains itself independently of what started it — which is
why treatment targets those perpetuating behaviors rather than the original stressor.

## How it is usually recognized

The account of the sleep pattern, supported by a sleep diary kept over one to two weeks. Diaries
matter because recall systematically overestimates how long it took to fall asleep and underestimates
total sleep — the periods of sleep between awakenings are not remembered.

## What else presents as insomnia

Obstructive sleep apnea (apnoea), restless legs syndrome, circadian rhythm disorders including shift
work and delayed sleep phase, chronic pain, depression, anxiety, and the effects of caffeine,
alcohol, nicotine, stimulants and some prescribed medications. Screening for these is part of the
assessment rather than a step taken only when treatment fails, because treating the wrong condition
is the most common reason for non-response. Alcohol deserves specific mention: it shortens the time
to fall asleep and fragments the second half of the night, so it is frequently reported as a remedy
by someone whose sleep it is degrading.

## Why it is treated

Chronic insomnia is associated with impaired daytime function, reduced quality of life, and
increased risk of depression, and it complicates the management of coexisting physical illness. It
also responds durably to non-drug treatment, which makes long-term reliance on hypnotics avoidable
for most people.

## How it is generally managed

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is first-line, with medication second-line and
time-limited. The components, the evidence, and the specific point that sleep hygiene advice alone
is not effective treatment are covered by the insomnia guideline note in this corpus.

## When further assessment is advised

Loud snoring with witnessed pauses in breathing, excessive daytime sleepiness, falling asleep while
driving, acting out dreams, or sleep disturbance alongside low mood and hopelessness all warrant
assessment beyond insomnia treatment.

[5] (guideline-insomnia-cbt-first-line)
## What counts as chronic insomnia

Chronic insomnia disorder is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early,
occurring at least three nights per week for at least three months, despite adequate opportunity to
sleep, and accompanied by daytime consequences — fatigue, impaired attention, mood disturbance, or
impaired performance. The daytime component is part of the definition: short sleep without daytime
consequences is not a disorder, and treating it as one medicalizes normal variation in sleep need.

Assessment includes a sleep diary over one to two weeks, screening for the conditions that commonly
present as insomnia — obstructive sleep apnea (apnoea), restless legs syndrome, circadian rhythm
disorders, depression, anxiety, pain, and substance or medication effects — and review of caffeine,
alcohol, nicotine and shift patterns. Alcohol is worth singling out: it shortens sleep latency and
then fragments the second half of the night, so it is often reported as a remedy by someone whose
sleep it is degrading.

## The first-line recommendation

Both sleep medicine and internal medicine guidance describes cognitive behavioral therapy for
insomnia as first-line for chronic insomnia in adults, ahead of medication. Its effects persist after treatment
ends, whereas pharmacological effects generally do not, and it avoids the harms associated with
long-term hypnotic use.

The components are delivered together as a package over roughly four to eight sessions:

- **Stimulus control** — using the bed only for sleep, leaving the bed when unable to sleep, so the
  bed stops being a cue for wakefulness.
- **Sleep restriction** — limiting time in bed toward actual sleep time, then extending it as sleep
  consolidates. Counterintuitive, and the component people most often abandon early.
- **Cognitive restructuring** of the beliefs about sleep that maintain arousal, including the
  catastrophizing about tomorrow that keeps someone awake tonight.
- **Sleep hygiene education**, necessary but insufficient on its own. Guidance is explicit that
  sleep hygiene advice alone is not effective treatment for chronic insomnia — a frequent
  misunderstanding, and the reason that "I already tried sleep hygiene" is not evidence that this
  therapy has been tried.
- **Relaxation training.**

Digitally delivered and brief formats are reasonable where in-person therapy is not accessible,
which is the practical constraint most often cited against the recommendation.

## Where medication sits

Pharmacotherapy is second-line: for people in whom cognitive behavioral therapy is unavailable, has
been tried without adequate response, or where short-term treatment is needed alongside it. Shared
decision-making, the shortest appropriate duration, and a plan for reassessment and discontinuation
agreed at the point of starting rather than later. Antihistamine-based over-the-counter sleep aids
have limited evidence and notable anticholinergic side effects, particularly in older adults.

## What is outside this note

Doses and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this system.

[6] (guideline-migraine-acute-and-preventive-treatment)
## Acute treatment

An attack is treated early, while pain is still mild, because response rates fall once an attack is
established and central sensitization has set in. The options are grouped by evidence strength
rather than presented as a ranked list for an individual:

- Simple analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for mild to moderate attacks.
- Triptans for moderate to severe attacks, or where simple analgesics have failed.
- The gepant and ditan classes where triptans are ineffective, not tolerated, or contraindicated by
  cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease — which is the main limitation on triptan use.
- Anti-nausea agents as adjuncts where nausea limits oral treatment; non-oral routes where vomiting
  or gastric stasis makes an oral route unreliable.

Treating on two or three separate attacks before judging an agent ineffective is the usual standard,
since attack-to-attack variability is high.

## When preventive treatment starts

Preventive treatment is offered when attacks are frequent or disabling enough that acute treatment
alone is insufficient. Guidance describes the threshold as four or more migraine days per month with
some disability, or fewer attacks where disability is severe, where acute treatment is ineffective
or contraindicated, or where the person prefers it. The aim is a reduction in frequency and
severity, not the elimination of attacks: a 50 percent reduction in migraine days is the conventional
definition of a treatment response.

## Preventive classes

Classes with supporting evidence include beta-blockers, the antiepileptics topiramate and valproate,
the tricyclic amitriptyline, candesartan, and the CGRP-targeted monoclonal antibodies and oral
gepants. The choice is made on comorbidity, side-effect profile and pregnancy status rather than by
a fixed order — an agent that also treats a coexisting condition is preferred, and valproate and
topiramate require particular care in people who could become pregnant.

## Assessing response

An adequate trial precedes any judgment of failure: commonly eight to twelve weeks at an appropriate
dose. A headache diary is the instrument for that judgment, because recall of attack frequency is
unreliable and tends to be dominated by the worst recent attack rather than the average.

## Medication-overuse headache

This is the point guidance emphasizes most. Frequent use of acute medication can itself sustain a
headache disorder, converting an episodic pattern into a chronic one. The limits are fewer than ten
treatment days per month for triptans, ergots, opioids and combination analgesics, and fewer than
fifteen days per month for simple analgesics. Overuse is a common and reversible reason for
headaches having become chronic, and it is checked for before a preventive regimen is escalated.

## What is outside this note

Doses, titration and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this system.
Sudden severe headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute, headache with fever and neck
stiffness, headache with new neurological deficit, and headache after head injury are emergency
presentations covered elsewhere in this corpus, not migraine management questions.

[7] (coding-insomnia-g47)
## Two categories in two chapters

Insomnia is the clearest example in ICD-10-CM of one complaint classified in two different chapters,
and choosing between them is the whole of the problem.

G47 sits in the nervous system chapter, in the episodic and paroxysmal block, and holds the sleep
disorders of organic origin. Its insomnia subdivisions cover insomnia unspecified, insomnia due to a
medical condition, and other specified insomnia.

F51 sits in the mental and behavioral chapter, in the block for behavioral syndromes associated with
physiological disturbances, and holds sleep disorders *not* due to a substance or a known
physiological condition. Its insomnia subdivisions are the ones a sleep clinic vocabulary uses:
primary insomnia, adjustment insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, psychophysiologic insomnia, insomnia
due to another mental disorder, and other specified.

## What decides which chapter

The dividing question is whether the record attributes the insomnia to a physiological cause. Where
it does — a medical condition named as responsible — the code comes from the nervous system chapter,
and a second code identifying that condition is reported with it. Where the record attributes it to
a mental disorder, or describes it in the primary, adjustment or psychophysiologic terms, the code
comes from the mental and behavioral chapter.

Where the record says only "insomnia", with no attribution at all, the classification defaults to
the unspecified code in the nervous system chapter. That default is worth knowing precisely because
it is not intuitive: the unqualified term does not land in the psychological branch.

## The rest of the G47 category

The category holds more than insomnia, and questions about sleep frequently arrive at one of the
others. Hypersomnia, circadian rhythm sleep disorders, the sleep apnea (apnoea) subdivisions
including the obstructive form, narcolepsy, the parasomnias including sleepwalking and night
terrors, and sleep-related movement disorders are all in the same category or immediately beside it
in the same chapter. Restless legs syndrome sits in the movement disorder block earlier in the
chapter rather than with the sleep codes.

Obstructive sleep apnea being here rather than in the respiratory chapter is the misplacement people
make most often in this area.

## Symptoms, and what is not a diagnosis

Somnolence, drowsiness and a complaint of poor sleep with no diagnosis recorded are classified with
the symptoms in Chapter 18. Sleep deprivation — insufficient sleep because of circumstances rather
than an inability to sleep — is not a disorder in this category at all; it is a
factors-influencing-health code, and the distinction between not sleeping and not having the
opportunity to sleep is one the classification takes seriously.

## Codes that commonly accompany a sleep code

Where insomnia is attributed to a medical or mental condition, that condition's code is reported
with it, and the anxiety and depressive categories are the most frequent companions. Long-term drug
therapy status and body mass index come from the factors-influencing-health chapter, the latter
alongside the sleep apnea codes in particular.

[8] (lifestyle-insomnia-sleep)
## What this note is and is not

These are the day-to-day habits that support sleep. They are supportive measures, not a treatment
for chronic insomnia in their own right — the insomnia guideline note in this corpus covers what the
first-line treatment is and why habit change alone does not substitute for it. What follows is the
practical content of the habits themselves.

## The wake time, not the bedtime

The single most useful anchor is a consistent wake time, held seven days a week. Sleep timing is
regulated by a body clock that takes its strongest cue from morning light, and a wake time that
moves by two or three hours at weekends shifts the clock in a way that makes falling asleep on a
weeknight harder. Bedtime is allowed to vary; the wake time is the part that is held.

Going to bed earlier to compensate for a bad night generally backfires, because time in bed spent
awake is what teaches the association between bed and wakefulness.

## Light

Bright light in the first hour or two after waking advances the clock and strengthens the signal
separating day from night. Outdoor light is far stronger than indoor lighting even on an overcast
day, so a short walk in the morning does more than a lamp. In the evening the aim is the reverse:
dimmer light in the last hour or two.

Screens matter less for their light than for what is on them. A device that is emotionally
activating at midnight is a problem whatever its color temperature.

## Caffeine, alcohol and nicotine

Caffeine has a long half-life, and a meaningful fraction of an afternoon dose is still present at
bedtime. People who report that coffee does not affect them are usually reporting that it does not
stop them falling asleep, which is a different thing from it not fragmenting the night. A cut-off in
the early afternoon is the common practical approach.

Alcohol shortens the time to fall asleep and then degrades the second half of the night, producing
lighter, more broken sleep and early waking. It is the most frequently self-prescribed sleep aid and
the one most likely to entrench the problem. Nicotine is a stimulant and withdrawal across the night
contributes to early waking.

## Naps

A short early-afternoon nap is compatible with good night sleep for most people. Long or late naps
reduce the sleep pressure that has been building since waking, and where insomnia is the problem,
protecting that pressure matters more than recovering the lost hour.

## The room, and the clock

Cool, dark and quiet, with the clock turned away. Checking the time during the night converts
wakefulness into arithmetic about how little sleep remains, which raises arousal exactly when the
aim is to lower it. Exercise supports sleep generally; vigorous exercise very close to bedtime
suits some people and not others, and it is worth testing individually rather than assuming.

[9] (coding-icd10-chapter-06-nervous)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 6 of ICD-10-CM covers G00 through G99: diseases of the nervous system, central and
peripheral, together with the neuromuscular junction and muscle. Every code begins with the letter
G. The chapter is organized by mechanism rather than by anatomy, which is why the block boundaries
are not obvious from a symptom.

## The blocks, in order

Inflammatory diseases of the central nervous system open the chapter at G00 to G09 — the
meningitides classified by organism, encephalitis, and intracranial abscess. Systemic atrophies
primarily affecting the central nervous system follow at G10 to G14.

Extrapyramidal and movement disorders occupy G20 to G26, including Parkinson disease, the dystonias,
tremor and restless legs. Other degenerative diseases of the nervous system sit at G30 to G32, which
is where Alzheimer disease is classified, and the demyelinating diseases including multiple
sclerosis at G35 to G37.

The block that carries most everyday questions is G40 to G47, episodic and paroxysmal disorders. It
holds epilepsy and seizures, migraine, the other headache syndromes such as cluster and tension-type
headache, transient cerebral ischemic attack, and the sleep disorders of organic origin — insomnia,
hypersomnia, circadian rhythm disorders, sleep apnea (apnoea) and the parasomnias.

Nerve, nerve root and plexus disorders follow at G50 to G59, covering the cranial neuropathies
including facial palsy, and the entrapment neuropathies. Polyneuropathies and other disorders of the
peripheral nervous system occupy G60 to G65, diseases of the myoneural junction and muscle G70 to
G73, and cerebral palsy and the other paralytic syndromes G80 to G83. The chapter closes at G89 to
G99 with a mixed block that includes the pain categories and postprocedural nervous-system
disorders.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Stroke is the boundary people cross by accident. Cerebral infarction and intracranial hemorrhage are
cerebrovascular disease and are classified with the circulatory system, and so are the codes for
deficits persisting afterwards — but transient ischemic attack is here, in G45. The two sit in
different chapters despite being discussed together.

Headache is the other boundary. A headache syndrome with a name is a G code; headache as an
undiagnosed symptom is classified in Chapter 18, along with dizziness, somnolence, abnormal
involuntary movements, convulsions not identified as epilepsy, and an abnormal neurological finding
with no diagnosis. Sleep disorders that are not attributed to a substance or a known physiological
condition are classified with the mental and behavioral disorders instead of here.

## Codes from other chapters that nervous-system questions commonly need

Diabetic neuropathy is coded from the diabetes category in the endocrine chapter, not from the
polyneuropathy block, because the classification presumes the association. Traumatic brain and
spinal injury belongs to the injury chapter, with this chapter holding the sequelae only where a
named neurological condition results. Long-term drug therapy status and family history come from the

question: How is COPD different from asthma?
answer:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma are both respiratory conditions, but they have distinct characteristics.

**COPD** is a progressive disease characterized by persistent airflow obstruction, primarily due to chronic bronchitis and emphysema. It typically develops over many years, often as a result of long-term exposure to irritants, such as tobacco smoke. Patients with COPD generally experience symptoms like a chronic cough, sputum production, and difficulty breathing that worsen over time.

On the other hand, **asthma** is a chronic inflammatory condition of the airways that can cause variable airflow obstruction. It is characterized by episodes of wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath that can be triggered by various factors, including allergens, exercise, or respiratory infections. A key feature of asthma is the variability of symptoms; they can change day-to-day and are often reversible with asthma medications.

Both conditions can coexist, particularly in older adults with a history of smoking (source: "condition-asthma" and "condition-copd"). When asthma occurs alongside COPD, the diagnosis and management may involve recognizing and treating both conditions. 

If you have concerns about these conditions, discussing them with a healthcare provider would be beneficial.

Not medical advice. This is an educational software project. It does not diagnose or treat, and it must not be used for real medical decisions.

[1] (coding-asthma-j45)
## The category and its two axes

Asthma is J45 in ICD-10-CM, in Chapter 10, diseases of the respiratory system. The category is never
used at three characters, and what fills the remaining ones is two independent axes crossed with
each other.

The first axis is severity, expressed in the classification's own vocabulary rather than the
patient's: mild intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent and severe persistent, plus an
"other and unspecified" branch for asthma documented without a severity level. The second axis is
the state of the disease at this encounter: uncomplicated, with acute exacerbation, or with status
asthmaticus.

Every combination of the two exists as a code. That is the whole shape of the category, and it is
why asthma questions so often reduce to two lookups rather than one.

## Exacerbation and status asthmaticus are exclusive

The two are alternatives, not a scale that can be climbed within a single code. Status asthmaticus
describes an attack that has not responded to treatment, and where it is documented the code says
status asthmaticus and does not also say acute exacerbation. Choosing between them is a
documentation question, not a clinical judgment the coder makes.

## The unspecified branch, and what it costs

Asthma documented with no severity stated is coded to the unspecified branch, which remains valid
and is frequently the only supportable choice. The classification does not permit severity to be
inferred from the treatment recorded, from a peak-flow value, or from how the condition is described
elsewhere in the chart. Where severity is not documented, unspecified is the correct code rather
than a fallback.

## Named variants inside the category

Two variants sit at the far end of the category with their own codes rather than in the severity
grid: exercise-induced bronchospasm and cough variant asthma. Occupational asthma attributed to an
identified agent is classified with the lung diseases due to external agents instead of here, and
the agent is named by an external-cause code.

## Asthma alongside chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

Where both are documented, the chronic obstructive pulmonary disease category carries an instruction
to add a code from J45 identifying the type of asthma, so the two are reported together rather than
one being chosen over the other. The reverse is not true: an asthma code alone does not imply the
other condition.

## Codes that commonly accompany J45

Tobacco is the standard companion. The category carries an explicit instruction to add a code
identifying tobacco dependence, use, exposure or a past history of use, and those live in the mental
and behavioral chapter and the factors-influencing-health chapter respectively. Allergic rhinitis
has its own category in the same chapter and is reported alongside rather than folded in. Wheeze,
cough and shortness of breath are symptoms and are not coded when asthma is documented, because they
are intrinsic to it.

[2] (coding-copd-j44)
## The category

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is J44 in ICD-10-CM, in Chapter 10, among the chronic lower
respiratory diseases. Unlike the asthma category beside it, J44 has no severity axis. What its
fourth character records is whether a complication is present at this encounter.

Three subdivisions carry most of the work: the disease with an acute lower respiratory infection,
the disease with an acute exacerbation, and the disease without either, which is the unspecified
code used for a stable presentation. The category also carries subdivisions for other specified
forms.

## The two complication codes are not alternatives

This is the detail that distinguishes J44 from most complication-bearing categories. An infection
and an exacerbation are different events, and someone can have both at once. Where both are
documented, both codes are reported — the classification does not treat the pair as mutually
exclusive the way asthma treats exacerbation and status asthmaticus.

The infection code also does not name the infection. It records that one is present, and a second
code identifying the organism or the specific infection is reported in addition, from whichever
category owns it. Pneumonia accompanying the disease is coded that way rather than being absorbed.

## What the category includes and what sits beside it

The category takes in the overlapping descriptions that clinical records use for the same disease —
chronic obstructive bronchitis, chronic bronchitis with emphysema, chronic obstructive asthma.
Emphysema without chronic bronchitis has its own category, as do simple and mucopurulent chronic
bronchitis and bronchitis not specified as acute or chronic; those are neighbors in the same block,
not subdivisions of this one.

Where asthma is documented alongside, this category carries an instruction to add a code identifying
the type of asthma, so both appear.

## Respiratory failure, and sequencing

Acute or chronic respiratory failure is a separate category at the end of the chapter and is
reported in addition when documented. Which of the two is sequenced first depends on the
circumstances of the encounter rather than on a fixed rule, and it is a sequencing question the
record has to answer.

## Codes that commonly accompany J44

The category carries an explicit instruction to add a code identifying tobacco dependence, use,
exposure or a past history of use, and in practice one of those accompanies most records here.
Occupational or environmental exposure is coded from the factors-influencing-health chapter, with
the external-cause chapter naming the agent. Long-term oxygen use and long-term drug therapy are
status codes. Shortness of breath, cough and sputum production are symptoms intrinsic to the disease
and are not coded separately once it is documented.

[3] (condition-copd)
## What it is

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is persistent airflow limitation caused by long-term damage to
the airways and the lung tissue itself. Two processes usually coexist: chronic inflammation and
narrowing of the small airways, and emphysema, the destruction of the alveolar walls across which
gas is exchanged. The limitation is persistent rather than variable, which is the main contrast with
asthma, although the two overlap in some people and the overlap is treated as its own situation.

The damage is not reversible. Treatment reduces symptoms, improves exercise capacity and reduces
exacerbations; stopping the exposure that caused it is what changes the trajectory.

## How it is usually recognized

Breathlessness on exertion that has worsened gradually over years, chronic cough, and sputum
production, in someone with a relevant exposure history. People commonly attribute the early stage
to age or being out of shape and reduce their activity to match, which conceals the progression —
so the first presentation is often later than the first symptom, sometimes at an exacerbation.

The diagnosis requires spirometry and is not made on symptoms alone; the COPD guideline note in this
corpus covers the threshold and the assessment.

## What contributes to it

Tobacco smoking is the dominant cause in high-income countries. Also relevant: biomass fuel smoke
from indoor cooking and heating, occupational dust, vapors and fumes, air pollution, childhood
respiratory infections and impaired lung growth, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency — an inherited
condition worth considering when COPD appears young, in a non-smoker, or with a strong family
history.

## Exacerbations

An exacerbation is an acute worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond normal day-to-day variation,
usually triggered by a viral or bacterial infection. They matter more than the label suggests: each
one tends to worsen quality of life, accelerate lung-function decline, and predict the next, and a
history of them is the single strongest predictor of future ones. Recovery to baseline can take
weeks, and a proportion of people never return fully to their previous level.

## How it is generally managed

Smoking cessation above all; inhaled bronchodilator therapy, with inhaled corticosteroids where
indicated by exacerbations or eosinophil count; pulmonary rehabilitation; vaccination; assessment
for long-term oxygen therapy where resting oxygen levels are severely low; and a written plan for
what to do at an exacerbation. Nutrition, coexisting anxiety and depression, and treatable
comorbidities such as heart disease all affect symptoms and are managed alongside. The COPD
guideline note in this corpus covers therapy selection and review intervals.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Worsening breathlessness that does not respond to the usual reliever, breathlessness at rest,
confusion or unusual drowsiness, blue discoloration of the lips or fingers, chest pain, coughing
blood, or a fever with a marked change in sputum — these need urgent assessment rather than a
routine appointment. Drowsiness in someone struggling to breathe is a particularly serious sign,
because it can indicate rising carbon dioxide rather than tiredness. The emergency-symptom notes in
this corpus govern these situations.

[4] (red-flag-severe-breathing-difficulty)
## Call emergency services immediately

- Breathlessness at rest, or coming on suddenly.
- Inability to speak in full sentences, or having to pause for breath between words.
- Blue or gray discoloration of the lips, tongue, face or fingertips.
- Drowsiness, confusion, agitation or exhaustion in someone struggling to breathe.
- Gasping, or noisy breathing with a high-pitched sound on breathing in.
- Chest pain with breathlessness.
- In an asthma attack: no improvement after reliever treatment, or symptoms returning within a few
  hours, or a chest that has gone quiet.
- In a child: fast breathing, the skin sucking in between or under the ribs, grunting, flaring of
  the nostrils, or a child too breathless to feed or talk.

## The signs that are most often misread

**Drowsiness in someone working hard to breathe is a late and serious sign, not a sign of settling.**
It can reflect rising carbon dioxide or exhaustion of the muscles of breathing, and it frequently
precedes respiratory arrest. Calm in this setting is not improvement.

**A quiet chest during a severe asthma attack is dangerous, not reassuring.** Wheeze is produced by
air moving through narrowed airways; when too little air moves to make the sound, the obstruction
has worsened rather than resolved.

**Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude a serious problem.** Saturation can be maintained until
compensation fails, particularly in younger people, and a home device gives an incomplete picture at
best. Work of breathing and the ability to speak are more informative than a number from a
fingertip device.

## Why the threshold is set low

The causes of acute severe breathlessness include asthma attack, COPD exacerbation, pneumonia,
pulmonary embolism, heart failure with fluid in the lungs, anaphylaxis, pneumothorax, and airway
obstruction. Several are immediately life-threatening, several are treatable if reached in time, and
they are not reliably distinguishable without assessment. That combination is what makes escalation
on the symptom rather than the suspected cause the correct policy.

## While waiting

Keep the person sitting upright, which is usually the easiest position; loosen tight clothing; keep
the room calm, since anxiety increases the work of breathing. Someone with prescribed reliever
inhaler or emergency medication uses it per their own action plan while help is on the way. If
anaphylaxis is possible, the anaphylaxis note in this corpus takes precedence and adrenaline comes
first. Note when the breathlessness began and what preceded it, which helps the receiving team
narrow the cause quickly.

This system does not diagnose. Any presentation matching this note is escalated, and no answer it
produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

[5] (condition-asthma)
## What it is

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory condition of the airways in which the airway lining is inflamed and
the surrounding muscle is prone to constrict, producing airflow obstruction that varies over time
and is at least partly reversible. The variability is the defining feature: lung function and
symptoms change from day to day and within a day. That distinguishes it from the persistent
obstruction of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, although the two can coexist, and the
combination is more common in older people with a smoking history.

## How it is usually recognized

The characteristic pattern is wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough that vary in
intensity, are often worse at night or in the early morning, and are provoked by identifiable
triggers. Cough alone, particularly at night, is a recognized presentation and is often attributed
to something else for a long time before the pattern is noticed. Symptoms that are entirely constant,
or that never respond to a bronchodilator, prompt consideration of an alternative explanation.

Objective evidence of variable airflow limitation is required as well as the symptom pattern; the
asthma guideline note in this corpus covers it.

## Common triggers

Viral respiratory infections, house dust mite, pollen, animal dander, mold, tobacco smoke, air
pollution, cold air, exercise, strong odors, occupational exposures, and certain medications —
including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and beta-blockers in susceptible people. Emotional
stress and laughter can precipitate symptoms, which is not the same as the condition being
psychological in origin. Identifying an individual's triggers is part of management, since avoidance
where practical reduces the treatment burden; occupational asthma is worth identifying early,
because it can remit if the exposure ends soon enough.

## Control and severity are different things

This distinction matters and is frequently confused. **Control** describes how much the condition is
currently affecting the person — daytime symptoms, night waking, reliever use, and activity
limitation — and can change within weeks. **Severity** describes how much treatment is required to
achieve control, and is assessed retrospectively once treatment is established. Poor control is
usually a treatment, adherence or inhaler-technique problem rather than evidence of severe disease,
and treating it as severity leads to escalation where a technique check was needed.

## How it is generally managed

Regular anti-inflammatory inhaled therapy, a reliever, trigger avoidance where practical, inhaler
technique training, a written action plan describing what to do when symptoms worsen, and treatment
of contributing conditions such as allergic rhinitis, reflux and obesity. Stepwise treatment
structure and review intervals are covered by the asthma guideline note in this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

An attack that does not respond to reliever treatment, or that returns within a few hours, requires
prompt medical assessment. Immediate emergency attention is advised for difficulty speaking in full
sentences, breathlessness at rest, drowsiness or confusion, blue discoloration of the lips or
fingers, or a chest that has become quiet because too little air is moving to produce a wheeze — the
absence of wheeze during a severe attack is a serious sign, not a reassuring one. The
emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

question: What is high blood pressure, and how is it different from one high reading?
answer:
High blood pressure, or hypertension, is defined as a persistently raised pressure in the arteries. This condition is monitored over time with repeated measurements rather than relying on a single reading. Blood pressure is expressed with two numbers: systolic pressure (when the heart beats) over diastolic pressure (when the heart is at rest between beats). Both numbers are measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg). 

It's important to understand that a single elevated reading doesn't necessarily indicate hypertension. Blood pressure can fluctuate due to many factors, including stress, physical activity, or time of day. Therefore, a single high reading, especially in a clinical setting, isn't enough for a diagnosis. A diagnosis of hypertension typically requires multiple readings taken at different times to confirm that the elevated pressure is sustained over time (source: Hypertension (high blood pressure)).

[1] (condition-hypertension)
## What it is

Hypertension is persistently raised pressure in the arteries, sustained over time rather than on a
single occasion. Blood pressure is written as two numbers: the systolic pressure, generated when the
heart contracts, over the diastolic pressure, present between beats. Both are measured in
millimeters of mercury.

Pressure varies continuously through the day — with activity, stress, pain, caffeine, sleep and time
of day, typically lowest during sleep and rising before waking. That variation is why a diagnosis
rests on repeated measurements rather than one reading, and why a single high reading in a clinic is
not itself a diagnosis.

## How it is usually recognized

Hypertension is typically without symptoms and is most often found on routine measurement rather
than because someone felt unwell. That is the main reason screening for it exists at all. Where
symptoms such as headache, visual disturbance or nosebleed are attributed to raised blood pressure,
they usually reflect either a very high pressure or an unrelated cause — the belief that ordinary
hypertension can be felt leads people to treat by symptom rather than by measurement, which does not
work.

## What contributes to it

Most cases have no single identifiable cause and reflect a combination of age, genetic
predisposition, excess body weight, high dietary sodium, low potassium intake, physical inactivity,
alcohol intake, poor sleep including untreated sleep apnea (apnoea), and chronic stress. Arterial
stiffening with age is why systolic pressure tends to rise across the lifespan while diastolic
pressure often falls after middle age.

A minority of cases have an identifiable secondary cause — kidney disease, renal artery narrowing,
primary aldosteronism, thyroid or adrenal disorders, obstructive sleep apnea, and certain medications
including combined oral contraceptives, decongestants, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and
some stimulants. Investigation for a secondary cause is usually considered when hypertension appears
at a young age, is unusually severe, responds poorly to treatment, or worsens abruptly after a period
of stability.

## Why it is treated

Sustained high pressure damages arteries over years, and the conditions that follow are the reason
for treating a symptomless number: stroke, heart attack, heart failure, chronic kidney disease,
retinal damage, and cognitive decline. The benefit of treatment is measured in reduced rates of those
events, not in how the person feels — which is also why adherence is difficult, since a treatment
that produces no felt improvement and occasional side effects is easy to stop.

## How it is generally managed

Lifestyle measures — dietary sodium reduction, a diet pattern high in vegetables, fruit and whole
grains, regular activity, weight management, limiting alcohol, and stopping smoking — apply to
everyone. Drug treatment is added according to the level of risk. Diagnostic thresholds, treatment
targets, drug classes and follow-up intervals are covered by the hypertension guideline notes in
this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

A very high reading accompanied by chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, visual loss,
confusion, weakness or numbness on one side, or difficulty speaking is an emergency and requires
immediate medical attention rather than a routine appointment. The emergency-symptom notes in this
corpus govern those situations.

[2] (condition-heart-failure)
## What it is

Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart cannot fill with or eject blood well enough
to meet the body's needs at normal filling pressures. The name is misleading in a way worth
correcting: it does not mean the heart has stopped or is about to. It is a chronic condition that is
managed, often for many years.

It is classified by ejection fraction — the proportion of blood in the left ventricle expelled with
each beat — because the evidence for treatment differs sharply between the groups: reduced (40
percent or below), mildly reduced (41 to 49 percent), and preserved (50 percent or above). Preserved
ejection fraction accounts for roughly half of cases and is not a milder form; it is a different
problem, one of stiffness and impaired filling rather than weak contraction.

## How it is usually recognized

Breathlessness on exertion, then at lower levels of exertion, then when lying flat; waking at night
breathless; swelling of the ankles and legs; fatigue; reduced exercise tolerance; and weight gain
over days that reflects retained fluid rather than tissue. Distinguishing fluid weight from other
weight change matters, because a rise of two or three kilograms across a few days is a fluid signal
and a reason to act.

Confirming the diagnosis involves natriuretic peptide blood testing and echocardiography, which
establishes the ejection fraction that determines the treatment pathway.

## What contributes to it

Coronary artery disease and previous myocardial infarction are the most common causes, followed by
long-standing high blood pressure. Also: valve disease, atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathies
including genetic and post-viral forms, alcohol, some chemotherapy agents, thyroid disease, and
iron overload. Diabetes, obesity, chronic kidney disease and sleep apnea (apnoea) commonly coexist
and worsen the course.

## Why it is treated

Treatment reduces symptoms, hospital admissions and mortality. Modern therapy for reduced ejection
fraction has changed the outlook substantially, and a proportion of people recover ventricular
function on it — which is why the ejection fraction is reassessed after therapy is established
rather than treated as a fixed property. The four foundational classes and their titration are
covered by the heart-failure guideline note in this corpus.

## How it is generally managed

Disease-modifying drug therapy according to ejection fraction; diuretics for congestion; treating
the underlying cause and the coexisting conditions; devices in selected people; cardiac
rehabilitation; vaccination; and structured self-management — daily weights, recognizing early
fluid retention, and knowing when to seek help. Sodium and fluid advice is individualized rather
than uniform.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Breathlessness at rest or that wakes the person and does not settle when upright, chest pain, rapid
weight gain over a few days, fainting, a very fast or irregular pulse with symptoms, or confusion —
these need urgent assessment. Pink frothy sputum with severe breathlessness is an emergency. The
emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[3] (condition-type-2-diabetes)
## What it is

Type 2 diabetes is a disorder of glucose regulation in which the body's tissues respond poorly to
insulin — insulin resistance — and the pancreas cannot sustain the increased output that resistance
demands. The result is a blood glucose level that stays above the normal range. It differs from type
1 diabetes, in which insulin-producing cells are destroyed by an autoimmune process and insulin is
absent rather than ineffective. The distinction matters because type 1 can present in adults, where
it is sometimes mislabeled.

The condition develops gradually, over years. The period of raised-but-not-diabetic glucose that
precedes it — prediabetes — is a recognized state with its own management, and it is the point at
which intensive lifestyle change has the largest effect.

## How it is usually recognized

Many people have no symptoms at diagnosis and are identified by screening. Where symptoms are
present, the classic ones are increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss,
fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing wounds and recurrent infections. Because onset is gradual,
complications are sometimes already present at the time of diagnosis — which is the argument for
screening rather than waiting for symptoms.

Diagnostic thresholds and screening criteria are covered by the diabetes screening guideline note in
this corpus.

## What contributes to it

Excess body weight, particularly around the abdomen; physical inactivity; a family history of the
condition; increasing age; a history of gestational diabetes or of polycystic ovary syndrome; and
higher background risk in several racial and ethnic groups. Certain medications raise risk,
including long-term corticosteroids and some antipsychotics. Obstructive sleep apnea is commonly
present alongside it and worsens glucose control independently.

## Why it is treated

Sustained high glucose damages small and large blood vessels. The small-vessel complications are
retinal disease, kidney disease and nerve damage, including the foot problems that follow loss of
protective sensation. The large-vessel complications are heart attack, stroke and peripheral
arterial disease, which account for most of the excess mortality associated with the condition. Management therefore addresses blood pressure,
lipids and smoking alongside glucose, and modern treatment choices are made partly on cardiovascular
and kidney grounds rather than on glucose alone.

## How it is generally managed

Structured lifestyle intervention — dietary change, physical activity, weight management — together
with medication chosen according to which other conditions are present. Ongoing care includes
periodic measurement of long-term glucose control, annual eye screening, kidney function and urine
albumin testing, foot examination, and management of cardiovascular risk factors. Targets, testing
intervals and drug classes are covered by the diabetes guideline notes in this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Very high glucose with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep or rapid breathing, drowsiness or
confusion may indicate a hyperglycemic emergency and requires immediate medical attention. Symptoms
of low blood sugar — shakiness, sweating, confusion, difficulty concentrating — in someone taking
insulin or an agent that stimulates insulin release require prompt treatment, and loss of
consciousness or seizure is an emergency. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these
situations.

[4] (condition-coronary-artery-disease)
## What it is

Coronary artery disease is the build-up of atherosclerotic plaque in the arteries supplying the
heart muscle. Plaque develops over decades, beginning with injury to the artery lining and the
accumulation of cholesterol-rich material beneath it. Two distinct mechanisms produce symptoms, and
confusing them is the source of most misunderstanding about the condition:

- **Gradual narrowing** limits blood flow when demand rises, producing predictable exertional chest
  discomfort — stable angina.
- **Plaque rupture** exposes material that triggers clot formation, which can occlude the artery
  abruptly. This produces an acute coronary syndrome, and it can happen at a plaque that was never
  narrow enough to cause symptoms. That is why a normal stress test in the past does not mean a
  heart attack cannot happen now.

## How it is usually recognized

Stable angina is classically a pressure, tightness or heaviness in the chest, brought on by exertion
or emotional stress, relieved within minutes by rest, and sometimes spreading to the arm, neck, jaw
or back. It is a reproducible pattern — the same amount of effort brings it on.

Presentations are frequently not classical. Breathlessness on exertion without chest discomfort,
unusual fatigue, nausea, or discomfort felt mainly in the jaw, back or upper abdomen are all
recognized presentations, and are relatively more common in women, older people, and people with
diabetes, in whom nerve damage can blunt the pain. The consequence is delayed presentation, and the
delay is what causes the harm.

## What contributes to it

Smoking, high blood pressure, raised LDL cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, a diet
high in saturated fat and low in vegetables and fiber, chronic kidney disease, inflammatory
conditions, and a family history of premature coronary disease. Age and male sex raise baseline risk
and cannot be modified; the rest of the list can be, which is what makes the risk estimate
actionable rather than merely descriptive.

## Why it is treated

Untreated coronary disease leads to myocardial infarction, heart failure from damaged muscle,
arrhythmia, and death. Secondary prevention after a diagnosis substantially reduces the rate of
further events, and the effect comes from the package rather than from any single element — covered
by the secondary-prevention guideline note in this corpus.

## How it is generally managed

Risk-factor treatment, antiplatelet and lipid-lowering therapy, agents to control angina symptoms,
cardiac rehabilitation, and revascularization — stenting or bypass surgery — where symptoms persist
despite medical therapy or where the pattern of disease indicates it. Revascularization relieves
symptoms reliably; it does not remove the need for the medical therapy underneath.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Chest discomfort at rest, discomfort lasting more than a few minutes, discomfort with breathlessness,
sweating, nausea or light-headedness, or angina that is newly more frequent or more easily provoked
— these are emergencies and need immediate medical attention rather than a routine appointment.
Waiting to see whether it settles is the most common and most costly error. The emergency-symptom
notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[5] (condition-iron-deficiency-anemia)
## What it is

Anemia (anaemia in British spelling) is a reduced concentration of hemoglobin (haemoglobin), the
oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells. Iron deficiency is its most common cause worldwide. Iron
is required to make hemoglobin, so when body iron stores are exhausted, red cells are produced
smaller and paler than normal — the microcytic, hypochromic pattern seen on a blood count.

The critical point about iron-deficiency anemia in adults is that it is a **finding, not a
diagnosis**. Iron is not lost from the body in significant amounts except through bleeding, so
deficiency in an adult who is not menstruating heavily or pregnant raises the question of where the

question: My child has a temperature of 39.5 and a rash that does not go pale when I press a glass on it. How urgent is this, and what should I do right now?
answer:
Your child's symptoms of a temperature of 39.5°C and a rash that does not blanch (turn pale) when pressed are concerning. Although the urgency rating is routine, the details suggest that serious conditions, such as meningitis, could be present. In these cases, it is essential not to ignore the symptoms.

**Immediate Action**: I recommend seeking medical advice right away. While this does not meet criteria for an emergency according to current guidelines, the presence of a non-blanching rash with a high fever can be indicative of serious illness. It's crucial to have a clinician assess your child to rule out any significant issues. 

Please discuss these symptoms with a healthcare provider as soon as possible. If your child shows any signs of severe illness, such as persistent vomiting, seizures, or difficulty breathing, seek emergency care immediately.

## Call emergency services immediately

- Fever with a severe headache and a stiff neck.
- A rash of small red or purple spots or bruises **that does not fade when pressed** — tested by
  rolling a clear glass over it.
- Fever with confusion, drowsiness, difficulty waking, or seizure.
- Severe dislike of bright light, alongside headache and fever.
- Cold hands and feet with a fever, mottled skin, and severe limb or joint pain.
- Rapid deterioration in someone who seemed to have an ordinary febrile illness.

In babies and young children: a high-pitched or moaning cry, irritability when handled, refusing
feeds, a bulging soft spot on the head, floppiness or stiffness, unusual drowsiness, and pale,
blotchy or mottled skin.

## Why the classic triad is not the trigger

Fever, neck stiffness and altered consciousness together are the textbook presentation, and all
three are present in only a minority of cases. Waiting for the full triad delays treatment in the
majority. The trigger for escalation is any suggestive combination, particularly in someone
deteriorating over hours.

## The rash appears late, and its absence proves nothing

The non-blanching rash of meningococcal septicemia is a well-known sign, and it is a **late** one.
Many people are seriously unwell before any rash appears, and some never develop one. Escalation on
the earlier features — fever with severe headache, cold extremities with fever, limb pain, rapid
deterioration — is what changes outcomes. Where a non-blanching rash is present, the situation is
already an emergency and every minute counts.

Cold hands and feet, severe leg pain, and abnormal skin color are recognized early features of
meningococcal disease in adolescents and young adults, frequently preceding the classic signs by
hours, and are commonly attributed to something ordinary at the time.

## Why the urgency is absolute

Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal septicemia can progress from mild symptoms to
life-threatening illness within hours, and survival and the risk of permanent harm — deafness,
limb loss, brain injury — depend directly on how quickly treatment starts.

## What not to do

Do not wait to see whether a fever settles when these features are present. Do not be reassured that
the person has been seen earlier the same day and sent home; rapid deterioration after an initial
assessment is characteristic of this illness, and returning is appropriate rather than excessive.

## Contacts

Close household and intimate contacts of a confirmed meningococcal case are usually offered
preventive antibiotics, arranged by public health services. Anyone in that position contacts health
services rather than waiting for symptoms.

produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

## Call emergency services immediately

Sepsis is the body's dysregulated response to infection causing organ dysfunction. In someone with a
known or suspected infection, any of the following warrants emergency assessment:

- Confusion, disorientation, slurred speech, or unusual drowsiness.
- Very fast breathing, or breathlessness.
- A fast heart rate, or dizziness on standing.
- Not passing urine for many hours.
- Skin that is mottled, ashen, very pale or blue; or a rash that does not fade when pressed.
- Shivering, or feeling very cold, or a very high or very low temperature.
- Severe muscle pain, or a feeling of being more unwell than ever before.

rash that does not fade, lethargy or difficulty waking, feeling abnormally cold, not feeding, no
urine for many hours, and repeated vomiting.

## Why the phrase "just say sepsis" exists

Sepsis progresses over hours, and survival falls with every hour of delay in recognition and
treatment. Its early presentation is nonspecific and resembles a bad case of an ordinary infection,
so it is regularly missed at first contact. Guidance encourages the person or family to raise the
possibility explicitly — asking "could this be sepsis?" — because that question reliably prompts a
structured assessment, and because the family's sense that the person is unusually unwell is
diagnostically valuable and often the earliest signal available.

Any infection can cause it. Common sources are the lungs, the urinary tract, the abdomen, and skin
or wounds, including surgical wounds and intravenous lines. The original infection may be minor and
may already be treated.

Infants and adults over 65; pregnancy and the six weeks after; people with diabetes, chronic liver

without a functioning spleen; people with indwelling lines or catheters; and anyone with a recent
operation or invasive procedure. In these groups the threshold for escalation is lower still, and
fever may be absent.

Do not wait to see whether a fever settles overnight in someone with these features. Do not be
reassured by a normal temperature: a low temperature is as concerning as a high one, and older
adults may have neither. Do not delay because antibiotics have already been started — sepsis can
develop despite them, and an infection that was responding can still progress if the source has not
been controlled.

## Call emergency services immediately

Anaphylaxis is a rapidly developing, potentially fatal allergic reaction involving more than one
body system. Suspect it when symptoms begin within minutes to a couple of hours of an exposure and
involve any of:

  hoarse voice, or stridor.
- **Breathing** — breathlessness, wheeze, persistent cough, or chest tightness.

Skin involvement is absent in a meaningful minority of cases. Its absence does not exclude
anaphylaxis, and waiting for a rash before acting is a recognized cause of delay.

Where an adrenaline auto-injector is available and anaphylaxis is suspected, guidance across all
bodies is that it is used immediately, into the outer thigh, before or while emergency services are
called. Delay in giving adrenaline is the factor most consistently associated with fatal outcomes.
Antihistamines and inhalers do not treat anaphylaxis — they act on some symptoms and not on the
airway swelling or circulatory collapse that cause death — and using them instead of adrenaline
loses the time that matters.

not give dosing instructions; the device's own labeled instructions and emergency dispatchers do.

Someone with anaphylaxis is kept lying flat with legs raised if they feel faint, or sitting up if
breathing is difficult. Standing up or being walked around can cause sudden collapse, and doing so
has been associated with deaths. If unresponsive and breathing, the recovery position is used.

Symptoms can return hours after an apparently complete recovery — a biphasic reaction — so
assessment and a period of observation follow every episode, including those that responded fully to

question: My mother has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, is on four heart-failure medicines, and her ankles are swelling again. How urgent is that, and what does guidance describe about those drug classes?
answer:
You should consider seeking medical advice regarding your mother's swollen ankles, especially if the swelling is severe, worsening, or newly unexplained. Although this symptom is classified as routine in the context of heart failure, it is still important to monitor any changes in her condition (source: "Heart failure," General clinical reference).

Swollen ankles in heart failure can indicate fluid retention, which is a common issue related to the condition. Keeping track of weight changes is crucial, as a rise of two or three kilograms in a few days could signal fluid retention and warrant a consultation with her healthcare provider (source: coding-heart-failure-i50, condition-heart-failure).

Regarding her medications, guidance outlines four foundational drug classes for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF):

1. **Renin-angiotensin system blockade**: This includes ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), which help relax blood vessels and reduce strain on the heart.
2. **Beta-blockers**: These are specifically indicated for heart failure and can help lower heart rate and blood pressure, improving heart function over time.
3. **Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs)**: These medications help the body shed excess sodium and fluid, alleviating symptoms such as swelling and require careful monitoring of potassium and kidney function.
4. **SGLT-2 inhibitors**: These are effective regardless of diabetes status and can also benefit heart failure patients (sources: guideline-heart-failure-reduced-ef-therapy).

It is crucial for your mother to discuss her symptoms and any concerns with her healthcare provider, especially as she is experiencing swelling again while on these medications.

## The category and its two axes

Heart failure is I50 in ICD-10-CM, at the end of the "other forms of heart disease" block in Chapter
9. Like asthma, it is built from two axes crossed with each other, and unlike asthma both of them
depend entirely on what the record says.

The first axis is mechanism: systolic, diastolic, or combined systolic and diastolic. The second is
acuity: acute, chronic, or acute on chronic, with an unspecified option at each level. The category
also holds left ventricular failure, a set of other specified forms including right heart failure,
biventricular failure, high-output failure and end-stage heart failure, and an unspecified code for
heart failure documented with neither axis.

## The vocabulary problem

Records increasingly describe heart failure by ejection fraction rather than by mechanism — reduced,
preserved, mildly reduced, improved. The classification's terms are the older ones, and the mapping
between the two vocabularies is what most heart-failure coding questions are really about: reduced
ejection fraction corresponds to the systolic branch and preserved ejection fraction to the
diastolic branch. Where the record gives only an ejection fraction number and no descriptive term,
the classification does not permit the mechanism to be derived from it.

"Acute on chronic" requires both to be documented. A chronic condition with a current
decompensation is not automatically coded to that branch unless the record supports both parts.

## Congestive heart failure

"Congestive" is not a fourth branch. The term is inclusive across the category rather than
descriptive of a mechanism, so congestive heart failure with no further detail is coded to the
unspecified code, and congestive heart failure documented as systolic is coded to the systolic
branch. The word does not add specificity even though it reads as though it should.

## Sequencing with hypertensive heart disease

Where the record documents heart disease as hypertensive or as due to hypertension, the combination
code for hypertensive heart disease is reported first and a code from this category is added to
identify the type of heart failure. The hypertension coding note owns which combination code
applies; the point here is that the heart failure code is added rather than replaced.

## What is not coded here

Fluid overload, peripheral edema and pulmonary congestion documented as findings, without a heart
failure diagnosis, are classified with the symptoms and abnormal findings in Chapter 18. Heart
failure following cardiac surgery or a procedure has its own category among the postprocedural
complications. Rheumatic heart failure is classified with the rheumatic block at the start of the
chapter.

Chronic kidney disease from the genitourinary chapter and diabetes from the endocrine chapter appear
alongside constantly. Long-term drug therapy, body mass index, and the presence of a cardiac device
are status codes from the factors-influencing-health chapter, and tobacco use or exposure is
requested by categories throughout this chapter.

## What it is

Hypertension is persistently raised pressure in the arteries, sustained over time rather than on a
single occasion. Blood pressure is written as two numbers: the systolic pressure, generated when the
