at a young age, is unusually severe, responds poorly to treatment, or worsens abruptly after a period
of stability.

## Why it is treated

Sustained high pressure damages arteries over years, and the conditions that follow are the reason
for treating a symptomless number: stroke, heart attack, heart failure, chronic kidney disease,
retinal damage, and cognitive decline. The benefit of treatment is measured in reduced rates of those
events, not in how the person feels — which is also why adherence is difficult, since a treatment
that produces no felt improvement and occasional side effects is easy to stop.

## How it is generally managed

Lifestyle measures — dietary sodium reduction, a diet pattern high in vegetables, fruit and whole
grains, regular activity, weight management, limiting alcohol, and stopping smoking — apply to
everyone. Drug treatment is added according to the level of risk. Diagnostic thresholds, treatment
targets, drug classes and follow-up intervals are covered by the hypertension guideline notes in
this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

A very high reading accompanied by chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, visual loss,
confusion, weakness or numbness on one side, or difficulty speaking is an emergency and requires
immediate medical attention rather than a routine appointment. The emergency-symptom notes in this
corpus govern those situations.

[5] (guideline-heart-failure-reduced-ef-therapy)
## The classification the guidance depends on

Heart failure guidance separates by ejection fraction, because the evidence differs sharply between
the groups:

- **Reduced ejection fraction** — 40 percent or below.
- **Mildly reduced ejection fraction** — 41 to 49 percent.
- **Preserved ejection fraction** — 50 percent or above.

The therapy below applies to the reduced group. Applying it wholesale to preserved ejection fraction
is a common error: several of these classes have not shown the same benefit there, and the one that
has — the SGLT-2 inhibitors — is the newest addition.

## The four foundational classes

Current guidance describes four classes as foundational, started together or in rapid sequence
rather than added one at a time over months:

1. **Renin-angiotensin system blockade** — an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor where
   suitable, otherwise an ACE inhibitor, otherwise an angiotensin receptor blocker.
2. **A beta-blocker** with evidence specifically in heart failure, started when the person is not
   congested, since starting during congestion can worsen it.
3. **A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist**, with potassium and kidney function monitored.
4. **An SGLT-2 inhibitor**, used for this indication irrespective of whether diabetes is present.

Each is titrated toward the doses used in the trials as blood pressure, kidney function and
potassium allow, with review at roughly two-week intervals during titration. The change from older
guidance is the emphasis on getting all four classes started at low intensity before maximizing any
one of them: the benefit of a fourth class at a low dose exceeds the benefit of pushing a third to
its ceiling. A modest early fall in kidney function or a small rise in potassium is anticipated and
is not by itself a reason to stop.

## Additional measures

Diuretic therapy relieves congestion and symptoms; it is not an outcome-modifying therapy and is
adjusted to the lowest dose that maintains euvolemia. Structured education in self-monitoring —
daily weights, recognizing increasing breathlessness or swelling, sodium and fluid advice — and
cardiac rehabilitation are part of the package. Iron deficiency is looked for and corrected, since
it is common and independently affects symptoms.

## Reassessment and device consideration

Ejection fraction is reassessed after at least three months of optimized therapy before an
implantable defibrillator or resynchronization device is considered, because function improves in a
substantial proportion of people once therapy is established. A device decision made on the
pre-treatment number is a decision made on the wrong number.

## Follow-up after admission

Early follow-up after a heart-failure admission — commonly within seven to fourteen days — is one of
the higher-yield contacts in the whole pathway, because the weeks after discharge carry the highest
readmission risk and are when titration most often stalls.

[6] (condition-osteoarthritis)
## What it is

Osteoarthritis is a disorder of the whole joint — cartilage, underlying bone, ligaments, joint
lining and surrounding muscle — in which cartilage is progressively lost and the bone underneath
remodels in response. It most often affects the knees, hips, hands and spine.

The description of it as "wear and tear" is inaccurate enough to be worth correcting, because it
leads people to rest the joint. The process is an active one involving inflammation and attempted
repair, not simple mechanical erosion, and the muscle weakness that follows from reduced use makes
the joint worse rather than protecting it. That is why exercise is the first-line treatment and not
merely an adjunct.

## How it is usually recognized

Joint pain that is worse with activity and better with rest, short-lived stiffness after inactivity
— characteristically under 30 minutes in the morning, which distinguishes it from inflammatory
arthritis — reduced range of movement, a grating sensation on movement, and bony swelling. Onset is
gradual, over months to years, and usually asymmetric.

The diagnosis is generally clinical in a person over 45 with activity-related pain and no prolonged
morning stiffness. Imaging is not required to make it, and the relationship between what an X-ray
shows and what a person feels is weak in both directions — substantial radiographic change with few
symptoms, and significant pain with modest change, are both common. Imaging that is done for
reassurance frequently achieves the opposite.

## What contributes to it

Age; previous joint injury or surgery, which is the dominant factor in a young person with knee
osteoarthritis; obesity, which acts both mechanically and metabolically; occupational and sporting
loading; joint shape and alignment; muscle weakness; genetic factors; and female sex, particularly
for hand and knee disease after menopause.

## Why it is treated

Pain and reduced function affect independence, sleep, mood and cardiovascular fitness, and the
inactivity that follows compounds all of them. Treatment aims to reduce pain and maintain function,
and the condition is manageable over long periods; it does not inevitably progress to joint
replacement.

## How it is generally managed

Structured exercise — combining muscle strengthening, range of movement and aerobic activity — is
the core treatment for every affected joint, together with weight management where relevant.
Education, pacing, appropriate footwear, walking aids where useful, and heat or cold for symptom
relief support it. Pharmacologic options are adjuncts rather than the foundation, with topical
agents preferred where the joint is accessible. Joint replacement is considered where pain and
functional limitation persist despite adequate non-surgical management. The osteoarthritis guideline
note in this corpus covers the sequence and the evidence behind it.

## When further assessment is advised

A hot, swollen, acutely painful joint with fever suggests infection or crystal arthritis and needs
urgent assessment — this is not an osteoarthritis flare. Prolonged morning stiffness, multiple
symmetric small-joint involvement, or systemic symptoms suggest inflammatory arthritis instead.
Sudden joint locking or giving way, or new neurological symptoms with spinal pain, also warrant
prompt assessment.

[7] (condition-influenza)
## What it is

Influenza is a respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses, of which types A and B cause
seasonal epidemics. Influenza A is subtyped by two surface proteins, hemagglutinin and
neuraminidase — the H and N in designations such as H1N1 and H3N2. The virus changes continuously
through small mutations, which is why immunity from one season is incomplete against the next and
why the vaccine is reformulated annually rather than given once.

It is more severe than a common cold in both symptoms and consequences, and it causes substantial
seasonal hospitalization and death, concentrated in older adults, young children, pregnant people
and those with chronic conditions.

## How it is usually recognized

Abrupt onset — people can often name the hour — with fever, chills, muscle aches, headache, marked
fatigue and dry cough. Sore throat and nasal symptoms occur but are less prominent than in a cold.
Fever typically lasts three to five days; cough and fatigue commonly persist two weeks or more.
Gastrointestinal symptoms occur more often in children than adults.

Laboratory confirmation is not required to manage a typical case during a known outbreak, and is
used where the result would change management — in hospital, in high-risk people, or where an
antiviral decision or outbreak control depends on it.

## Complications

Pneumonia is the main one, either from the virus itself or from a secondary bacterial infection.
Secondary bacterial pneumonia classically appears as a deterioration after several days of
improvement, which is a pattern worth recognizing. Other complications include worsening of
underlying asthma, COPD, heart failure or diabetes, and less commonly inflammation of the heart
muscle, brain or muscle tissue. Influenza is also associated with a transient increase in the risk
of myocardial infarction and stroke in the weeks after infection.

## How it is generally managed

Supportive care for most otherwise healthy people: rest, fluids, and symptomatic relief. Antiviral
treatment is targeted rather than universal, and is most effective when started early — the timing
threshold and the groups in whom treatment is recommended are covered by the influenza guideline
note in this corpus. Antibiotics have no effect on the virus and are reserved for a bacterial
complication.

Annual vaccination is the principal preventive measure, alongside staying home while febrile, hand
hygiene and respiratory etiquette.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Difficulty breathing or breathlessness at rest, chest pain, persistent dizziness or confusion,
inability to keep fluids down, seizures, severe muscle pain or weakness, or symptoms that improve
and then return with fever and worse cough — these need urgent assessment. In children, additional
signs include fast or labored breathing, blue lips, no tears when crying, and significantly reduced
wet diapers. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[8] (condition-copd)
## What it is

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is persistent airflow limitation caused by long-term damage to
the airways and the lung tissue itself. Two processes usually coexist: chronic inflammation and
narrowing of the small airways, and emphysema, the destruction of the alveolar walls across which
gas is exchanged. The limitation is persistent rather than variable, which is the main contrast with
asthma, although the two overlap in some people and the overlap is treated as its own situation.

The damage is not reversible. Treatment reduces symptoms, improves exercise capacity and reduces
exacerbations; stopping the exposure that caused it is what changes the trajectory.

## How it is usually recognized

Breathlessness on exertion that has worsened gradually over years, chronic cough, and sputum
production, in someone with a relevant exposure history. People commonly attribute the early stage
to age or being out of shape and reduce their activity to match, which conceals the progression —
so the first presentation is often later than the first symptom, sometimes at an exacerbation.

The diagnosis requires spirometry and is not made on symptoms alone; the COPD guideline note in this
corpus covers the threshold and the assessment.

## What contributes to it

Tobacco smoking is the dominant cause in high-income countries. Also relevant: biomass fuel smoke
from indoor cooking and heating, occupational dust, vapors and fumes, air pollution, childhood
respiratory infections and impaired lung growth, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency — an inherited
condition worth considering when COPD appears young, in a non-smoker, or with a strong family
history.

## Exacerbations

An exacerbation is an acute worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond normal day-to-day variation,
usually triggered by a viral or bacterial infection. They matter more than the label suggests: each
one tends to worsen quality of life, accelerate lung-function decline, and predict the next, and a
history of them is the single strongest predictor of future ones. Recovery to baseline can take
weeks, and a proportion of people never return fully to their previous level.

## How it is generally managed

Smoking cessation above all; inhaled bronchodilator therapy, with inhaled corticosteroids where
indicated by exacerbations or eosinophil count; pulmonary rehabilitation; vaccination; assessment
for long-term oxygen therapy where resting oxygen levels are severely low; and a written plan for
what to do at an exacerbation. Nutrition, coexisting anxiety and depression, and treatable
comorbidities such as heart disease all affect symptoms and are managed alongside. The COPD
guideline note in this corpus covers therapy selection and review intervals.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Worsening breathlessness that does not respond to the usual reliever, breathlessness at rest,
confusion or unusual drowsiness, blue discoloration of the lips or fingers, chest pain, coughing
blood, or a fever with a marked change in sputum — these need urgent assessment rather than a
routine appointment. Drowsiness in someone struggling to breathe is a particularly serious sign,
because it can indicate rising carbon dioxide rather than tiredness. The emergency-symptom notes in
this corpus govern these situations.

[9] (guideline-type-2-diabetes-first-line-therapy)
## The shape of current guidance

Older guidance set out a single sequence: metformin first, then agents added in order as control
worsened. Current guidance is structured differently — the first-line choice depends on which other
conditions are present, and for several of them the choice is made independently of the HbA1c value.
This is the substantive change, and it is the part most often stated in the old form.

## Where there is no compelling comorbidity

Metformin, alongside structured lifestyle intervention, is the usual initial agent: long experience,
low cost, weight neutrality, and little risk of causing low blood sugar on its own. Kidney function
is checked before starting and periodically after, since the dose is constrained below a threshold
of kidney function and the agent is avoided below a lower one. Gastrointestinal intolerance is the
common reason for stopping, and is reduced by gradual escalation and extended-release formulations.
Long-term use is associated with lower vitamin B12 levels, so periodic measurement is advised.

## Where cardiovascular, kidney or heart-failure disease is present

Guidance describes agents with demonstrated organ benefit as preferred, whether or not metformin is
also used, and independent of whether the HbA1c is at goal:

- **Established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease** — a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven
  cardiovascular benefit, or an SGLT-2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit.
- **Heart failure**, particularly with reduced ejection fraction — an SGLT-2 inhibitor.
- **Chronic kidney disease**, particularly with albuminuria — an SGLT-2 inhibitor, with a GLP-1
  receptor agonist as the alternative where an SGLT-2 inhibitor is not tolerated or not appropriate.

These are organ-protective therapies that also lower glucose, rather than later steps in a glucose
ladder. Class-specific cautions are part of the choice: SGLT-2 inhibitors carry a risk of genital
mycotic infection, volume depletion, and — uncommonly — ketoacidosis at near-normal glucose levels,
which is easy to miss precisely because the glucose is not high.

## Where weight is a major treatment goal

Agents with the greatest weight-reduction effect — the GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual incretin
agonists — are preferred where weight management is a primary objective, alongside structured
lifestyle intervention and, in selected people, metabolic surgery.

## Reassessment

The regimen is reviewed every three to six months. De-intensification is an explicit option, not a
failure: where the regimen has become more aggressive than the individualized target requires, or
where low blood sugar is occurring, stepping down is the appropriate response.

Doses, titration schedules and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this
system.

[10] (guideline-hypertension-first-line-treatment)
## Lifestyle measures are the shared foundation

Every major body recommends the same set of non-drug measures, whether or not medication is also
used: reducing dietary sodium, adopting a dietary pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains
and low-fat dairy and low in saturated fat, regular aerobic activity most days of the week, weight
reduction where body weight is above the healthy range, limiting alcohol, and stopping smoking.
Each produces a meaningful reduction on its own, and the effects are partly additive, so several
combined can move a person a full stage.

## When drug treatment starts

The decision is tied to cardiovascular risk, not to the blood-pressure number alone:

- **Stage 2 hypertension** — drug treatment alongside lifestyle measures, usually beginning with
  two agents, because a single agent rarely closes a gap of this size.
- **Stage 1 hypertension with established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney
  disease, or an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk at or above 10 percent** — drug treatment
  alongside lifestyle measures.
- **Stage 1 hypertension without those features** — lifestyle measures first, with reassessment
  after three to six months before drug treatment is considered.

## First-line drug classes

Four classes are first-line for most adults without a compelling indication for something else:
thiazide-type diuretics, angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers,
and dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers. An ACE inhibitor and an angiotensin receptor blocker
are not combined — the combination adds harm without adding benefit. Single-pill combinations are
preferred where two agents are needed, because adherence falls as pill count rises.

Comorbidity shifts the choice. Renin-angiotensin blockade is preferred where diabetes with
albuminuria or chronic kidney disease is present; a beta-blocker is not first-line for uncomplicated
hypertension but becomes appropriate where there is a separate indication such as heart failure or
recent myocardial infarction. Doses are outside the scope of this note and of this system.

## Resistant hypertension

Blood pressure above target on three agents including a diuretic, all at appropriate doses, is
described as resistant hypertension. Before treatment is escalated further, the sequence is to
confirm the readings out of office, review adherence, review agents that raise blood pressure —
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, decongestants, some stimulants, combined oral contraceptives
— and investigate for a secondary cause. Apparent resistance is more often measurement, adherence
or an interfering agent than a need for a fourth drug.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on how aggressively to treat low-risk stage 1 hypertension, which follows from the
threshold disagreement in the diagnostic note: where guidance describes hypertension as beginning at
140/90 mm Hg, much of the population that United States guidance calls stage 1 is instead advised on
lifestyle alone.

## Follow-up interval

Monthly review until the target is reached, including adherence and a check of kidney function and
potassium after starting an agent acting on the renin-angiotensin system, then review every three
to six months once stable.

[11] (guideline-coronary-artery-disease-secondary-prevention)
## What secondary prevention means

Secondary prevention is the set of measures used for someone who already has established coronary
artery disease — a previous heart attack, a revascularization procedure, or angiographic disease —
to reduce the chance of a further event. It is a package rather than a single intervention: no one
element carries the effect, and the benefit measured in trials comes from applying them together.
Partial application is the common failure, and it is usually the non-drug elements that are dropped.

## The components

- **Antiplatelet therapy** — long-term single antiplatelet therapy for most people, with a defined
  period of dual antiplatelet therapy after an acute coronary syndrome or stent placement, its
  duration individualized against bleeding risk.
- **High-intensity statin therapy**. United States guidance describes the intensity; European
  guidance describes an LDL goal instead. Where the response is inadequate, additional
  non-statin agents are added rather than the statin abandoned.
- **Blood-pressure control**, with a target below 130/80 mm Hg for most people.
- **Renin-angiotensin blockade** where diabetes, reduced left ventricular function, or chronic
  kidney disease is also present.
- **Beta-blockade** after myocardial infarction, with the strongest and longest-standing evidence
  where left ventricular function is reduced.
- **Cardiac rehabilitation referral** — a structured program of supervised exercise, education and
  risk-factor management, and consistently one of the most underused elements relative to the
  strength of the evidence behind it.
- **Smoking cessation**, the single largest modifiable factor, with combined behavioral and
  pharmacologic support more effective than advice alone.
- **Annual influenza vaccination**, included as a cardiovascular measure rather than only a
  respiratory one.
- **Structured management of diabetes** where present, preferring agents with demonstrated
  cardiovascular benefit.

## Review interval

Review at least annually once the regimen is stable, with earlier review after any change in
symptoms, after a hospital admission, and four to twelve weeks after any change in lipid-lowering
intensity. Each review is an opportunity to check adherence, which falls measurably in the year
after an event as the acute experience recedes.

## What warrants urgent reassessment

New, worsening, or rest-onset chest discomfort in someone with known coronary disease is not a
routine review matter and requires urgent assessment. A pattern of angina that is becoming more
frequent, more easily provoked, or longer-lasting is a change in category rather than a change in
degree. The emergency-symptom notes elsewhere in this corpus govern these situations, and this note
does not substitute for them.

[12] (guideline-migraine-acute-and-preventive-treatment)
## Acute treatment

An attack is treated early, while pain is still mild, because response rates fall once an attack is
established and central sensitization has set in. The options are grouped by evidence strength
rather than presented as a ranked list for an individual:

- Simple analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for mild to moderate attacks.
- Triptans for moderate to severe attacks, or where simple analgesics have failed.
- The gepant and ditan classes where triptans are ineffective, not tolerated, or contraindicated by
  cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease — which is the main limitation on triptan use.
- Anti-nausea agents as adjuncts where nausea limits oral treatment; non-oral routes where vomiting
  or gastric stasis makes an oral route unreliable.

Treating on two or three separate attacks before judging an agent ineffective is the usual standard,
since attack-to-attack variability is high.

## When preventive treatment starts

Preventive treatment is offered when attacks are frequent or disabling enough that acute treatment
alone is insufficient. Guidance describes the threshold as four or more migraine days per month with
some disability, or fewer attacks where disability is severe, where acute treatment is ineffective
or contraindicated, or where the person prefers it. The aim is a reduction in frequency and
severity, not the elimination of attacks: a 50 percent reduction in migraine days is the conventional
definition of a treatment response.

## Preventive classes

Classes with supporting evidence include beta-blockers, the antiepileptics topiramate and valproate,
the tricyclic amitriptyline, candesartan, and the CGRP-targeted monoclonal antibodies and oral
gepants. The choice is made on comorbidity, side-effect profile and pregnancy status rather than by
a fixed order — an agent that also treats a coexisting condition is preferred, and valproate and
topiramate require particular care in people who could become pregnant.

## Assessing response

An adequate trial precedes any judgment of failure: commonly eight to twelve weeks at an appropriate
dose. A headache diary is the instrument for that judgment, because recall of attack frequency is
unreliable and tends to be dominated by the worst recent attack rather than the average.

## Medication-overuse headache

This is the point guidance emphasizes most. Frequent use of acute medication can itself sustain a
headache disorder, converting an episodic pattern into a chronic one. The limits are fewer than ten
treatment days per month for triptans, ergots, opioids and combination analgesics, and fewer than
fifteen days per month for simple analgesics. Overuse is a common and reversible reason for
headaches having become chronic, and it is checked for before a preventive regimen is escalated.

## What is outside this note

Doses, titration and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this system.
Sudden severe headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute, headache with fever and neck
stiffness, headache with new neurological deficit, and headache after head injury are emergency
presentations covered elsewhere in this corpus, not migraine management questions.

question: I have stage 3 kidney disease and high blood pressure. Does the classification link the two, and what target does guidance describe for someone like me?
answer:
You should seek care from your healthcare provider to discuss your condition, as stage 3 kidney disease and high blood pressure require careful management.

Stage 3 kidney disease indicates moderate kidney dysfunction, and it often occurs alongside high blood pressure, which can impact the management of both conditions. This connection is recognized in coding guidelines that classify hypertension with chronic kidney disease together (source: coding-hypertension-i10). 

Current guidance suggests that the target blood pressure for most individuals with stage 3 kidney disease is typically below 130/80 mm Hg (source: "Coronary artery disease: secondary prevention after a diagnosis"). Regular monitoring of your blood pressure, kidney function, and potassium levels is essential, particularly if you are on certain medications (source: guideline-hypertension-first-line-treatment).

Discuss specific targets and treatment plans with your healthcare provider, as these should be tailored to fit your overall health and situation. Lifestyle changes, such as dietary modifications and increased physical activity, can also be beneficial for managing both your blood pressure and kidney health (sources: lifestyle-hypertension-diet and lifestyle-hypertension-activity).

[1] (coding-type-2-diabetes-e11)
## The category

Type 2 diabetes mellitus is E11 in ICD-10-CM, in Chapter 4, endocrine, nutritional and metabolic
diseases. The chapter separates diabetes by cause rather than by treatment: diabetes due to an
underlying condition, drug- or chemical-induced diabetes, type 1, type 2, and other specified
diabetes each have their own three-character category. Where the record says only "diabetes
mellitus" with no type stated, the classification defaults to type 2.

That default is worth knowing in both directions. It means an unqualified diagnosis does not stall
the coding, and it means a record that meant type 1 but did not say so is classified as the wrong
disease. Insulin use does not change the category — a person with type 2 diabetes taking insulin is
still coded to E11, with long-term insulin use recorded as a separate status code.

## E11 is a family, not a single code

E11 is never used at three characters. The fourth and subsequent characters name the complication,
which is what makes this one of the larger combination-code families in the classification. The
subcategories cover kidney involvement, retinal involvement subdivided by severity and by whether
macular edema is present, neuropathy including the polyneuropathy and autonomic forms, circulatory
involvement of the limbs with or without gangrene, skin, oral and joint complications, and the
metabolic states of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia, the latter distinguished by whether coma
occurred. Diabetes documented without complications has its own code ending in the digit 9, which is
the source of the frequently quoted E11.9.

Several of these still require a second code. Diabetic chronic kidney disease is paired with a code
for the stage of kidney disease; a diabetic foot ulcer is paired with a code giving its site and
depth. The combination code names the association, and the additional code carries the detail.

## The "with" convention

The reason this family works the way it does is a general convention rather than a diabetes rule.
Where the alphabetic index links two conditions with the word "with", the classification reads that
as "associated with" or "due to" and presumes the relationship, without requiring the record to
state it explicitly. A record listing type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease is therefore coded
as diabetic kidney disease unless the documentation says the two are unrelated.

This presumption is the single most consequential detail in coding diabetes, and it is also the one
most often applied too enthusiastically. It holds only for the pairings the index actually lists,
and a condition merely appearing on the same problem list is not automatically a diabetic
complication.

## Codes that commonly accompany E11

Long-term use of insulin, of injectable non-insulin agents, and of oral glucose-lowering drugs each
have distinct status codes, and body mass index has its own set. Screening for diabetes in someone
without symptoms is an encounter code rather than a diagnosis. Prediabetes and abnormal glucose
findings that fall short of a diabetes diagnosis are not coded to E11 at all; they sit with the
abnormal laboratory findings in the symptoms and abnormal findings chapter.

[2] (coding-hypertension-i10)
## The code

Essential, or primary, hypertension is I10 in ICD-10-CM. It sits in Chapter 9, diseases of the
circulatory system, in the hypertensive-disease block that runs from I10 to I16.

I10 is unusual in being a complete code at three characters. Most ICD-10-CM categories require a
fourth, fifth or sixth character before the code is billable; I10 takes none, so a request to
"add more specificity to I10" is a request the classification cannot satisfy. What the category
includes is broad: high blood pressure described as arterial, essential, primary or systemic all map
to the same code. The benign-versus-malignant split that the previous US classification carried was
not brought forward, which is why searching for a "malignant hypertension" code returns nothing
separate.

## What I10 is not used for

A single raised reading, or a series of readings, in someone who has not been given a diagnosis of
hypertension is a finding rather than a disease, and it is classified with the abnormal findings in
Chapter 18 instead. The distinction is documentation-driven: the diagnosis in the record, not the
number, is what moves a case to I10. The same chapter holds the code for low blood pressure.

Hypertension complicating pregnancy, childbirth or the period after delivery is excluded outright
and is classified in the obstetric chapter; the pregnancy code is used in place of I10, not
alongside it. Hypertension affecting the vessels of the brain or of the eye is handled differently
again — those are separate conditions that may be coded in addition to the hypertension rather than
instead of it.

## When hypertension stops being I10

I10 applies when hypertension stands alone. Once organ involvement is in the picture, the
classification prefers a combination code:

- Documented hypertensive heart disease moves the case to I11, subdivided by whether heart failure
  is present. When it is, the type of heart failure is added from I50 as a second code.
- Hypertension with chronic kidney disease moves to I12, with a second code identifying the stage of
  kidney disease.
- Both together move to I13.
- Hypertension attributed to an identifiable underlying cause — renal, endocrine, or another — is
  secondary hypertension in I15, coded together with the cause.
- Hypertensive urgency and hypertensive emergency are distinguished within I16.

The heart and kidney rules differ in an important way. The classification presumes a causal link
between hypertension and chronic kidney disease and pairs them without being told to. It makes no
such presumption for heart disease: unless the record states that the heart condition is
hypertensive or due to the hypertension, the two are coded separately and I11 is not used.

## Related codes that appear on the same encounter

Screening for cardiovascular disorders in someone without symptoms has its own encounter code in the
factors-influencing-health chapter, as does a personal history of, or long-term drug therapy for, a
circulatory condition. Tobacco use or dependence is frequently added, because many categories in
Chapter 9 carry an explicit instruction to identify it.

## What this guidance covers

How adult office blood pressure is classified, what is required before a diagnosis of hypertension
is made, and the treatment target most bodies set once treatment has begun.

## Classification of office blood pressure in adults

United States society guidance classifies adult office readings as:

- **Normal** — systolic below 120 mm Hg *and* diastolic below 80 mm Hg.
- **Elevated** — systolic 120 to 129 mm Hg *and* diastolic below 80 mm Hg.
- **Stage 1 hypertension** — systolic 130 to 139 mm Hg *or* diastolic 80 to 89 mm Hg.
- **Stage 2 hypertension** — systolic at least 140 mm Hg *or* diastolic at least 90 mm Hg.

When the systolic and diastolic values fall into different categories, the higher category applies.
"Elevated" is not a stage of hypertension: it marks a group at raised future risk in whom lifestyle
measures are advised and drug treatment is not.

## Measurement technique, which changes the number

A reading taken carelessly is not a milder version of a correct reading — it is a different
measurement. The technique that the classification above assumes is a validated device, a cuff
sized to the arm, the person seated with back supported and feet flat, arm supported at heart
level, no caffeine, exercise or smoking in the preceding 30 minutes, five minutes of rest
beforehand, and no talking during the measurement. An undersized cuff and an unsupported arm both
push the reading up, each by an amount comparable to the width of a whole stage.

## Confirming the diagnosis

A diagnosis is not made from a single reading. The standard is an average of two or more readings
taken on two or more separate occasions. Out-of-office measurement — home readings or 24-hour
ambulatory monitoring — confirms the diagnosis and identifies two patterns that office readings
alone cannot: white-coat hypertension, where office readings are raised but out-of-office readings
are not, and masked hypertension, where the reverse holds and the risk is underestimated.

## Treatment target

For most treated adults, United States guidance describes a target below 130/80 mm Hg. The target is
individualized for older adults with frailty, limited life expectancy, or a heavy burden of other
conditions, where the balance of benefit and harm differs and where postural drops matter more.

## Where guidance differs

The 130/80 mm Hg diagnostic threshold is a United States position. European guidance describes office
hypertension as beginning at 140/90 mm Hg, and treats the 130 to 139 / 80 to 89 band as high-normal
blood pressure rather than as stage 1 disease. The same reading is therefore labeled differently
depending on which body's guidance is applied, and the size of the population called hypertensive
changes substantially between the two. Any answer that quotes a threshold should say which
convention it is using.

## Follow-up interval

After treatment starts or changes, reassessment at roughly monthly intervals until the target is
reached, then review every three to six months once readings are stable.

## The range and what it holds

Chapter 9 of ICD-10-CM covers I00 through I99. Every code begins with the letter I. It takes in the
heart, the arteries and veins, the lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes, and the blood supply to the
brain. Its blocks run in anatomical and mechanistic order rather
than alphabetical, so codes sitting near each other describe related processes and knowing where a
block begins narrows a lookup.

## The blocks, in order

Acute rheumatic fever opens the chapter at I00 to I02, followed by chronic rheumatic heart disease
at I05 to I09 — the valve damage, mostly mitral and aortic, left behind by earlier infection.

Hypertensive disease occupies I10 to I16, a short block carrying combination codes that fold
hypertension together with heart or kidney disease attributed to it.

Ischemic heart disease — coronary artery disease — runs from I20 to I25, moving from angina through
acute myocardial infarction to the chronic atherosclerotic disease that follows. Pulmonary heart disease and disorders of the
pulmonary circulation sit at I26 to I28: pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, and the
right-sided heart disease that follows lung disease.

The largest block, I30 to I52, is other forms of heart disease, heterogeneous by design —
inflammatory disease of the pericardium, endocardium and myocardium; non-rheumatic valve disorders;
cardiomyopathy; the conduction disorders and the arrhythmias, atrial fibrillation among them;
cardiac arrest; and heart failure at the end of the block.

Cerebrovascular disease is I60 to I69, ordered by mechanism: subarachnoid and intracerebral bleeding
first, then infarction, then occlusion and stenosis, closing with the sequelae category for
deficits persisting after the event.

Diseases of the arteries, arterioles and capillaries follow at I70 to I79 — atherosclerosis
identified by site, aneurysm and dissection, peripheral arterial disease. Veins, lymphatic vessels
and lymph nodes occupy I80 to I89: thrombosis and phlebitis, varicose veins, lymphedema. A short
closing block at I95 to I99 holds low blood pressure, post-procedural disorders, and the
unspecified residual.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Transient ischemic attack is classified with the nervous system rather than with cerebrovascular
disease — the most common misplacement in this area. Congenital malformations of the heart and great
vessels belong to the congenital chapter, and stay there for an adult. Circulatory disorders
complicating pregnancy or childbirth are classified in the obstetric chapter. Giant cell arteritis
and the systemic vasculitides sit with the connective-tissue disorders in the musculoskeletal
chapter.

Symptoms are the other boundary: chest pain, palpitations, an abnormal cardiac finding and a raised
blood-pressure reading in someone with no diagnosis stay with the symptoms and abnormal findings in
Chapter 18 until a diagnosis is recorded.

## Codes from other chapters that circulatory questions commonly need

Many categories here carry an explicit instruction to add a code identifying tobacco use,
dependence or exposure, split between the mental and behavioral chapter and the
factors-influencing-health chapter. Stage of chronic kidney disease comes from the genitourinary
chapter and diabetes from the endocrine chapter. Long-term drug therapy, body mass index, family
history and screening encounters all come from the factors-influencing-health chapter.

[5] (guideline-hypertension-first-line-treatment)
## Lifestyle measures are the shared foundation

Every major body recommends the same set of non-drug measures, whether or not medication is also
used: reducing dietary sodium, adopting a dietary pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains
and low-fat dairy and low in saturated fat, regular aerobic activity most days of the week, weight
reduction where body weight is above the healthy range, limiting alcohol, and stopping smoking.
Each produces a meaningful reduction on its own, and the effects are partly additive, so several
combined can move a person a full stage.

## When drug treatment starts

The decision is tied to cardiovascular risk, not to the blood-pressure number alone:

- **Stage 2 hypertension** — drug treatment alongside lifestyle measures, usually beginning with
  two agents, because a single agent rarely closes a gap of this size.
- **Stage 1 hypertension with established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney
  disease, or an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk at or above 10 percent** — drug treatment
  alongside lifestyle measures.
- **Stage 1 hypertension without those features** — lifestyle measures first, with reassessment
  after three to six months before drug treatment is considered.

## First-line drug classes

Four classes are first-line for most adults without a compelling indication for something else:
thiazide-type diuretics, angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers,
and dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers. An ACE inhibitor and an angiotensin receptor blocker
are not combined — the combination adds harm without adding benefit. Single-pill combinations are
preferred where two agents are needed, because adherence falls as pill count rises.

Comorbidity shifts the choice. Renin-angiotensin blockade is preferred where diabetes with
albuminuria or chronic kidney disease is present; a beta-blocker is not first-line for uncomplicated
hypertension but becomes appropriate where there is a separate indication such as heart failure or
recent myocardial infarction. Doses are outside the scope of this note and of this system.

## Resistant hypertension

Blood pressure above target on three agents including a diuretic, all at appropriate doses, is
described as resistant hypertension. Before treatment is escalated further, the sequence is to
confirm the readings out of office, review adherence, review agents that raise blood pressure —
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, decongestants, some stimulants, combined oral contraceptives
— and investigate for a secondary cause. Apparent resistance is more often measurement, adherence
or an interfering agent than a need for a fourth drug.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on how aggressively to treat low-risk stage 1 hypertension, which follows from the
threshold disagreement in the diagnostic note: where guidance describes hypertension as beginning at
140/90 mm Hg, much of the population that United States guidance calls stage 1 is instead advised on
lifestyle alone.

## Follow-up interval

Monthly review until the target is reached, including adherence and a check of kidney function and
potassium after starting an agent acting on the renin-angiotensin system, then review every three
to six months once stable.

## The dietary pattern with the most evidence

The dietary approach most consistently described for blood pressure emphasizes vegetables, fruit,
whole grains, low-fat dairy, poultry, fish, beans, nuts and vegetable oils, while limiting saturated
fat, full-fat dairy, fatty meat, sweets and sugar-sweetened drinks. It is a whole pattern rather
than a single food, and the trials that established it changed everything on the plate at once —
which is why substituting one "blood pressure food" into an otherwise unchanged diet does not
reproduce the result.

The reduction seen with the pattern alone is meaningful, and combining it with sodium reduction
produces a larger effect than either alone.

## Sodium

Sodium reduction is the single most-studied dietary change for blood pressure. Commonly stated
targets are under 2,300 mg per day, with a further benefit described at 1,500 mg for many adults.
Any reduction helps: the relationship is graded, so moving from very high intake to merely high
intake is worthwhile even if a target is not reached.

The practical point that surprises people: most dietary sodium does not come from the salt shaker.
The large majority is already in packaged and restaurant food — bread, processed meat, cheese,
sauces, soups, snacks and prepared meals. Cooking at home from unprocessed ingredients does more
than removing salt from the table, and reading labels for sodium per serving is more effective than
any single substitution.

Salt substitutes containing potassium chloride are described as reducing blood pressure, but they
are not appropriate for everyone — particularly people with chronic kidney disease or on medication
that raises potassium — and are a matter for the person's own clinician.

## Potassium

Higher dietary potassium is associated with lower blood pressure, and increasing it through food —
vegetables, fruit, beans, dairy — is the described route rather than supplements. The same caution
about kidney disease and potassium-raising medication applies.

## Alcohol

Alcohol raises blood pressure in a dose-related way, and reducing intake lowers it. Commonly stated
limits are up to two drinks per day for men and one for women, with less being better. For someone
drinking well above that, reduction is one of the more reliable non-drug interventions available.

## Weight

Weight reduction lowers blood pressure roughly in proportion to the amount lost, and the effect
begins early rather than requiring a target weight to be reached. A modest, sustained reduction is
described as worthwhile in its own right.

## What is not established

Specific "superfoods", vinegar, garlic supplements and similar single-ingredient remedies do not
have evidence comparable to the whole-pattern approach. Caffeine raises blood pressure acutely but
habitual intake has little sustained effect in most people. The hypertension guideline notes in this
corpus cover thresholds, targets and when drug treatment is added.

[7] (lifestyle-type-2-diabetes-adherence)
## Why this has its own note

Diabetes is largely self-managed. Most decisions affecting the outcome are made by the person
between appointments, and adherence to glucose-lowering medication is measurably imperfect in
practice. Treating non-adherence as a character issue misses what the evidence shows: cost,
complexity, side effects, low health literacy, depression, and simply forgetting account for most of
it, and each has a different remedy.

## Diabetes self-management education

Structured education and support is described as a core part of care rather than an optional extra,
with specific points at which it is offered: at diagnosis, annually where treatment targets are not
met, when complicating factors develop, and when transitions in care occur. It improves glucose
control and quality of life, and it is consistently underused.

## Making the regimen easier to follow

- **Simplify where possible.** Fewer daily doses and fixed-dose combinations improve adherence.
  Where a regimen has become more complex than the individualized target requires,
  de-intensification is an appropriate response rather than a concession.
- **Name the cost problem out loud.** Cost-related underuse — skipping doses, splitting tablets, not
  filling prescriptions — is common and is rarely volunteered unless asked about directly.
- **Tie doses to existing routines** rather than to clock times, and use pill organizers, blister
  packs or reminders.
- **Anticipate side effects.** Gastrointestinal effects with metformin and genital mycotic infections
  with SGLT-2 inhibitors are common early reasons for silent discontinuation, and both are usually
  manageable if raised.
- **Screen for depression.** It is more common in diabetes and materially reduces self-care; treating
  it improves both.

## Monitoring that is actually used

Glucose monitoring only helps if the readings change something. Guidance describes agreeing in
advance what the person will do in response to particular readings, rather than recording numbers
that are reviewed only at the next appointment. Where continuous monitoring is available, the same
principle applies to time-in-range.

## The review schedule

Long-term glucose control is measured at least twice yearly when stable and at goal, and quarterly
otherwise. Alongside it, ongoing care includes annual eye screening, kidney function and urine
albumin testing, foot examination, blood pressure and lipid review, dental care, and vaccination.
These are separate from glucose control and are frequently the parts that lapse.

## Sick days and travel

Illness raises glucose and changes requirements, and glucose-lowering medication is not simply
stopped because someone is not eating — that combination is a recognized route into a
hyperglycemic emergency. A sick-day plan agreed in advance with the person's own clinician is the
described approach. This system does not provide one, and does not give dosing instructions.

## What is generally recommended

The commonly stated target for adults is 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic
activity, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, or an equivalent combination, plus muscle-strengthening
activity on two or more days. For blood pressure specifically, the aerobic component carries most of
the evidence, and the reduction it produces is comparable in size to what a single
antihypertensive agent achieves in some people.

Moderate intensity means breathing harder and able to talk but not sing — brisk walking, cycling on
the flat, swimming, dancing, gardening that raises the heart rate. Vigorous means being unable to
say more than a few words without pausing.

## The part that matters most

Sessions can be accumulated across the week in whatever blocks fit, and short bouts count. The
older advice that only sustained ten-minute blocks counted has been dropped, and the practical
consequence is that stairs, brisk walks between tasks and short bursts of activity all contribute.

The largest single gain is from moving from doing nothing to doing something. The dose-response
curve is steepest at the low end, so someone currently inactive gains more from the first 60 minutes
a week than an already-active person gains from the last 60.

## Strength training

Resistance training two or more days per week is described as lowering blood pressure independently
of aerobic activity, and the two together are better than either alone. Isometric exercise — such as
sustained handgrip or wall-sit protocols — has attracted attention for a comparatively large effect
on blood pressure in trials, though the evidence base is smaller than for aerobic work and it is
usually described as an adjunct rather than a replacement.

## Reducing sedentary time

Prolonged uninterrupted sitting is associated with worse cardiovascular outcomes partly
independently of how much a person exercises. Breaking up long periods of sitting is described as a
separate target from the weekly activity total, not a substitute for it.

## Building it sustainably

Starting below the target and increasing gradually is more effective than beginning at the target,
because the failure mode is not insufficient ambition but abandonment. Activity that fits an
existing routine, and that the person is willing to keep doing, outperforms a theoretically superior
program that stops after three weeks.

## When medical review comes first

Anyone with chest pain on exertion, breathlessness disproportionate to effort, fainting, palpitations
with exercise, known heart disease, or very high uncontrolled blood pressure should be assessed
before starting vigorous activity. Anyone who develops chest discomfort, severe breathlessness or
faintness during exercise should stop and seek assessment. The emergency-symptom notes in this
corpus govern those situations.

[9] (lifestyle-asthma-adherence)
## Technique is the adherence problem people do not know they have

An inhaler taken faithfully every day with poor technique delivers a fraction of what it should, and
the record shows perfect adherence. Incorrect technique is common, it persists for years unless
someone checks it, and it is the first thing usually reviewed when treatment appears to be failing —
ahead of changing the drug.

The errors depend on the device. Pressurized inhalers are most often let down by poor coordination
between actuation and breath, and by breathing in too fast; dry powder inhalers need a fast, deep
breath in, which is the opposite instruction, and they fail when someone breathes out into the
device and dampens the powder. Someone using both device types is being asked to do two
contradictory things, which is worth naming rather than assuming.

A **spacer** used with a pressurized inhaler removes the coordination problem almost entirely and
improves delivery to the lungs. Technique is worth having checked at review appointments rather than
assumed, and a demonstration is more useful than a leaflet.

## Rinsing, and the side effect that drives people to stop

Rinsing the mouth and spitting after an inhaled corticosteroid reduces hoarseness and oral thrush.
These are minor problems clinically and major ones practically, because they are among the reasons
people quietly stop taking a controller inhaler.

## The controller and reliever confusion

The most consequential misunderstanding in asthma is between an inhaler taken every day whether or
not there are symptoms and one taken for immediate relief. Because the daily inhaler produces no
sensation and the relief inhaler produces an immediate one, the daily inhaler is the one dropped
first when someone feels well — which is precisely when it is working.

Knowing which device is which, by name and by appearance, is worth confirming explicitly. Rising use
of a relief inhaler is a signal that the underlying condition is not controlled rather than a sign
that the relief inhaler is doing its job; the asthma guideline note in this corpus covers what
modern guidance says about reliever-only treatment.

## The written action plan

A personalized written plan states what to take daily, what to do when symptoms worsen, and at what
point to seek help. It converts a decision made while breathless into one made in advance, and
having a copy where it can be found — on a phone, and with family — is part of the point.

## Refills, routines and the practical rest

A prescription collected less often than the dose requires is a straightforward indicator of missed
doses, and is worth tracking as information rather than treated as an accusation. Anchoring the
daily inhaler to an existing habit such as brushing teeth is the most durable reminder most people
find. Checking dose counters before a trip, keeping a relief inhaler where it will actually be, and
reducing exposure to identified triggers at home all belong to the same practical category.

## Why sodium matters here for a different reason

Sodium restriction in high blood pressure is about lowering a number. In heart failure it is about
volume: sodium holds water in the circulation, and a heart that cannot move that volume forward
backs it up into the lungs and the legs. The symptom being managed is congestion rather than
pressure, which is why a single high-sodium meal can produce breathlessness within a day or two in
someone whose blood pressure never moves.

The commonly stated targets sit in a similar range to those for blood pressure, and the practical
detail — that most dietary sodium is already in packaged and restaurant food rather than added at
the table — is covered in the blood-pressure diet note in this corpus and applies unchanged here.

What differs is the tolerance for a lapse. Guidance describes the evidence for aggressive
restriction as less settled than it was once assumed to be, and very strict limits can worsen
appetite and nutrition in people who are already eating poorly, so the target is a matter for the
person's own clinician rather than a number to be applied as hard as possible.

## Fluid

Fluid restriction is not universal. It is generally reserved for people with more advanced disease,
persistent congestion despite treatment, or a low blood sodium level, and where it applies the limit
is set individually. Applying a restriction that has not been advised carries its own risks,
particularly during hot weather, illness with vomiting or diarrhea, or a change in diuretic dose.

Where a limit does apply, everything liquid at room temperature counts — soup, ice, gelatin desserts
and the water taken with medication included. Thirst is managed with ice chips, sugar-free gum, hard
candy and rinsing the mouth rather than by drinking, because thirst in this setting is often driven
by sodium intake and dry mouth rather than by genuine volume need.

## The daily weight

Weighing daily is the feedback loop that makes the rest of it visible. The same scale, at the same
time of day, after waking and using the bathroom and before eating, recorded somewhere it can be
compared across days.

Weight is a proxy for fluid, and it moves faster than fluid symptoms do. A gain of a few pounds over
two or three days, or a larger gain over a week, is fluid rather than tissue and is the standard
prompt to make contact before breathlessness or swelling develops. Many people are given an action
plan specifying the thresholds and what to do at each; where one exists, it is the authority.

## Alcohol and other points

Alcohol is a direct depressant of heart muscle and is generally limited or avoided, particularly
where alcohol is thought to have contributed to the condition. Potassium and other electrolytes
interact with several heart failure medications in both directions, so supplements and salt
substitutes containing potassium chloride are decisions for the person's own clinician rather than
independent choices.

[11] (guideline-type-2-diabetes-glycemic-targets)
## The general target

Diabetes association guidance describes an HbA1c below 7 percent as a reasonable goal for many
non-pregnant adults, on the basis that this level of control reduces the small-vessel complications of diabetes — retinal, kidney and nerve
disease — over the following years. The evidence for large-vessel benefit from tighter glucose
control alone is weaker, which is why the target sits alongside blood pressure and lipid management
rather than above them.

The target is individualized rather than applied uniformly:

- **A more stringent goal**, such as below 6.5 percent, where it can be reached without significant
  low blood sugar or other harm — typically shorter duration of diabetes, longer life expectancy,
  and no significant cardiovascular disease.
- **A less stringent goal**, such as below 8 percent, where there is a history of severe low blood
  sugar, limited life expectancy, advanced complications, extensive other illness, or where the
  target has proved difficult to reach despite appropriate management.

## Monitoring intervals

HbA1c is measured at least twice a year in people meeting their goal on a stable regimen, and
quarterly in people not at goal or whose therapy has recently changed. It reflects average glucose
over roughly the preceding three months, which is why a shorter retest interval adds little: a test
repeated at six weeks is still reporting mostly the old period.

Continuous glucose monitoring and self-monitoring of blood glucose are complementary to HbA1c
rather than alternatives to it. They show the variability and the low readings that an average
conceals — two people with the same HbA1c can have very different exposure to hypoglycemia — and
they matter most for anyone using insulin or an agent that stimulates insulin release.
Time-in-range metrics derived from continuous monitoring are increasingly reported alongside HbA1c.

## Hypoglycemia is a target too

Guidance treats low blood sugar as an outcome to be measured, not only a side effect to be
mentioned. Episodes are classified by severity, with any episode requiring the assistance of another
person counted as severe, and a history of severe hypoglycemia is one of the explicit reasons to
relax the HbA1c goal rather than pursue it.

## Targets other than glucose

Glycemic control is one of several targets and not the most important one for cardiovascular
outcomes. Blood-pressure control, lipid management, smoking cessation, and — where indicated by
other conditions — the choice of glucose-lowering agent with demonstrated cardiovascular or kidney
benefit sit alongside the HbA1c goal.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on how firmly to state a single number. Some guidance describes 7 percent as the
default with individualization around it; other guidance describes the individualized range as
primary and declines to headline a figure at all, on the grounds that a headline number is applied more rigidly in practice
than its authors intend.

[12] (guideline-coronary-artery-disease-secondary-prevention)
## What secondary prevention means

Secondary prevention is the set of measures used for someone who already has established coronary
artery disease — a previous heart attack, a revascularization procedure, or angiographic disease —
to reduce the chance of a further event. It is a package rather than a single intervention: no one
element carries the effect, and the benefit measured in trials comes from applying them together.
Partial application is the common failure, and it is usually the non-drug elements that are dropped.

## The components

- **Antiplatelet therapy** — long-term single antiplatelet therapy for most people, with a defined
  period of dual antiplatelet therapy after an acute coronary syndrome or stent placement, its
  duration individualized against bleeding risk.
- **High-intensity statin therapy**. United States guidance describes the intensity; European
  guidance describes an LDL goal instead. Where the response is inadequate, additional
  non-statin agents are added rather than the statin abandoned.
- **Blood-pressure control**, with a target below 130/80 mm Hg for most people.
- **Renin-angiotensin blockade** where diabetes, reduced left ventricular function, or chronic
  kidney disease is also present.
- **Beta-blockade** after myocardial infarction, with the strongest and longest-standing evidence
  where left ventricular function is reduced.
- **Cardiac rehabilitation referral** — a structured program of supervised exercise, education and
  risk-factor management, and consistently one of the most underused elements relative to the
  strength of the evidence behind it.
- **Smoking cessation**, the single largest modifiable factor, with combined behavioral and
  pharmacologic support more effective than advice alone.
- **Annual influenza vaccination**, included as a cardiovascular measure rather than only a
  respiratory one.
- **Structured management of diabetes** where present, preferring agents with demonstrated
  cardiovascular benefit.

## Review interval

Review at least annually once the regimen is stable, with earlier review after any change in
symptoms, after a hospital admission, and four to twelve weeks after any change in lipid-lowering
intensity. Each review is an opportunity to check adherence, which falls measurably in the year
after an event as the acute experience recedes.

## What warrants urgent reassessment

New, worsening, or rest-onset chest discomfort in someone with known coronary disease is not a
routine review matter and requires urgent assessment. A pattern of angina that is becoming more
frequent, more easily provoked, or longer-lasting is a change in category rather than a change in
degree. The emergency-symptom notes elsewhere in this corpus govern these situations, and this note
does not substitute for them.

[13] (guideline-lipid-screening-and-statin-initiation)
## Screening

The screening test is a lipid panel — total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and
triglycerides. A non-fasting sample is acceptable for initial screening in most adults; a fasting
sample is preferred where triglycerides are markedly raised, since the triglyceride value and the
calculated LDL derived from it are the parts most affected by a recent meal.

The usual screening interval is every four to six years for adults aged 20 to 75 who are at low risk
and not on lipid-lowering therapy, and shorter where risk factors are present or where risk is being
reassessed before a treatment decision.

## Risk stratification

The central move in current guidance is that the decision is driven by estimated 10-year
atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk, not by the LDL number alone. Risk is estimated from age, sex,
race, total and HDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, treatment for hypertension, diabetes and
smoking status. The four named risk categories, for adults aged 40 to 75 without established
disease, are:

- **Low** — estimated 10-year risk below 5 percent.
- **Borderline** — 5 percent to below 7.5 percent.
- **Intermediate** — 7.5 percent to below 20 percent.
- **High** — 20 percent or above.

Risk-enhancing features shift a decision within the borderline and intermediate bands rather than
replacing the estimate: family history of premature cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease,
chronic inflammatory conditions, persistently raised triglycerides, metabolic syndrome, conditions
specific to pregnancy such as pre-eclampsia, and, where the decision remains uncertain, a coronary
artery calcium score.

## Groups in which therapy is indicated

- **Established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease** — high-intensity statin therapy as
  secondary prevention.
- **LDL cholesterol at or above 190 mg/dL** — high-intensity statin therapy regardless of the
  calculated risk score, which is not designed for this group.
- **Diabetes, aged 40 to 75** — at least moderate-intensity statin therapy.
- **Intermediate risk** — moderate-intensity statin therapy after a risk discussion.
- **Borderline risk** — guidance describes a risk discussion rather than a default action, with
  therapy favored where risk-enhancing features are present and reasonably deferred where they are
  not.

## Monitoring interval

The lipid panel is repeated four to twelve weeks after starting therapy or changing intensity, which
assesses response and adherence together, then every three to twelve months once stable. Routine
liver enzyme monitoring is not part of ongoing care in the absence of symptoms; a baseline
measurement is usual.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on whether to state numeric LDL targets. United States guidance describes statin
intensity and percentage reduction from baseline; European guidance describes explicit LDL goals
that fall as risk category rises, pursued with combination therapy where a statin alone falls short. Answers should say
which framing they are using rather than blending the two, since "at goal" means different things
under each.

[14] (condition-hypertension)
## What it is

Hypertension is persistently raised pressure in the arteries, sustained over time rather than on a
single occasion. Blood pressure is written as two numbers: the systolic pressure, generated when the
heart contracts, over the diastolic pressure, present between beats. Both are measured in
millimeters of mercury.

Pressure varies continuously through the day — with activity, stress, pain, caffeine, sleep and time
of day, typically lowest during sleep and rising before waking. That variation is why a diagnosis
rests on repeated measurements rather than one reading, and why a single high reading in a clinic is
not itself a diagnosis.

## How it is usually recognized

Hypertension is typically without symptoms and is most often found on routine measurement rather
than because someone felt unwell. That is the main reason screening for it exists at all. Where
symptoms such as headache, visual disturbance or nosebleed are attributed to raised blood pressure,
they usually reflect either a very high pressure or an unrelated cause — the belief that ordinary
hypertension can be felt leads people to treat by symptom rather than by measurement, which does not
work.

## What contributes to it

Most cases have no single identifiable cause and reflect a combination of age, genetic
predisposition, excess body weight, high dietary sodium, low potassium intake, physical inactivity,
alcohol intake, poor sleep including untreated sleep apnea (apnoea), and chronic stress. Arterial
stiffening with age is why systolic pressure tends to rise across the lifespan while diastolic
pressure often falls after middle age.

A minority of cases have an identifiable secondary cause — kidney disease, renal artery narrowing,
primary aldosteronism, thyroid or adrenal disorders, obstructive sleep apnea, and certain medications
including combined oral contraceptives, decongestants, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and
some stimulants. Investigation for a secondary cause is usually considered when hypertension appears
at a young age, is unusually severe, responds poorly to treatment, or worsens abruptly after a period
of stability.

## Why it is treated

Sustained high pressure damages arteries over years, and the conditions that follow are the reason
for treating a symptomless number: stroke, heart attack, heart failure, chronic kidney disease,
retinal damage, and cognitive decline. The benefit of treatment is measured in reduced rates of those
events, not in how the person feels — which is also why adherence is difficult, since a treatment
that produces no felt improvement and occasional side effects is easy to stop.

## How it is generally managed

Lifestyle measures — dietary sodium reduction, a diet pattern high in vegetables, fruit and whole
grains, regular activity, weight management, limiting alcohol, and stopping smoking — apply to
everyone. Drug treatment is added according to the level of risk. Diagnostic thresholds, treatment
targets, drug classes and follow-up intervals are covered by the hypertension guideline notes in
this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

A very high reading accompanied by chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, visual loss,
confusion, weakness or numbness on one side, or difficulty speaking is an emergency and requires
immediate medical attention rather than a routine appointment. The emergency-symptom notes in this
corpus govern those situations.

[15] (condition-heart-failure)
## What it is

Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart cannot fill with or eject blood well enough
to meet the body's needs at normal filling pressures. The name is misleading in a way worth
correcting: it does not mean the heart has stopped or is about to. It is a chronic condition that is
managed, often for many years.

It is classified by ejection fraction — the proportion of blood in the left ventricle expelled with
each beat — because the evidence for treatment differs sharply between the groups: reduced (40
percent or below), mildly reduced (41 to 49 percent), and preserved (50 percent or above). Preserved
ejection fraction accounts for roughly half of cases and is not a milder form; it is a different
problem, one of stiffness and impaired filling rather than weak contraction.

## How it is usually recognized

Breathlessness on exertion, then at lower levels of exertion, then when lying flat; waking at night
breathless; swelling of the ankles and legs; fatigue; reduced exercise tolerance; and weight gain
over days that reflects retained fluid rather than tissue. Distinguishing fluid weight from other
weight change matters, because a rise of two or three kilograms across a few days is a fluid signal
and a reason to act.

Confirming the diagnosis involves natriuretic peptide blood testing and echocardiography, which
establishes the ejection fraction that determines the treatment pathway.

## What contributes to it

Coronary artery disease and previous myocardial infarction are the most common causes, followed by
long-standing high blood pressure. Also: valve disease, atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathies
including genetic and post-viral forms, alcohol, some chemotherapy agents, thyroid disease, and
iron overload. Diabetes, obesity, chronic kidney disease and sleep apnea (apnoea) commonly coexist
and worsen the course.

## Why it is treated

Treatment reduces symptoms, hospital admissions and mortality. Modern therapy for reduced ejection
fraction has changed the outlook substantially, and a proportion of people recover ventricular
function on it — which is why the ejection fraction is reassessed after therapy is established
rather than treated as a fixed property. The four foundational classes and their titration are
covered by the heart-failure guideline note in this corpus.

## How it is generally managed

Disease-modifying drug therapy according to ejection fraction; diuretics for congestion; treating
the underlying cause and the coexisting conditions; devices in selected people; cardiac
rehabilitation; vaccination; and structured self-management — daily weights, recognizing early
fluid retention, and knowing when to seek help. Sodium and fluid advice is individualized rather
than uniform.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Breathlessness at rest or that wakes the person and does not settle when upright, chest pain, rapid
weight gain over a few days, fainting, a very fast or irregular pulse with symptoms, or confusion —
these need urgent assessment. Pink frothy sputum with severe breathlessness is an emergency. The
emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[16] (condition-type-2-diabetes)
## What it is

Type 2 diabetes is a disorder of glucose regulation in which the body's tissues respond poorly to
insulin — insulin resistance — and the pancreas cannot sustain the increased output that resistance
demands. The result is a blood glucose level that stays above the normal range. It differs from type
1 diabetes, in which insulin-producing cells are destroyed by an autoimmune process and insulin is
absent rather than ineffective. The distinction matters because type 1 can present in adults, where
it is sometimes mislabeled.

The condition develops gradually, over years. The period of raised-but-not-diabetic glucose that
precedes it — prediabetes — is a recognized state with its own management, and it is the point at
which intensive lifestyle change has the largest effect.

## How it is usually recognized

Many people have no symptoms at diagnosis and are identified by screening. Where symptoms are
present, the classic ones are increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss,
fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing wounds and recurrent infections. Because onset is gradual,
complications are sometimes already present at the time of diagnosis — which is the argument for
screening rather than waiting for symptoms.

this corpus.

## What contributes to it

Excess body weight, particularly around the abdomen; physical inactivity; a family history of the
condition; increasing age; a history of gestational diabetes or of polycystic ovary syndrome; and
higher background risk in several racial and ethnic groups. Certain medications raise risk,
including long-term corticosteroids and some antipsychotics. Obstructive sleep apnea is commonly
present alongside it and worsens glucose control independently.

## Why it is treated

Sustained high glucose damages small and large blood vessels. The small-vessel complications are
retinal disease, kidney disease and nerve damage, including the foot problems that follow loss of
protective sensation. The large-vessel complications are heart attack, stroke and peripheral
arterial disease, which account for most of the excess mortality associated with the condition. Management therefore addresses blood pressure,
lipids and smoking alongside glucose, and modern treatment choices are made partly on cardiovascular
and kidney grounds rather than on glucose alone.
