[1] (guideline-gerd-initial-management-and-alarm-features)
## The empiric approach

For an adult with typical symptoms — heartburn and regurgitation — and no alarm features, the
initial approach to gastroesophageal reflux disease (gastro-oesophageal in British spelling) is an
one guidance describes: an empiric eight-week trial of acid suppression with a proton pump inhibitor
taken before a meal, rather than investigation first. Typical symptoms plus response to acid suppression is informative
enough in this group that endoscopy first would change management in few people. Timing matters as
much as the agent: these drugs act on activated pumps, so a dose taken with or after food is a
common reason for apparent non-response. Doses are outside the scope of this note.

## Lifestyle measures

Weight reduction where body weight is above the healthy range has the strongest supporting evidence.
Others are elevating the head of the bed for people with night-time symptoms, avoiding meals within
two to three hours of lying down, stopping smoking, and avoiding individually identified trigger
foods rather than applying a blanket elimination diet, which is poorly supported.

## Alarm features that change the approach

Prompt endoscopy rather than an empiric trial where any of the following are present:

- Difficulty swallowing, or pain on swallowing.
- Unintentional weight loss.
- Gastrointestinal bleeding — vomiting blood, or black tarry stools.
- Iron-deficiency anemia (anaemia).
- Persistent vomiting.
- A palpable mass, or a family history of upper gastrointestinal cancer.
- New onset of symptoms at an older age.

## After the trial

Where symptoms respond, the next step is stepping down to the lowest effective therapy, or to
on-demand use, rather than continuing indefinitely at the initial intensity. Where symptoms do not
respond, adherence and timing relative to meals are confirmed first, then referral for endoscopy
and, in selected people, esophageal pH or pH-impedance testing performed off therapy to establish
whether acid reflux is in fact the cause. A substantial share of non-responders turn out to have
functional heartburn, reflux hypersensitivity, or a motility disorder — conditions that more acid
suppression will not improve, which is why escalating the dose indefinitely is not the answer to
non-response.

## Long-term therapy

Where long-term acid suppression is genuinely needed — erosive esophagitis (oesophagitis), Barrett's
esophagus (oesophagus), or symptom recurrence on withdrawal — it is continued at the lowest
effective intensity with periodic review, rather than renewed indefinitely without reassessment.

## An important overlap

Chest discomfort cannot be attributed to reflux without considering a cardiac cause, particularly
where it is exertional, associated with breathlessness or sweating, or occurring in someone with
cardiovascular risk factors. Cardiac assessment takes precedence, and the emergency-symptom notes
elsewhere in this corpus govern that case.

[2] (guideline-type-2-diabetes-first-line-therapy)
## The shape of current guidance

Older guidance set out a single sequence: metformin first, then agents added in order as control
worsened. Current guidance is structured differently — the first-line choice depends on which other
conditions are present, and for several of them the choice is made independently of the HbA1c value.
This is the substantive change, and it is the part most often stated in the old form.

## Where there is no compelling comorbidity

Metformin, alongside structured lifestyle intervention, is the usual initial agent: long experience,
low cost, weight neutrality, and little risk of causing low blood sugar on its own. Kidney function
is checked before starting and periodically after, since the dose is constrained below a threshold
of kidney function and the agent is avoided below a lower one. Gastrointestinal intolerance is the
common reason for stopping, and is reduced by gradual escalation and extended-release formulations.
Long-term use is associated with lower vitamin B12 levels, so periodic measurement is advised.

## Where cardiovascular, kidney or heart-failure disease is present

Guidance describes agents with demonstrated organ benefit as preferred, whether or not metformin is
also used, and independent of whether the HbA1c is at goal:

- **Established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease** — a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven
  cardiovascular benefit, or an SGLT-2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit.
- **Heart failure**, particularly with reduced ejection fraction — an SGLT-2 inhibitor.
- **Chronic kidney disease**, particularly with albuminuria — an SGLT-2 inhibitor, with a GLP-1
  receptor agonist as the alternative where an SGLT-2 inhibitor is not tolerated or not appropriate.

These are organ-protective therapies that also lower glucose, rather than later steps in a glucose
ladder. Class-specific cautions are part of the choice: SGLT-2 inhibitors carry a risk of genital
mycotic infection, volume depletion, and — uncommonly — ketoacidosis at near-normal glucose levels,
which is easy to miss precisely because the glucose is not high.

## Where weight is a major treatment goal

Agents with the greatest weight-reduction effect — the GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual incretin
agonists — are preferred where weight management is a primary objective, alongside structured
lifestyle intervention and, in selected people, metabolic surgery.

## Reassessment

The regimen is reviewed every three to six months. De-intensification is an explicit option, not a
failure: where the regimen has become more aggressive than the individualized target requires, or
where low blood sugar is occurring, stepping down is the appropriate response.

Doses, titration schedules and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this
system.

[3] (guideline-asthma-diagnosis-and-stepwise-therapy)
## Confirming the diagnosis

Asthma requires both a compatible symptom pattern and objective evidence of variable expiratory
airflow limitation. The symptom pattern is variable wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and
cough, worse at night or early morning and provoked by exercise, allergens, cold air or viral
infection. The objective test is spirometry before and after a bronchodilator, with reversibility
supporting the diagnosis.

A normal spirometry result when the person is well does not exclude asthma — variability is the
point, and a measurement taken on a good day measures the good day. Repeat testing while
symptomatic, peak-flow variability over two weeks, or bronchial challenge testing are the usual next
steps where the diagnosis remains uncertain. Confirming it before committing someone to long-term
inhaled therapy matters, because a substantial share of people carrying an asthma label do not have
objective confirmation of it.

## The central change in modern guidance

Treating asthma with a short-acting bronchodilator alone is no longer appropriate at any severity.
Every adult and adolescent with asthma receives inhaled-corticosteroid-containing therapy, because
reliever-only treatment leaves the underlying inflammation untreated and is associated with severe
exacerbations even in people whose symptoms are infrequent. Heavy reliever use — several canisters a
year — is a marker of risk in its own right.

## The stepwise structure

Treatment is arranged in steps, with the step chosen from current symptom control and exacerbation
history and reviewed rather than fixed:

- **Lower steps** — as-needed inhaled corticosteroid combined with a fast-onset long-acting
  bronchodilator, or regular low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with an as-needed reliever.
- **Middle steps** — regular low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting bronchodilator, with
  the same combination inhaler used as the reliever in one of the described regimens.
- **Higher steps** — medium- or high-dose combination therapy, the addition of a long-acting
  muscarinic antagonist, then referral for severe-asthma assessment including biologic agents
  targeted to inflammatory phenotype.

Stepping down is considered after three or more months of good control. Before stepping up, inhaler
technique and adherence are checked, since between them they account for a large share of apparent
treatment failure, and a step-up that compensates for poor technique treats the wrong problem.

## Where guidance differs

The preferred reliever in mild asthma is a genuine point of divergence. Global strategy guidance
describes an inhaled-corticosteroid-and-formoterol combination as the preferred reliever across
steps; some national panel guidance describes a short-acting bronchodilator reliever alongside a
regular controller as remaining appropriate in mild disease. Answers should name which position they are describing.

## Review interval

Review one to three months after starting or changing therapy, then every three to twelve months,
and within one week after an exacerbation — the period when the reason for the exacerbation is still
recoverable.

[4] (guideline-hypertension-first-line-treatment)
## Lifestyle measures are the shared foundation

Every major body recommends the same set of non-drug measures, whether or not medication is also
used: reducing dietary sodium, adopting a dietary pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains
and low-fat dairy and low in saturated fat, regular aerobic activity most days of the week, weight
reduction where body weight is above the healthy range, limiting alcohol, and stopping smoking.
Each produces a meaningful reduction on its own, and the effects are partly additive, so several
combined can move a person a full stage.

## When drug treatment starts

The decision is tied to cardiovascular risk, not to the blood-pressure number alone:

- **Stage 2 hypertension** — drug treatment alongside lifestyle measures, usually beginning with
  two agents, because a single agent rarely closes a gap of this size.
- **Stage 1 hypertension with established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney
  disease, or an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk at or above 10 percent** — drug treatment
  alongside lifestyle measures.
- **Stage 1 hypertension without those features** — lifestyle measures first, with reassessment
  after three to six months before drug treatment is considered.

## First-line drug classes

Four classes are first-line for most adults without a compelling indication for something else:
thiazide-type diuretics, angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers,
and dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers. An ACE inhibitor and an angiotensin receptor blocker
are not combined — the combination adds harm without adding benefit. Single-pill combinations are
preferred where two agents are needed, because adherence falls as pill count rises.

Comorbidity shifts the choice. Renin-angiotensin blockade is preferred where diabetes with
albuminuria or chronic kidney disease is present; a beta-blocker is not first-line for uncomplicated
hypertension but becomes appropriate where there is a separate indication such as heart failure or
recent myocardial infarction. Doses are outside the scope of this note and of this system.

## Resistant hypertension

Blood pressure above target on three agents including a diuretic, all at appropriate doses, is
described as resistant hypertension. Before treatment is escalated further, the sequence is to
confirm the readings out of office, review adherence, review agents that raise blood pressure —
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, decongestants, some stimulants, combined oral contraceptives
— and investigate for a secondary cause. Apparent resistance is more often measurement, adherence
or an interfering agent than a need for a fourth drug.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on how aggressively to treat low-risk stage 1 hypertension, which follows from the
threshold disagreement in the diagnostic note: where guidance describes hypertension as beginning at
140/90 mm Hg, much of the population that United States guidance calls stage 1 is instead advised on
lifestyle alone.

## Follow-up interval

Monthly review until the target is reached, including adherence and a check of kidney function and
potassium after starting an agent acting on the renin-angiotensin system, then review every three
to six months once stable.

[5] (guideline-insomnia-cbt-first-line)
## What counts as chronic insomnia

Chronic insomnia disorder is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early,
occurring at least three nights per week for at least three months, despite adequate opportunity to
sleep, and accompanied by daytime consequences — fatigue, impaired attention, mood disturbance, or
impaired performance. The daytime component is part of the definition: short sleep without daytime
consequences is not a disorder, and treating it as one medicalizes normal variation in sleep need.

Assessment includes a sleep diary over one to two weeks, screening for the conditions that commonly
present as insomnia — obstructive sleep apnea (apnoea), restless legs syndrome, circadian rhythm
disorders, depression, anxiety, pain, and substance or medication effects — and review of caffeine,
alcohol, nicotine and shift patterns. Alcohol is worth singling out: it shortens sleep latency and
then fragments the second half of the night, so it is often reported as a remedy by someone whose
sleep it is degrading.

## The first-line recommendation

Both sleep medicine and internal medicine guidance describes cognitive behavioral therapy for
insomnia as first-line for chronic insomnia in adults, ahead of medication. Its effects persist after treatment
ends, whereas pharmacological effects generally do not, and it avoids the harms associated with
long-term hypnotic use.

The components are delivered together as a package over roughly four to eight sessions:

- **Stimulus control** — using the bed only for sleep, leaving the bed when unable to sleep, so the
  bed stops being a cue for wakefulness.
- **Sleep restriction** — limiting time in bed toward actual sleep time, then extending it as sleep
  consolidates. Counterintuitive, and the component people most often abandon early.
- **Cognitive restructuring** of the beliefs about sleep that maintain arousal, including the
  catastrophizing about tomorrow that keeps someone awake tonight.
- **Sleep hygiene education**, necessary but insufficient on its own. Guidance is explicit that
  sleep hygiene advice alone is not effective treatment for chronic insomnia — a frequent
  misunderstanding, and the reason that "I already tried sleep hygiene" is not evidence that this
  therapy has been tried.
- **Relaxation training.**

Digitally delivered and brief formats are reasonable where in-person therapy is not accessible,
which is the practical constraint most often cited against the recommendation.

## Where medication sits

Pharmacotherapy is second-line: for people in whom cognitive behavioral therapy is unavailable, has
been tried without adequate response, or where short-term treatment is needed alongside it. Shared
decision-making, the shortest appropriate duration, and a plan for reassessment and discontinuation
agreed at the point of starting rather than later. Antihistamine-based over-the-counter sleep aids
have limited evidence and notable anticholinergic side effects, particularly in older adults.

## What is outside this note

Doses and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this system.

[6] (guideline-coronary-artery-disease-secondary-prevention)
## What secondary prevention means

Secondary prevention is the set of measures used for someone who already has established coronary
artery disease — a previous heart attack, a revascularization procedure, or angiographic disease —
to reduce the chance of a further event. It is a package rather than a single intervention: no one
element carries the effect, and the benefit measured in trials comes from applying them together.
Partial application is the common failure, and it is usually the non-drug elements that are dropped.

## The components

- **Antiplatelet therapy** — long-term single antiplatelet therapy for most people, with a defined
  period of dual antiplatelet therapy after an acute coronary syndrome or stent placement, its
  duration individualized against bleeding risk.
- **High-intensity statin therapy**. United States guidance describes the intensity; European
  guidance describes an LDL goal instead. Where the response is inadequate, additional
  non-statin agents are added rather than the statin abandoned.
- **Blood-pressure control**, with a target below 130/80 mm Hg for most people.
- **Renin-angiotensin blockade** where diabetes, reduced left ventricular function, or chronic
  kidney disease is also present.
- **Beta-blockade** after myocardial infarction, with the strongest and longest-standing evidence
  where left ventricular function is reduced.
- **Cardiac rehabilitation referral** — a structured program of supervised exercise, education and
  risk-factor management, and consistently one of the most underused elements relative to the
  strength of the evidence behind it.
- **Smoking cessation**, the single largest modifiable factor, with combined behavioral and
  pharmacologic support more effective than advice alone.
- **Annual influenza vaccination**, included as a cardiovascular measure rather than only a
  respiratory one.
- **Structured management of diabetes** where present, preferring agents with demonstrated
  cardiovascular benefit.

## Review interval

Review at least annually once the regimen is stable, with earlier review after any change in
symptoms, after a hospital admission, and four to twelve weeks after any change in lipid-lowering
intensity. Each review is an opportunity to check adherence, which falls measurably in the year
after an event as the acute experience recedes.

## What warrants urgent reassessment

New, worsening, or rest-onset chest discomfort in someone with known coronary disease is not a
routine review matter and requires urgent assessment. A pattern of angina that is becoming more
frequent, more easily provoked, or longer-lasting is a change in category rather than a change in
degree. The emergency-symptom notes elsewhere in this corpus govern these situations, and this note
does not substitute for them.

[7] (guideline-heart-failure-reduced-ef-therapy)
## The classification the guidance depends on

Heart failure guidance separates by ejection fraction, because the evidence differs sharply between
the groups:

- **Reduced ejection fraction** — 40 percent or below.
- **Mildly reduced ejection fraction** — 41 to 49 percent.
- **Preserved ejection fraction** — 50 percent or above.

The therapy below applies to the reduced group. Applying it wholesale to preserved ejection fraction
is a common error: several of these classes have not shown the same benefit there, and the one that
has — the SGLT-2 inhibitors — is the newest addition.

## The four foundational classes

Current guidance describes four classes as foundational, started together or in rapid sequence
rather than added one at a time over months:

1. **Renin-angiotensin system blockade** — an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor where
   suitable, otherwise an ACE inhibitor, otherwise an angiotensin receptor blocker.
2. **A beta-blocker** with evidence specifically in heart failure, started when the person is not
   congested, since starting during congestion can worsen it.
3. **A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist**, with potassium and kidney function monitored.
4. **An SGLT-2 inhibitor**, used for this indication irrespective of whether diabetes is present.

Each is titrated toward the doses used in the trials as blood pressure, kidney function and
potassium allow, with review at roughly two-week intervals during titration. The change from older
guidance is the emphasis on getting all four classes started at low intensity before maximizing any
one of them: the benefit of a fourth class at a low dose exceeds the benefit of pushing a third to
its ceiling. A modest early fall in kidney function or a small rise in potassium is anticipated and
is not by itself a reason to stop.

## Additional measures

Diuretic therapy relieves congestion and symptoms; it is not an outcome-modifying therapy and is
adjusted to the lowest dose that maintains euvolemia. Structured education in self-monitoring —
daily weights, recognizing increasing breathlessness or swelling, sodium and fluid advice — and
cardiac rehabilitation are part of the package. Iron deficiency is looked for and corrected, since
it is common and independently affects symptoms.

## Reassessment and device consideration

Ejection fraction is reassessed after at least three months of optimized therapy before an
implantable defibrillator or resynchronization device is considered, because function improves in a
substantial proportion of people once therapy is established. A device decision made on the
pre-treatment number is a decision made on the wrong number.

## Follow-up after admission

Early follow-up after a heart-failure admission — commonly within seven to fourteen days — is one of
the higher-yield contacts in the whole pathway, because the weeks after discharge carry the highest
readmission risk and are when titration most often stalls.

[8] (guideline-hypothyroidism-testing-and-monitoring)
## The testing sequence

Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone is the initial test in suspected thyroid dysfunction, because it
responds to small changes in thyroid hormone before the hormone levels themselves leave the
reference range — the relationship is logarithmic, so a modest fall in thyroxine produces a large
rise in the stimulating hormone. Where the result is raised, free thyroxine is measured to
distinguish two situations:

- **Overt hypothyroidism** — raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with free thyroxine below the
  reference range.
- **Subclinical hypothyroidism** — raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with free thyroxine within
  the reference range.

Thyroid peroxidase antibodies establish autoimmune thyroiditis as the cause and help estimate how
likely subclinical disease is to progress. Routine thyroid ultrasound is not part of the workup for
an abnormal blood test in the absence of a palpable nodule or goiter.

## Confirming before treating

An abnormal result is confirmed with a repeat measurement after several weeks before long-term
therapy starts. The hormone fluctuates, is suppressed during acute illness and recovery from it, and
shows diurnal variation with higher values overnight and early morning. Treating a single abnormal
value is a common and avoidable error, and non-thyroidal illness is the usual explanation for an
abnormal panel in someone who is acutely unwell.

## Monitoring interval

This is the interval most often asked about and most often got wrong. Thyroid-stimulating hormone is
rechecked six to eight weeks after starting levothyroxine or after any dose change, because it takes
that long to re-equilibrate to the new steady state. A test taken at two or three weeks still
largely reflects the old state and invites an unnecessary further change, producing an oscillation
that takes months to settle. Once the level is stable on an unchanged dose, testing moves to six to
twelve month intervals.

## Absorption and interference

Levothyroxine is taken consistently with respect to food, and separated from calcium salts, iron
salts, proton pump inhibitors and several other agents that reduce its absorption. Where a dose that
was previously adequate stops working, adherence and interfering agents are reviewed before the dose
is increased — a newly started supplement is a more common explanation than a change in the thyroid
itself.

## Where guidance differs

Whether to treat subclinical hypothyroidism is a genuine and unresolved disagreement. There is broad
agreement on treating when thyroid-stimulating hormone is persistently above about 10 mIU/L. In the
band between the upper reference limit and 10 mIU/L, some guidance describes a trial of treatment
where symptoms, positive antibodies, or cardiovascular risk are present, while other guidance
describes monitoring alone for most people, citing trials in older adults that showed no
symptomatic benefit from treatment. Bodies also differ on whether the reference range should be
adjusted upward for older adults, in whom a mildly raised value may be normal for age. Pregnancy is
treated separately under trimester-specific ranges, with a lower threshold for treatment.

[9] (guideline-lipid-screening-and-statin-initiation)
## Screening

The screening test is a lipid panel — total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and
triglycerides. A non-fasting sample is acceptable for initial screening in most adults; a fasting
sample is preferred where triglycerides are markedly raised, since the triglyceride value and the
calculated LDL derived from it are the parts most affected by a recent meal.

The usual screening interval is every four to six years for adults aged 20 to 75 who are at low risk
and not on lipid-lowering therapy, and shorter where risk factors are present or where risk is being
reassessed before a treatment decision.

## Risk stratification

The central move in current guidance is that the decision is driven by estimated 10-year
atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk, not by the LDL number alone. Risk is estimated from age, sex,
race, total and HDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, treatment for hypertension, diabetes and
smoking status. The four named risk categories, for adults aged 40 to 75 without established
disease, are:

- **Low** — estimated 10-year risk below 5 percent.
- **Borderline** — 5 percent to below 7.5 percent.
- **Intermediate** — 7.5 percent to below 20 percent.
- **High** — 20 percent or above.

Risk-enhancing features shift a decision within the borderline and intermediate bands rather than
replacing the estimate: family history of premature cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease,
chronic inflammatory conditions, persistently raised triglycerides, metabolic syndrome, conditions
specific to pregnancy such as pre-eclampsia, and, where the decision remains uncertain, a coronary
artery calcium score.

## Groups in which therapy is indicated

- **Established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease** — high-intensity statin therapy as
  secondary prevention.
- **LDL cholesterol at or above 190 mg/dL** — high-intensity statin therapy regardless of the
  calculated risk score, which is not designed for this group.
- **Diabetes, aged 40 to 75** — at least moderate-intensity statin therapy.
- **Intermediate risk** — moderate-intensity statin therapy after a risk discussion.
- **Borderline risk** — guidance describes a risk discussion rather than a default action, with
  therapy favored where risk-enhancing features are present and reasonably deferred where they are
  not.

## Monitoring interval

The lipid panel is repeated four to twelve weeks after starting therapy or changing intensity, which
assesses response and adherence together, then every three to twelve months once stable. Routine
liver enzyme monitoring is not part of ongoing care in the absence of symptoms; a baseline
measurement is usual.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on whether to state numeric LDL targets. United States guidance describes statin
intensity and percentage reduction from baseline; European guidance describes explicit LDL goals
that fall as risk category rises, pursued with combination therapy where a statin alone falls short. Answers should say
which framing they are using rather than blending the two, since "at goal" means different things
under each.

[10] (condition-type-2-diabetes)
## What it is

Type 2 diabetes is a disorder of glucose regulation in which the body's tissues respond poorly to
insulin — insulin resistance — and the pancreas cannot sustain the increased output that resistance
demands. The result is a blood glucose level that stays above the normal range. It differs from type
1 diabetes, in which insulin-producing cells are destroyed by an autoimmune process and insulin is
absent rather than ineffective. The distinction matters because type 1 can present in adults, where
it is sometimes mislabeled.

The condition develops gradually, over years. The period of raised-but-not-diabetic glucose that
precedes it — prediabetes — is a recognized state with its own management, and it is the point at
which intensive lifestyle change has the largest effect.

## How it is usually recognized

Many people have no symptoms at diagnosis and are identified by screening. Where symptoms are
present, the classic ones are increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss,
fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing wounds and recurrent infections. Because onset is gradual,
complications are sometimes already present at the time of diagnosis — which is the argument for
screening rather than waiting for symptoms.

Diagnostic thresholds and screening criteria are covered by the diabetes screening guideline note in
this corpus.

## What contributes to it

Excess body weight, particularly around the abdomen; physical inactivity; a family history of the
condition; increasing age; a history of gestational diabetes or of polycystic ovary syndrome; and
higher background risk in several racial and ethnic groups. Certain medications raise risk,
including long-term corticosteroids and some antipsychotics. Obstructive sleep apnea is commonly
present alongside it and worsens glucose control independently.

## Why it is treated

Sustained high glucose damages small and large blood vessels. The small-vessel complications are
retinal disease, kidney disease and nerve damage, including the foot problems that follow loss of
protective sensation. The large-vessel complications are heart attack, stroke and peripheral
arterial disease, which account for most of the excess mortality associated with the condition. Management therefore addresses blood pressure,
lipids and smoking alongside glucose, and modern treatment choices are made partly on cardiovascular
and kidney grounds rather than on glucose alone.

## How it is generally managed

Structured lifestyle intervention — dietary change, physical activity, weight management — together
with medication chosen according to which other conditions are present. Ongoing care includes
periodic measurement of long-term glucose control, annual eye screening, kidney function and urine
albumin testing, foot examination, and management of cardiovascular risk factors. Targets, testing
intervals and drug classes are covered by the diabetes guideline notes in this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Very high glucose with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep or rapid breathing, drowsiness or
confusion may indicate a hyperglycemic emergency and requires immediate medical attention. Symptoms
of low blood sugar — shakiness, sweating, confusion, difficulty concentrating — in someone taking
insulin or an agent that stimulates insulin release require prompt treatment, and loss of
consciousness or seizure is an emergency. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these
situations.

[11] (coding-icd10-chapter-04-endocrine)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 4 of ICD-10-CM covers E00 through E89 and takes in three things that are grouped together
more by tradition than by mechanism: disorders of the endocrine glands, nutritional disorders, and
inherited and acquired disorders of metabolism. Every code begins with the letter E.

## The blocks, in order

Disorders of the thyroid gland open the chapter at E00 to E07, running from the iodine-deficiency
states through hypothyroidism, thyrotoxicosis, thyroiditis and goiter to the residual categories.

Diabetes mellitus occupies E08 to E13, and the split within it is by cause rather than by treatment:
diabetes due to an underlying condition, drug- or chemical-induced diabetes, type 1, type 2, and
other specified diabetes each hold a separate three-character category. E15 to E16 continue with the
other disorders of glucose regulation and of pancreatic internal secretion, including the
hypoglycemia categories used when diabetes is not the cause.

Disorders of other endocrine glands follow at E20 to E35 — parathyroid, pituitary, adrenal, ovarian
and testicular dysfunction, and the polyglandular syndromes.

The nutritional blocks come next. Malnutrition occupies E40 to E46, other nutritional deficiencies
E50 to E64, and overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation E65 to E68. Metabolic disorders make
up the long final block at E70 to E88: the inherited disorders of amino-acid, carbohydrate and lipid
metabolism, disorders of mineral metabolism, cystic fibrosis, amyloidosis, volume depletion and the
fluid, electrolyte and acid-base disturbances. A short closing block at E89 covers endocrine and
metabolic complications following a procedure.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Transitory endocrine and metabolic disorders specific to the newborn are classified in the perinatal
chapter rather than here. Endocrine disorders arising in pregnancy, including gestational diabetes,
belong to the obstetric chapter. Neoplasms of endocrine glands are neoplasms, though the functional
disturbance a tumor causes may be coded from this chapter in addition.

The boundary with abnormal findings is the one that catches people. Prediabetes, impaired fasting
glucose, impaired glucose tolerance and an isolated raised or lowered glucose result with no
diagnosis recorded are all abnormal laboratory findings, and they are classified in Chapter 18 —
not in the diabetes block. An abnormal thyroid function test without a diagnosis sits in Chapter 18
for the same reason.

## Codes from other chapters that endocrine questions commonly need

Body mass index has its own category in the factors-influencing-health chapter and is reported
alongside an obesity diagnosis rather than in place of one. Long-term use of insulin, of injectable
non-insulin agents and of oral glucose-lowering drugs is coded from that chapter too, as are
screening encounters and family history. Diabetic complication codes reach outward constantly: stage
of chronic kidney disease from the genitourinary chapter, ulcer site and depth from the skin
chapter, and retinal detail from the eye chapter.

[12] (lifestyle-type-2-diabetes-adherence)
## Why this has its own note

Diabetes is largely self-managed. Most decisions affecting the outcome are made by the person
between appointments, and adherence to glucose-lowering medication is measurably imperfect in
practice. Treating non-adherence as a character issue misses what the evidence shows: cost,
complexity, side effects, low health literacy, depression, and simply forgetting account for most of
it, and each has a different remedy.

## Diabetes self-management education

Structured education and support is described as a core part of care rather than an optional extra,
with specific points at which it is offered: at diagnosis, annually where treatment targets are not
met, when complicating factors develop, and when transitions in care occur. It improves glucose
control and quality of life, and it is consistently underused.

## Making the regimen easier to follow

- **Simplify where possible.** Fewer daily doses and fixed-dose combinations improve adherence.
  Where a regimen has become more complex than the individualized target requires,
  de-intensification is an appropriate response rather than a concession.
- **Name the cost problem out loud.** Cost-related underuse — skipping doses, splitting tablets, not
  filling prescriptions — is common and is rarely volunteered unless asked about directly.
- **Tie doses to existing routines** rather than to clock times, and use pill organizers, blister
  packs or reminders.
- **Anticipate side effects.** Gastrointestinal effects with metformin and genital mycotic infections
  with SGLT-2 inhibitors are common early reasons for silent discontinuation, and both are usually
  manageable if raised.
- **Screen for depression.** It is more common in diabetes and materially reduces self-care; treating
  it improves both.

## Monitoring that is actually used

Glucose monitoring only helps if the readings change something. Guidance describes agreeing in
advance what the person will do in response to particular readings, rather than recording numbers
that are reviewed only at the next appointment. Where continuous monitoring is available, the same
principle applies to time-in-range.

## The review schedule

Long-term glucose control is measured at least twice yearly when stable and at goal, and quarterly
otherwise. Alongside it, ongoing care includes annual eye screening, kidney function and urine
albumin testing, foot examination, blood pressure and lipid review, dental care, and vaccination.
These are separate from glucose control and are frequently the parts that lapse.

## Sick days and travel

Illness raises glucose and changes requirements, and glucose-lowering medication is not simply
stopped because someone is not eating — that combination is a recognized route into a
hyperglycemic emergency. A sick-day plan agreed in advance with the person's own clinician is the
described approach. This system does not provide one, and does not give dosing instructions.

[13] (guideline-copd-diagnosis-and-stepwise-management)
## The diagnosis is spirometric

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is not diagnosed from symptoms alone. A post-bronchodilator
ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity below 0.70 confirms
persistent airflow limitation, in a person with compatible symptoms — breathlessness on exertion,
chronic cough, sputum production — and a relevant exposure history, most often tobacco smoke, and
also biomass fuel and occupational dust or fumes. The degree of airflow limitation is graded
separately, using the forced expiratory volume as a percentage of predicted, and correlates only
loosely with how the person actually feels.

## Assessment combines symptoms and exacerbations

Two axes are assessed rather than severity alone. Symptom burden is measured with a standard
questionnaire or breathlessness scale, and exacerbation history over the past year is recorded, with
particular weight on any exacerbation requiring hospital admission. Together they place the person
in a group that determines initial therapy. The exacerbation axis, not the symptom axis, identifies
the group at highest risk — and the best predictor of a future exacerbation is a past one.

## Initial pharmacologic therapy

Guidance describes initial therapy by group rather than by severity of airflow limitation:

- **Low symptom burden, no significant exacerbation history** — a long-acting bronchodilator.
- **High symptom burden, no significant exacerbation history** — dual long-acting bronchodilator
  therapy, combining a muscarinic antagonist and a beta-agonist.
- **Significant exacerbation history** — dual long-acting bronchodilator therapy, with an inhaled
  corticosteroid added where the blood eosinophil count is high or where features of coexisting
  asthma are present.

The blood eosinophil count is the marker used to predict who benefits from an inhaled
corticosteroid. The decision rests on a marker rather than being applied to everyone because
inhaled corticosteroid use in this population carries an increased risk of pneumonia, so the benefit
has to be identifiable to be worth the harm.

## The measures with the largest effect are not inhalers

Smoking cessation is the only intervention shown to alter the rate of decline in lung function.
Pulmonary rehabilitation improves breathlessness and exercise capacity more than any inhaler does.
Vaccination against influenza, pneumococcal disease, COVID-19 and, where recommended, RSV reduces
exacerbations. Long-term oxygen therapy is assessed for in people with severe resting hypoxemia,
where it affects survival — and is not indicated for breathlessness in the absence of that
hypoxemia, which is a frequent misunderstanding.

## Review interval

Review at least annually, after every exacerbation, and after any change in inhaled therapy, with
inhaler technique checked at each review. Escalation without a technique check is one of the more
common avoidable errors in the pathway.

[14] (guideline-anxiety-screening-and-first-line-care)
## Screening

Preventive-services guidance describes screening adults for anxiety disorders where systems are in
place to ensure accurate diagnosis and follow-up, with the strongest statement made for adults under
65. For older adults the evidence is judged insufficient to make a recommendation either way — a
statement about the evidence, not a recommendation against screening, and one that is frequently
misread as the latter.

The seven-item generalized anxiety disorder questionnaire (generalised in British spelling) is the
instrument most often used, both to screen and to track severity. The commonly used severity bands
are 5 for mild, 10 for moderate and 15 for severe, with 10 the threshold at which further assessment
usually follows. A questionnaire score is not a diagnosis: it prompts a diagnostic assessment, which
includes ruling out physical causes such as thyroid disease and arrhythmia, reviewing substance,
caffeine and medication effects, and assessing for co-occurring depression, which is common enough
that finding one is a reason to look for the other.

## First-line treatment

Two first-line options of broadly comparable effectiveness, chosen with the person rather than for
them:

- **Cognitive behavioral therapy**, delivered individually, in a group, or through a guided digital
  program, with the largest evidence base of the psychological therapies.
- **Pharmacotherapy** with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor or a serotonin-noradrenaline
  reuptake inhibitor.

Combining the two is usual for more severe or non-responding presentations. Availability, waiting
times and preference legitimately drive the choice, since a treatment that starts is better than a
better treatment that does not.

## Timing of review

Response is reviewed at four to six weeks after medication starts, with the caveat that anxiety
symptoms can transiently worsen in the first days — a predictable effect worth warning about in
advance, because it is a common reason for stopping early. Eight to twelve weeks at an adequate dose
precedes any conclusion that an agent has failed. Where a first agent fails, switching within or
between classes comes before adding further agents.

## Duration and stopping

Where treatment is effective, it continues for six to twelve months before a gradual taper is
considered, because early discontinuation is associated with relapse. Tapering is gradual and
monitored rather than abrupt, and discontinuation symptoms are distinguished from a return of the
underlying disorder, which they closely resemble and which they precede in time.

## Benzodiazepines

Benzodiazepines are not first-line for generalized anxiety disorder and are inappropriate for
long-term use: tolerance, dependence, cognitive effects, falls in older adults, and no effect on the
underlying disorder. Where used at all, the role is short and bounded.

## What is outside this note

Doses and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this system. Thoughts of
self-harm or suicide are an urgent situation covered by the emergency guidance elsewhere in this
corpus, not by routine review.

[15] (condition-coronary-artery-disease)
## What it is

Coronary artery disease is the build-up of atherosclerotic plaque in the arteries supplying the
heart muscle. Plaque develops over decades, beginning with injury to the artery lining and the
accumulation of cholesterol-rich material beneath it. Two distinct mechanisms produce symptoms, and
confusing them is the source of most misunderstanding about the condition:

- **Gradual narrowing** limits blood flow when demand rises, producing predictable exertional chest
  discomfort — stable angina.
- **Plaque rupture** exposes material that triggers clot formation, which can occlude the artery
  abruptly. This produces an acute coronary syndrome, and it can happen at a plaque that was never
  narrow enough to cause symptoms. That is why a normal stress test in the past does not mean a
  heart attack cannot happen now.

## How it is usually recognized

Stable angina is classically a pressure, tightness or heaviness in the chest, brought on by exertion
or emotional stress, relieved within minutes by rest, and sometimes spreading to the arm, neck, jaw
or back. It is a reproducible pattern — the same amount of effort brings it on.

Presentations are frequently not classical. Breathlessness on exertion without chest discomfort,
unusual fatigue, nausea, or discomfort felt mainly in the jaw, back or upper abdomen are all
recognized presentations, and are relatively more common in women, older people, and people with
diabetes, in whom nerve damage can blunt the pain. The consequence is delayed presentation, and the
delay is what causes the harm.

## What contributes to it

Smoking, high blood pressure, raised LDL cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, a diet
high in saturated fat and low in vegetables and fiber, chronic kidney disease, inflammatory
conditions, and a family history of premature coronary disease. Age and male sex raise baseline risk
and cannot be modified; the rest of the list can be, which is what makes the risk estimate
actionable rather than merely descriptive.

## Why it is treated

Untreated coronary disease leads to myocardial infarction, heart failure from damaged muscle,
arrhythmia, and death. Secondary prevention after a diagnosis substantially reduces the rate of
further events, and the effect comes from the package rather than from any single element — covered
by the secondary-prevention guideline note in this corpus.

## How it is generally managed

Risk-factor treatment, antiplatelet and lipid-lowering therapy, agents to control angina symptoms,
cardiac rehabilitation, and revascularization — stenting or bypass surgery — where symptoms persist
despite medical therapy or where the pattern of disease indicates it. Revascularization relieves
symptoms reliably; it does not remove the need for the medical therapy underneath.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Chest discomfort at rest, discomfort lasting more than a few minutes, discomfort with breathlessness,
sweating, nausea or light-headedness, or angina that is newly more frequent or more easily provoked
— these are emergencies and need immediate medical attention rather than a routine appointment.
Waiting to see whether it settles is the most common and most costly error. The emergency-symptom
notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[16] (lifestyle-gerd-diet)
## The two dietary changes with the best support

Meal size and meal timing carry more weight than food choice, and they are the two most people have
not tried systematically.

A large meal distends the stomach and raises the pressure working against the valve at the top of
it, so the same food divided into smaller portions produces fewer symptoms than it does in one
sitting. Timing matters because lying down removes gravity from the equation: a stomach that is
still full when someone becomes horizontal has nothing holding its contents down. Leaving a gap of
several hours between the last meal and lying down is the change most often described, and for
people whose symptoms are mainly nocturnal it tends to do more than any food substitution.

Weight reduction where body weight is above the healthy range has the strongest supporting evidence
of any lifestyle measure here; the reflux guideline note in this corpus places it among the
recommendations.

## The trigger-food list, and why blanket avoidance is not advised

Coffee, chocolate, alcohol, citrus, tomato, mint, fatty and fried food, spicy food and carbonated
drinks appear on almost every list handed to someone with reflux. The evidence that removing all of
them helps is weak, and the cost is real: a diet stripped of most of what a person enjoys is hard to
sustain and tends to be abandoned wholesale, including the parts that were working.

The approach usually described instead is individual identification. Symptoms are recorded alongside
what was eaten for a couple of weeks, the foods that repeatedly precede symptoms are removed, and
the rest stay. Most people find they have two or three genuine triggers rather than twenty, and the
list is not the same from person to person.

Two items have a mechanism behind them that generalizes a little better than the rest. Alcohol
relaxes the valve and increases acid exposure, and carbonated drinks add gas that distends the
stomach directly.

## Fat, and what it actually does

Fatty meals slow stomach emptying, which extends the window during which reflux can occur. This is
part of why a heavy late dinner is a reliable provoker where the same food at midday is not — the
effect is as much about how long the meal stays in the stomach as about the fat itself.

## What is not established

Alkaline water, apple cider vinegar, aloe preparations and similar remedies do not have evidence
comparable to the measures above. Milk gives brief relief and is followed by a rebound in many
people. Chewing gum after a meal increases saliva and has some supporting evidence, which puts it
among the more plausible of the folk measures rather than among the established ones.

Symptoms that persist despite these changes, or that come with difficulty swallowing, unintended
weight loss, vomiting or bleeding, are a reason for assessment rather than further dietary
adjustment.

[17] (condition-insomnia)
## What it is

Insomnia is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking earlier than intended, despite
adequate opportunity to sleep, together with daytime consequences. Both halves are required. Sleeping
six hours and functioning well is not insomnia; sleeping six hours and being impaired by it may be.
The condition is defined by the mismatch between sleep obtained and sleep needed, not by a clock
value.

Short-term insomnia lasting days to weeks, usually with an identifiable precipitant, is common and
often self-limiting. Chronic insomnia disorder — at least three nights per week for at least three
months — is a distinct condition that persists after the original precipitant has resolved.

## Why it persists after the trigger goes

This is the part that explains the treatment. An episode is typically precipitated by stress,
illness or a schedule change. What perpetuates it are the responses: going to bed earlier to
"catch up", staying in bed awake, daytime napping, and increasing effort to fall asleep. Time in bed
rises while sleep does not, so the bed becomes associated with wakefulness, and the effort itself
increases arousal. The condition then maintains itself independently of what started it — which is
why treatment targets those perpetuating behaviors rather than the original stressor.

## How it is usually recognized

The account of the sleep pattern, supported by a sleep diary kept over one to two weeks. Diaries
matter because recall systematically overestimates how long it took to fall asleep and underestimates
total sleep — the periods of sleep between awakenings are not remembered.

## What else presents as insomnia

Obstructive sleep apnea (apnoea), restless legs syndrome, circadian rhythm disorders including shift
work and delayed sleep phase, chronic pain, depression, anxiety, and the effects of caffeine,
alcohol, nicotine, stimulants and some prescribed medications. Screening for these is part of the
assessment rather than a step taken only when treatment fails, because treating the wrong condition
is the most common reason for non-response. Alcohol deserves specific mention: it shortens the time
to fall asleep and fragments the second half of the night, so it is frequently reported as a remedy
by someone whose sleep it is degrading.

## Why it is treated

Chronic insomnia is associated with impaired daytime function, reduced quality of life, and
increased risk of depression, and it complicates the management of coexisting physical illness. It
also responds durably to non-drug treatment, which makes long-term reliance on hypnotics avoidable
for most people.

## How it is generally managed

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is first-line, with medication second-line and
time-limited. The components, the evidence, and the specific point that sleep hygiene advice alone
is not effective treatment are covered by the insomnia guideline note in this corpus.

## When further assessment is advised

Loud snoring with witnessed pauses in breathing, excessive daytime sleepiness, falling asleep while
driving, acting out dreams, or sleep disturbance alongside low mood and hopelessness all warrant
assessment beyond insomnia treatment.

[18] (condition-gerd)
## What it is

Gastroesophageal reflux disease — gastro-oesophageal in British spelling, and abbreviated GERD or
GORD accordingly — is the condition in which stomach contents move back into the esophagus often
enough, or with enough consequence, to cause troublesome symptoms or damage to the esophageal
lining. Some reflux is normal and happens in everyone; what makes it a disease is the symptom burden
or the injury, not the presence of reflux itself.

The usual mechanism is transient relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, the ring of muscle at
the junction between esophagus (oesophagus) and stomach, sometimes with a hiatus hernia that
displaces the junction and weakens the barrier further.

## How it is usually recognized

The typical symptoms are heartburn — a burning discomfort rising behind the breastbone — and
regurgitation of acid or food into the throat, often worse after meals, on bending forward, and when
lying down. The pattern, particularly its relation to meals and position, is more informative than
the severity.

Less typical presentations include chronic cough, hoarseness, throat clearing, a sensation of a lump
in the throat, dental erosion, and non-cardiac chest pain. These are considerably less specific:
many people with them turn out to have another explanation, which is why attributing them to reflux
without considering alternatives is unreliable and why they respond less predictably to acid
suppression.

## What contributes to it

Excess body weight, particularly abdominal; hiatus hernia; pregnancy; smoking; large or late meals;
and alcohol. Several medications can worsen it, including calcium-channel blockers, nitrates and
others that relax the lower esophageal sphincter. Individual food triggers vary and are far less
consistent between people than is usually assumed, which is the argument for identifying a person's
own triggers rather than applying a standard list.

## Why it is treated

Beyond symptom burden, which can be substantial and affects sleep and quality of life, persistent
acid exposure can cause esophagitis, stricture with narrowing and difficulty swallowing, and
Barrett's esophagus — a change in the lining that carries a small increased risk of esophageal
cancer. That risk is the reason long-standing or alarm-feature-associated reflux is investigated
rather than treated indefinitely on assumption.

## How it is generally managed

Weight management where relevant, meal timing and portion changes, elevating the head of the bed for
night-time symptoms, smoking cessation, and acid-suppressing treatment with a defined trial period
and reassessment rather than open-ended use. Alarm features, endoscopy indications and the step-down
approach are covered by the GERD guideline note in this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Chest discomfort must not be assumed to be reflux. Discomfort brought on by exertion, or coming with
breathlessness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to the arm, neck or jaw, or occurring in someone
with cardiovascular risk factors, requires emergency assessment for a cardiac cause first —
heartburn and cardiac pain are not reliably distinguishable by how they feel. Difficulty swallowing,
painful swallowing, vomiting blood, black tarry stools, or unintentional weight loss also require
prompt medical assessment. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[19] (coding-gerd-k21)
## The category

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (gastro-oesophageal in British spelling) is K21 in ICD-10-CM, in the
esophagus, stomach and duodenum block of Chapter 11. The category is short, and the single
distinction it draws is whether esophagitis is present.

Reflux disease with esophagitis is one branch, further divided by whether bleeding is documented;
reflux disease without esophagitis is the other. Both are complete codes, and the second is the one
used for the large majority of records, because the distinction rests on an endoscopic finding that
most records do not contain.

## What decides the branch

Esophagitis is a mucosal finding, not a symptom severity. The classification takes it from
documentation of the finding, and does not permit it to be inferred from how bad the heartburn is,
from the treatment prescribed, or from the duration of the condition. A record describing severe
reflux symptoms with no endoscopy is coded to the without-esophagitis branch.

Bleeding, where it subdivides the esophagitis branch, likewise has to be documented rather than
assumed from an anemia elsewhere in the chart.

## Neighboring categories that are not this one

Esophagitis without reflux disease has its own category immediately before this one, and reflux
disease is not assumed from it. Barrett esophagus is a separate category further along the block,
subdivided by whether dysplasia is present and by its grade; it is reported in addition to the
reflux code rather than instead of it, because the two are different conditions and one does not
include the other.

Hiatal hernia is a hernia and is coded from the hernia block, so a record documenting both a hiatal
hernia and reflux disease carries two codes from two blocks. Esophageal stricture, ulcer and
dysmotility are likewise separate categories.

Newborn reflux is excluded from this category outright and is classified in the perinatal chapter.

## Symptoms, and when they are coded instead

Heartburn, chest discomfort of esophageal origin, regurgitation, dysphagia and nausea are symptoms.
Where reflux disease is documented, they are intrinsic to it and are not separately coded. Where it
is not — where the record says heartburn and stops — the symptom code from Chapter 18 is what the
encounter supports, and reaching for the disease code instead is the error the boundary exists to
prevent. Dysphagia is the exception worth knowing: it is not routinely part of uncomplicated reflux
disease, and where it is documented it is reported in addition.

## Codes that commonly accompany K21

Long-term drug therapy status is coded from the factors-influencing-health chapter, as is body mass
index. Tobacco and alcohol use are coded from their own chapters. Where reflux disease is documented
alongside asthma or chronic cough, those are coded from the respiratory chapter and neither implies
the other.

[20] (coding-type-2-diabetes-e11)
## The category

Type 2 diabetes mellitus is E11 in ICD-10-CM, in Chapter 4, endocrine, nutritional and metabolic
diseases. The chapter separates diabetes by cause rather than by treatment: diabetes due to an
underlying condition, drug- or chemical-induced diabetes, type 1, type 2, and other specified
diabetes each have their own three-character category. Where the record says only "diabetes
mellitus" with no type stated, the classification defaults to type 2.

That default is worth knowing in both directions. It means an unqualified diagnosis does not stall
the coding, and it means a record that meant type 1 but did not say so is classified as the wrong
disease. Insulin use does not change the category — a person with type 2 diabetes taking insulin is
still coded to E11, with long-term insulin use recorded as a separate status code.

## E11 is a family, not a single code

E11 is never used at three characters. The fourth and subsequent characters name the complication,
which is what makes this one of the larger combination-code families in the classification. The
subcategories cover kidney involvement, retinal involvement subdivided by severity and by whether
macular edema is present, neuropathy including the polyneuropathy and autonomic forms, circulatory
involvement of the limbs with or without gangrene, skin, oral and joint complications, and the
metabolic states of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia, the latter distinguished by whether coma
occurred. Diabetes documented without complications has its own code ending in the digit 9, which is
the source of the frequently quoted E11.9.

Several of these still require a second code. Diabetic chronic kidney disease is paired with a code
for the stage of kidney disease; a diabetic foot ulcer is paired with a code giving its site and
depth. The combination code names the association, and the additional code carries the detail.

## The "with" convention

The reason this family works the way it does is a general convention rather than a diabetes rule.
Where the alphabetic index links two conditions with the word "with", the classification reads that
as "associated with" or "due to" and presumes the relationship, without requiring the record to
state it explicitly. A record listing type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease is therefore coded
as diabetic kidney disease unless the documentation says the two are unrelated.

This presumption is the single most consequential detail in coding diabetes, and it is also the one
most often applied too enthusiastically. It holds only for the pairings the index actually lists,
and a condition merely appearing on the same problem list is not automatically a diabetic
complication.

## Codes that commonly accompany E11

Long-term use of insulin, of injectable non-insulin agents, and of oral glucose-lowering drugs each
have distinct status codes, and body mass index has its own set. Screening for diabetes in someone
without symptoms is an encounter code rather than a diagnosis. Prediabetes and abnormal glucose
findings that fall short of a diabetes diagnosis are not coded to E11 at all; they sit with the
abnormal laboratory findings in the symptoms and abnormal findings chapter.

[21] (coding-icd10-cm-versus-who-icd10)
## Two things share one name

ICD-10 is the World Health Organization's international classification of diseases, used across
countries chiefly for mortality and morbidity statistics. ICD-10-CM is the United States clinical
modification of it, developed and maintained by the National Center for Health Statistics, and it is
what US diagnosis coding actually uses.

The relationship is one of extension rather than translation. The clinical modification keeps the
chapter structure, the letter ranges and most of the three-character categories of the international
version, and then subdivides them much further. A question answered from a WHO ICD-10 reference can
therefore be right about the chapter and wrong about the code.

## What the modification adds

Three additions account for most of the difference in size.

**Laterality.** A large number of categories distinguish right, left, bilateral and unspecified,
which the international version generally does not. This alone multiplies the site-specific
categories in the musculoskeletal and injury chapters.

**Seventh characters.** Injuries, and some obstetric and other categories, carry a character
recording the episode of care rather than anything about the condition — initial encounter,
subsequent encounter, sequela — so one injury generates several valid codes across an episode.

**Greater clinical detail.** Severity, acuteness, laterality and complication status are pushed into
the code itself rather than left to a separate field, and combination codes fold pairs of conditions
together. The diabetes and asthma categories are the clearest examples.

## Procedures are a separate system

The clinical modification covers diagnoses only. Inpatient hospital procedures are coded in
ICD-10-PCS, a structurally unrelated system maintained by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid
Services in which every code is seven characters and each position carries a fixed meaning. Neither
the WHO classification nor the diagnosis modification contains it, and outpatient procedure coding
in the US uses a different system again.

## Updates, and what that means for a stored answer

The clinical modification is revised on an annual cycle, with changes taking effect at the start of
the federal fiscal year on October 1. Categories are added, subdivided and occasionally retired, so
a code that was valid in one year may not be valid in another. Any stored or cached code answer
carries an implicit date, and a lookup against a current file is the only thing that settles
whether a code is still valid.

## Other national modifications, and ICD-11

Several other countries maintain their own clinical modifications of the same international
classification, with their own subdivisions, so "the ICD-10 code" is an underspecified phrase
without a country attached. The World Health Organization has since released ICD-11, which is a
different classification with a different structure rather than a further revision of this one; the
United States has not adopted it for diagnosis coding, and codes do not carry across between them.

[22] (coding-icd10-chapter-11-digestive)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 11 of ICD-10-CM covers K00 through K95 and follows the digestive tract in anatomical order
from the mouth to the anus, then adds the organs that drain into it. Every code begins with the
letter K.

## The blocks, in order

Diseases of the oral cavity and salivary glands open the chapter at K00 to K14, covering the teeth
and their supporting structures, the jaws, the salivary glands, the tongue and the lips.

Diseases of the esophagus (oesophagus), stomach and duodenum occupy K20 to K31. Esophagitis comes
first, then gastroesophageal reflux disease, then the Barrett and other esophageal categories,
followed by the peptic ulcer categories divided by site — gastric, duodenal, peptic unspecified and
gastrojejunal — and then gastritis, duodenitis and the functional stomach disorders.

Diseases of the appendix follow at K35 to K38 and hernia at K40 to K46, where the block is organized
first by site and then by whether obstruction or gangrene is present.

Noninfective enteritis and colitis occupy K50 to K52, which is where Crohn disease and ulcerative
colitis are classified. Other diseases of the intestines follow at K55 to K64: vascular disorders of
the bowel, ileus and obstruction, diverticular disease, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, anal
and rectal conditions, and the categories for gastrointestinal bleeding when no more specific source
is documented. Diseases of the peritoneum and retroperitoneum sit at K65 to K68.

Diseases of the liver occupy K70 to K77, ordered from alcoholic and toxic liver disease through
hepatic failure, chronic hepatitis and fibrosis to cirrhosis. Disorders of the gallbladder, biliary
tract and pancreas follow at K80 to K87, and the chapter closes at K90 to K95 with malabsorption,
postprocedural digestive disorders and the residual categories.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Infectious gastroenteritis and colitis are classified in the infectious-disease chapter, not here,
and the distinction turns on whether an organism is documented. Viral hepatitis is likewise an
infection rather than a liver disease for coding purposes, though its chronic sequelae may be coded
from this chapter in addition. Neoplasms of any digestive organ are neoplasms. Hernia complicating
pregnancy and digestive disorders arising in pregnancy belong to the obstetric chapter.

change in bowel habit and an abnormal liver function test with no diagnosis recorded are classified
in Chapter 18. A few bleeding presentations are exceptions: hematemesis, melena and unspecified
gastrointestinal hemorrhage have categories inside this chapter rather than with the symptoms.

reported alongside the liver categories here. Adverse effects of drugs come from the injury and

screening encounters such as colorectal cancer screening all come from the factors-influencing-health

## The category and its two axes

Heart failure is I50 in ICD-10-CM, at the end of the "other forms of heart disease" block in Chapter
9. Like asthma, it is built from two axes crossed with each other, and unlike asthma both of them
depend entirely on what the record says.

The first axis is mechanism: systolic, diastolic, or combined systolic and diastolic. The second is
acuity: acute, chronic, or acute on chronic, with an unspecified option at each level. The category
also holds left ventricular failure, a set of other specified forms including right heart failure,
biventricular failure, high-output failure and end-stage heart failure, and an unspecified code for
heart failure documented with neither axis.

## The vocabulary problem

Records increasingly describe heart failure by ejection fraction rather than by mechanism — reduced,
preserved, mildly reduced, improved. The classification's terms are the older ones, and the mapping
between the two vocabularies is what most heart-failure coding questions are really about: reduced
ejection fraction corresponds to the systolic branch and preserved ejection fraction to the
diastolic branch. Where the record gives only an ejection fraction number and no descriptive term,
the classification does not permit the mechanism to be derived from it.

"Acute on chronic" requires both to be documented. A chronic condition with a current
decompensation is not automatically coded to that branch unless the record supports both parts.

## Congestive heart failure

"Congestive" is not a fourth branch. The term is inclusive across the category rather than
descriptive of a mechanism, so congestive heart failure with no further detail is coded to the
unspecified code, and congestive heart failure documented as systolic is coded to the systolic
branch. The word does not add specificity even though it reads as though it should.

Where the record documents heart disease as hypertensive or as due to hypertension, the combination
code for hypertensive heart disease is reported first and a code from this category is added to
identify the type of heart failure. The hypertension coding note owns which combination code
applies; the point here is that the heart failure code is added rather than replaced.

failure diagnosis, are classified with the symptoms and abnormal findings in Chapter 18. Heart
failure following cardiac surgery or a procedure has its own category among the postprocedural
complications. Rheumatic heart failure is classified with the rheumatic block at the start of the
chapter.

alongside constantly. Long-term drug therapy, body mass index, and the presence of a cardiac device
are status codes from the factors-influencing-health chapter, and tobacco use or exposure is
requested by categories throughout this chapter.

question: My husband's face is drooping on one side and he can't speak properly. Is this a stroke?
answer:

[1] (red-flag-stroke-symptoms)
## Call emergency services immediately

Any sudden onset of the following is treated as a stroke until proven otherwise:

- **Face** — drooping on one side, or an uneven smile.
- **Arm** — weakness or numbness in one arm, or one arm drifting downward when both are raised.
- **Speech** — slurred speech, difficulty finding words, or difficulty understanding others.
- **Time** — note the time symptoms began, or the last time the person was known to be well, and
  call emergency services now.

Symptoms beyond the four above that carry the same urgency: sudden numbness or weakness of the leg
or of one whole side; sudden confusion; sudden loss or blurring of vision in one or both eyes;
sudden difficulty walking, dizziness, or loss of balance and coordination; and sudden severe
headache with no known cause.

## Why the time of onset matters so much

Treatments that restore blood flow to the brain — clot-dissolving drugs and mechanical clot removal
— are effective only within a limited window from symptom onset, and their benefit falls steeply
with every passing minute. The single most useful piece of information a caller can provide is when
the person was last known to be well. Where symptoms were present on waking, the relevant time is
when the person was last seen normal, not when they woke.

Brain tissue is lost continuously while an artery is blocked. This is the reason emergency services
are called rather than waiting for a routine appointment or driving to a clinic, and the reason a
stroke is treated as time-critical in the same way as a heart attack.

## Symptoms that resolve are still an emergency

Symptoms that disappear within minutes may indicate a transient ischemic attack. The event itself
has ended, but the risk of a full stroke in the following days is substantially raised, and it is
highest in the first 48 hours. Resolution is not reassurance and does not convert this into a
routine appointment — urgent assessment is what reduces the subsequent risk.

## What not to do

Do not give food, drink, or medication, including aspirin, to someone with suspected stroke:
swallowing may be impaired, and the type of stroke — clot or bleed — determines the treatment and
cannot be established without imaging. Do not wait to see whether symptoms improve. Do not let the
person drive.

## While waiting

Keep the person resting, comfortable and observed, note the time of onset and what was observed, and
gather a list of their medications if it can be done without leaving them unattended. Anticoagulant
use is particularly important for the receiving team to know.

This system does not diagnose. Any presentation matching this note is escalated, and no answer it
produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

[2] (red-flag-severe-breathing-difficulty)
## Call emergency services immediately

- Breathlessness at rest, or coming on suddenly.
- Inability to speak in full sentences, or having to pause for breath between words.
- Blue or gray discoloration of the lips, tongue, face or fingertips.
- Drowsiness, confusion, agitation or exhaustion in someone struggling to breathe.
- Gasping, or noisy breathing with a high-pitched sound on breathing in.
- Chest pain with breathlessness.
- In an asthma attack: no improvement after reliever treatment, or symptoms returning within a few
  hours, or a chest that has gone quiet.
- In a child: fast breathing, the skin sucking in between or under the ribs, grunting, flaring of
  the nostrils, or a child too breathless to feed or talk.

## The signs that are most often misread

**Drowsiness in someone working hard to breathe is a late and serious sign, not a sign of settling.**
It can reflect rising carbon dioxide or exhaustion of the muscles of breathing, and it frequently
precedes respiratory arrest. Calm in this setting is not improvement.

**A quiet chest during a severe asthma attack is dangerous, not reassuring.** Wheeze is produced by
air moving through narrowed airways; when too little air moves to make the sound, the obstruction
has worsened rather than resolved.

**Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude a serious problem.** Saturation can be maintained until
compensation fails, particularly in younger people, and a home device gives an incomplete picture at
best. Work of breathing and the ability to speak are more informative than a number from a
fingertip device.

## Why the threshold is set low

The causes of acute severe breathlessness include asthma attack, COPD exacerbation, pneumonia,
pulmonary embolism, heart failure with fluid in the lungs, anaphylaxis, pneumothorax, and airway
obstruction. Several are immediately life-threatening, several are treatable if reached in time, and
they are not reliably distinguishable without assessment. That combination is what makes escalation
on the symptom rather than the suspected cause the correct policy.

## While waiting

Keep the person sitting upright, which is usually the easiest position; loosen tight clothing; keep
the room calm, since anxiety increases the work of breathing. Someone with prescribed reliever
inhaler or emergency medication uses it per their own action plan while help is on the way. If
anaphylaxis is possible, the anaphylaxis note in this corpus takes precedence and adrenaline comes
first. Note when the breathlessness began and what preceded it, which helps the receiving team
narrow the cause quickly.
