[1] (red-flag-acute-abdominal-pain)
## Call emergency services immediately

- Sudden, severe abdominal pain, particularly if it came on within minutes.
- Abdominal pain with a rigid, board-like or exquisitely tender abdomen.
- Abdominal pain with fever, a fast heart rate, dizziness, fainting, or confusion.
- Abdominal pain with vomiting blood, or black tarry stools.
- Abdominal pain with an inability to pass stool or gas, and a distended abdomen.
- Severe pain in the abdomen or back in someone over 60, particularly with fainting or a pulsating
  abdominal sensation.
- Abdominal or pelvic pain in pregnancy, or in anyone who could be pregnant, with bleeding,
  faintness or shoulder-tip pain.
- Severe pain in the testicle or scrotum of sudden onset, with or without abdominal pain.

## Seek same-day medical assessment

Persistent pain lasting more than a few hours that is worsening, pain that localizes to the right
lower abdomen, pain with persistent vomiting, pain with jaundice or dark urine, and new severe pain
in anyone immunosuppressed, elderly, or recently operated on.

## Why some of these are time-critical

Several abdominal emergencies have a window measured in hours. A twisted testicle loses viability
within about six hours, and the presentation is sudden severe pain — sometimes referred to the
abdomen, which is why it belongs on an abdominal list. An ectopic pregnancy can rupture and bleed
internally, and shoulder-tip pain reflects blood irritating the diaphragm. A leaking abdominal
aortic aneurysm presents as sudden severe abdominal or back pain, often with collapse. A perforated
organ produces the rigid abdomen. Bowel that has lost its blood supply causes pain strikingly out of
proportion to what examination finds — a pattern worth knowing precisely because it invites
under-reaction.

## What not to do

Do not take painkillers, particularly non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, in the hope of settling
severe undiagnosed abdominal pain — they can worsen bleeding and ulceration. Do not eat or drink
while waiting, in case surgery is needed. Do not apply heat to an acutely painful abdomen. Do not
treat presumed constipation with laxatives when the abdomen is distended and nothing is passing,
since obstruction is the concern.

## Groups where the signs are blunted

Older adults, people on corticosteroids or immunosuppressants, people with diabetes, and people in
late pregnancy can have serious intra-abdominal disease with unimpressive examination findings and
little fever. The threshold for assessment in these groups is lower, and a reassuring examination
carries less weight than it otherwise would.

This system does not diagnose. Any presentation matching this note is escalated, and no answer it
produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

[2] (red-flag-stroke-symptoms)
## Call emergency services immediately

Any sudden onset of the following is treated as a stroke until proven otherwise:

- **Face** — drooping on one side, or an uneven smile.
- **Arm** — weakness or numbness in one arm, or one arm drifting downward when both are raised.
- **Speech** — slurred speech, difficulty finding words, or difficulty understanding others.
- **Time** — note the time symptoms began, or the last time the person was known to be well, and
  call emergency services now.

Symptoms beyond the four above that carry the same urgency: sudden numbness or weakness of the leg
or of one whole side; sudden confusion; sudden loss or blurring of vision in one or both eyes;
sudden difficulty walking, dizziness, or loss of balance and coordination; and sudden severe
headache with no known cause.

## Why the time of onset matters so much

Treatments that restore blood flow to the brain — clot-dissolving drugs and mechanical clot removal
— are effective only within a limited window from symptom onset, and their benefit falls steeply
with every passing minute. The single most useful piece of information a caller can provide is when
the person was last known to be well. Where symptoms were present on waking, the relevant time is
when the person was last seen normal, not when they woke.

Brain tissue is lost continuously while an artery is blocked. This is the reason emergency services
are called rather than waiting for a routine appointment or driving to a clinic, and the reason a
stroke is treated as time-critical in the same way as a heart attack.

## Symptoms that resolve are still an emergency

Symptoms that disappear within minutes may indicate a transient ischemic attack. The event itself
has ended, but the risk of a full stroke in the following days is substantially raised, and it is
highest in the first 48 hours. Resolution is not reassurance and does not convert this into a
routine appointment — urgent assessment is what reduces the subsequent risk.

## What not to do

Do not give food, drink, or medication, including aspirin, to someone with suspected stroke:
swallowing may be impaired, and the type of stroke — clot or bleed — determines the treatment and
cannot be established without imaging. Do not wait to see whether symptoms improve. Do not let the
person drive.

## While waiting

Keep the person resting, comfortable and observed, note the time of onset and what was observed, and
gather a list of their medications if it can be done without leaving them unattended. Anticoagulant
use is particularly important for the receiving team to know.

This system does not diagnose. Any presentation matching this note is escalated, and no answer it
produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

[3] (red-flag-meningitis-signs)
## Call emergency services immediately

- Fever with a severe headache and a stiff neck.
- A rash of small red or purple spots or bruises **that does not fade when pressed** — tested by
  rolling a clear glass over it.
- Fever with confusion, drowsiness, difficulty waking, or seizure.
- Severe dislike of bright light, alongside headache and fever.
- Cold hands and feet with a fever, mottled skin, and severe limb or joint pain.
- Rapid deterioration in someone who seemed to have an ordinary febrile illness.

In babies and young children: a high-pitched or moaning cry, irritability when handled, refusing
feeds, a bulging soft spot on the head, floppiness or stiffness, unusual drowsiness, and pale,
blotchy or mottled skin.

## Why the classic triad is not the trigger

Fever, neck stiffness and altered consciousness together are the textbook presentation, and all
three are present in only a minority of cases. Waiting for the full triad delays treatment in the
majority. The trigger for escalation is any suggestive combination, particularly in someone
deteriorating over hours.

## The rash appears late, and its absence proves nothing

The non-blanching rash of meningococcal septicemia is a well-known sign, and it is a **late** one.
Many people are seriously unwell before any rash appears, and some never develop one. Escalation on
the earlier features — fever with severe headache, cold extremities with fever, limb pain, rapid
deterioration — is what changes outcomes. Where a non-blanching rash is present, the situation is
already an emergency and every minute counts.

Cold hands and feet, severe leg pain, and abnormal skin color are recognized early features of
meningococcal disease in adolescents and young adults, frequently preceding the classic signs by
hours, and are commonly attributed to something ordinary at the time.

## Why the urgency is absolute

Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal septicemia can progress from mild symptoms to
life-threatening illness within hours, and survival and the risk of permanent harm — deafness,
limb loss, brain injury — depend directly on how quickly treatment starts.

## What not to do

Do not wait to see whether a fever settles when these features are present. Do not be reassured that
the person has been seen earlier the same day and sent home; rapid deterioration after an initial
assessment is characteristic of this illness, and returning is appropriate rather than excessive.

## Contacts

Close household and intimate contacts of a confirmed meningococcal case are usually offered
preventive antibiotics, arranged by public health services. Anyone in that position contacts health
services rather than waiting for symptoms.

This system does not diagnose. Any presentation matching this note is escalated, and no answer it
produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

[4] (red-flag-chest-pain)
## Call emergency services immediately

Chest discomfort with any of the following is treated as a possible heart attack until proven
otherwise:

- Pressure, tightness, squeezing, heaviness or burning in the center or left of the chest, lasting
  more than a few minutes, or going away and coming back.
- Discomfort spreading to one or both arms, the shoulders, neck, jaw, back, or upper abdomen.
- Chest discomfort with breathlessness, cold sweat, nausea or vomiting, light-headedness, or a sense
  of impending doom.
- Chest discomfort at rest, or brought on by less exertion than usual in someone with known angina.
- Any chest discomfort in someone with known coronary artery disease, diabetes, or several
  cardiovascular risk factors.

Emergency services are called rather than arranging transport privately. Paramedics can record an
ECG, begin treatment on the way, and route to a hospital capable of intervention. Self-transport
loses all three, and it is dangerous if the person deteriorates during the journey.

## Why the threshold is set low

Time is the determining factor in the outcome of a heart attack: heart muscle dies progressively
from the moment the artery occludes, and treatment that restores flow early preserves function that
cannot be recovered later. The most common and most costly error is waiting — to see whether it
settles, to avoid embarrassment at a false alarm, or because the discomfort is mild.

A false alarm is a good outcome. This is the clearest case in medicine where over-escalation is the
correct policy, and it is why this system escalates on the possibility rather than the probability.

## Presentations that are missed

Not all heart attacks present with severe chest pain. Breathlessness alone, unusual fatigue,
indigestion-like discomfort, nausea, or discomfort felt mainly in the jaw, back or upper abdomen are
recognized presentations, and are relatively more common in women, in older adults, and in people
with diabetes, in whom nerve damage can blunt pain. The absence of classic pain is not reassuring.

Heartburn and cardiac pain are not reliably distinguishable by how they feel, and a history of
reflux does not exclude a cardiac cause. Antacid relief does not rule it out either.

## Other emergencies presenting as chest pain

Sudden tearing chest or back pain, sudden pleuritic chest pain with breathlessness, and chest pain
with collapse can indicate aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, or another immediately
life-threatening condition. All are emergencies, and none is distinguishable from cardiac pain
without assessment.

## While waiting

Stay with the person, keep them still and seated or resting, and be ready to describe when the
symptoms started. If the person becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally, emergency
dispatchers can guide chest compressions over the phone.

This system does not diagnose. Any presentation matching this note is escalated, and no answer it
produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

[5] (red-flag-sudden-severe-headache)
## Call emergency services immediately

- A headache that comes on abruptly and reaches maximum intensity within about a minute — often
  described as the worst headache of one's life, or as being hit on the head. This is a thunderclap
  headache.
- Headache with fever and a stiff neck, or with a rash that does not fade under pressure.
- Headache with new confusion, drowsiness, seizure, weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, or
  visual loss.
- Headache after a head injury, particularly with vomiting, drowsiness or worsening over hours.
- Headache with sudden severe eye pain, a red eye, and blurred vision or halos around lights.

## Seek same-day medical assessment

- A new type of headache beginning after age 50.
- Headache that steadily worsens over days or weeks, or that is consistently worse on waking, on
  lying flat, or on coughing, straining or bending.
- New headache in someone with cancer, HIV, immunosuppression, or on anticoagulation.
- New headache in pregnancy or the postpartum period, particularly with visual changes, swelling or
  upper abdominal pain.
- Headache with scalp tenderness or jaw pain on chewing in someone over 50.

## Why thunderclap headache is treated as an emergency

The pattern is the concern, not the severity. A headache that reaches peak intensity almost
instantly can indicate bleeding around the brain from a ruptured aneurysm, and several other serious
causes present the same way. The mortality is high and depends on how quickly it is treated.

The critical point is that a thunderclap headache warrants emergency assessment **even if it then
settles completely**, including where simple painkillers appear to have relieved it. Resolution does
not exclude the diagnosis, and a warning bleed can precede a much larger one by days.

## Why the others are on the list

Fever with a stiff neck raises meningitis; a non-blanching rash raises meningococcal infection.
Headache worse on waking or on straining raises raised pressure inside the skull. Scalp tenderness
and jaw claudication over 50 raise giant cell arteritis, which can cause irreversible blindness
within days and is one of the few headache causes where hours of delay change the outcome
permanently. Eye pain with a red eye and halos raises acute angle-closure glaucoma, also
sight-threatening.

## What this note is not for

Most headaches are not dangerous. Migraine and tension-type headache are common, recurrent, and
recognizable by pattern, and they are covered by the migraine notes in this corpus. The purpose here
is to identify the minority of presentations where the pattern itself — sudden onset, new type,
progressive course, or accompanying neurological or systemic features — is the warning, independent
of how severe the pain feels.

This system does not diagnose. Any presentation matching this note is escalated, and no answer it
produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

[6] (condition-upper-respiratory-infection)
## What it is

An upper respiratory infection is a viral infection of the nose, sinuses, throat and upper airway.
Rhinoviruses cause the largest share; coronaviruses, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza,
adenovirus and others account for the rest. It is self-limiting in the great majority of otherwise
healthy people.

The distinction from influenza is clinically useful. A cold begins gradually, is dominated by nasal
symptoms and sore throat, and rarely produces high fever or prostration in adults. Influenza
typically begins abruptly with fever, muscle aches and marked malaise, with respiratory symptoms
following. The distinction is not reliable enough to be certain in an individual, but it usefully
shifts the probability.

## How it is usually recognized

Nasal congestion and discharge, sneezing, sore throat, cough, mild headache and malaise, sometimes a
low-grade fever. Symptoms typically peak at two to three days and resolve over seven to ten days.
Cough frequently outlasts everything else, persisting two to three weeks, which is normal and not by
itself evidence of a bacterial infection or of treatment failure.

Discharge changing from clear to yellow or green is part of the normal course, reflecting immune
cells rather than bacterial infection. This is the single most common reason people seek antibiotics
for a cold, and it is not an indication for them.

## What contributes to it

Exposure to infected people, which is why incidence rises with young children in the household and
in the colder months when people are indoors. Transmission is by respiratory droplets and by
contaminated hands and surfaces reaching the eyes or nose. Hand hygiene reduces transmission
measurably; the belief that cold exposure itself causes colds does not survive examination.

## How it is generally managed

Supportive care: rest, fluids, and symptomatic relief. Antibiotics have no effect on viral infection
and carry real harms — adverse effects, disruption of normal flora, and antimicrobial resistance —
which is why antibiotic stewardship for these presentations is an explicit guideline topic rather
than a matter of preference. Over-the-counter symptomatic treatments have modest effects on symptoms
and none on duration, and several are not appropriate for young children.

## When further assessment is advised

Symptoms worsening after an initial improvement, fever returning after it had settled, symptoms
persisting beyond ten days without improvement, severe facial pain or one-sided facial swelling,
severe sore throat with difficulty swallowing or drooling, or breathlessness — these suggest a
complication such as bacterial sinusitis, pneumonia, or a throat infection needing assessment.

People at higher risk of complications — infants, older adults, pregnancy, and anyone with chronic
lung, heart, kidney or liver disease, diabetes, or a weakened immune system — warrant earlier
assessment than an otherwise healthy adult.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Difficulty breathing, chest pain, a stiff neck with severe headache, confusion, persistent vomiting
preventing fluid intake, or signs of dehydration require urgent assessment. The emergency-symptom
notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[7] (condition-urinary-tract-infection)
## What it is

A urinary tract infection is bacterial infection of the urinary system. Most involve the bladder and
urethra — a lower tract infection, or cystitis. Infection reaching the kidney is pyelonephritis, an
upper tract infection, and it is a materially different and more serious illness rather than a worse
version of the same one. *Escherichia coli* causes the large majority.

The distinction that drives management is between **uncomplicated** infection — in a non-pregnant
adult with a normal urinary tract and normal immune function — and **complicated** infection, which
covers infection in pregnancy, in men, in people with structural or functional urinary abnormality,
catheters, kidney stones, diabetes with poor control, or immunosuppression. The same organism in the
same place is treated differently depending on which category applies.

## How it is usually recognized

Lower tract infection: burning or pain on urination, urinary frequency and urgency, passing small
volumes, lower abdominal discomfort, and cloudy or strong-smelling urine. Blood in the urine occurs
and is not by itself a sign of something worse in this context, though it warrants follow-up to
confirm resolution.

Upper tract infection adds fever, chills, flank or back pain, nausea and vomiting, and a general
sense of being unwell. Fever and flank pain are the features that move the presentation out of the
routine category.

Presentation is frequently atypical in older adults, where confusion, falls or functional decline
may dominate. This is genuinely difficult territory: asymptomatic bacteria in the urine are common
in older adults and generally not treated, so a positive urine test in a confused older person is
not on its own a diagnosis, and treating it as one both misses the real cause and contributes to
resistance.

## What contributes to it

Female anatomy, with a shorter urethra; sexual activity; certain contraceptives including
spermicides and diaphragms; post-menopausal changes in vaginal flora; incomplete bladder emptying;
urinary catheters; kidney stones; diabetes; and previous infections. In men, infections are less
common and more often associated with prostatic enlargement or another structural factor, which is
why they are treated as complicated by default.

## How it is generally managed

Short-course antibiotic treatment for uncomplicated lower tract infection, guided by local
resistance patterns, with urine culture reserved for cases where the diagnosis is uncertain, the
infection is complicated or recurrent, or the first treatment has failed. Fluids and symptomatic
relief support the treatment without replacing it. Antibiotic choice, culture indications and
recurrence prevention are covered by the urinary tract infection guideline note in this corpus.
Doses are outside the scope of this system.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Fever with flank or back pain, shaking chills, vomiting preventing fluid intake, confusion,
symptoms in pregnancy, symptoms in someone with a single kidney or a transplant, or symptoms that
worsen despite 48 hours of treatment — these need prompt assessment. Fever, rapid heart rate,
low blood pressure and confusion together suggest sepsis and are an emergency; the emergency-symptom
notes in this corpus govern that situation.

[8] (condition-osteoarthritis)
## What it is

Osteoarthritis is a disorder of the whole joint — cartilage, underlying bone, ligaments, joint
lining and surrounding muscle — in which cartilage is progressively lost and the bone underneath
remodels in response. It most often affects the knees, hips, hands and spine.

The description of it as "wear and tear" is inaccurate enough to be worth correcting, because it
leads people to rest the joint. The process is an active one involving inflammation and attempted
repair, not simple mechanical erosion, and the muscle weakness that follows from reduced use makes
the joint worse rather than protecting it. That is why exercise is the first-line treatment and not
merely an adjunct.

## How it is usually recognized

Joint pain that is worse with activity and better with rest, short-lived stiffness after inactivity
— characteristically under 30 minutes in the morning, which distinguishes it from inflammatory
arthritis — reduced range of movement, a grating sensation on movement, and bony swelling. Onset is
gradual, over months to years, and usually asymmetric.

The diagnosis is generally clinical in a person over 45 with activity-related pain and no prolonged
morning stiffness. Imaging is not required to make it, and the relationship between what an X-ray
shows and what a person feels is weak in both directions — substantial radiographic change with few
symptoms, and significant pain with modest change, are both common. Imaging that is done for
reassurance frequently achieves the opposite.

## What contributes to it

Age; previous joint injury or surgery, which is the dominant factor in a young person with knee
osteoarthritis; obesity, which acts both mechanically and metabolically; occupational and sporting
loading; joint shape and alignment; muscle weakness; genetic factors; and female sex, particularly
for hand and knee disease after menopause.

## Why it is treated

Pain and reduced function affect independence, sleep, mood and cardiovascular fitness, and the
inactivity that follows compounds all of them. Treatment aims to reduce pain and maintain function,
and the condition is manageable over long periods; it does not inevitably progress to joint
replacement.

## How it is generally managed

Structured exercise — combining muscle strengthening, range of movement and aerobic activity — is
the core treatment for every affected joint, together with weight management where relevant.
Education, pacing, appropriate footwear, walking aids where useful, and heat or cold for symptom
relief support it. Pharmacologic options are adjuncts rather than the foundation, with topical
agents preferred where the joint is accessible. Joint replacement is considered where pain and
functional limitation persist despite adequate non-surgical management. The osteoarthritis guideline
note in this corpus covers the sequence and the evidence behind it.

## When further assessment is advised

A hot, swollen, acutely painful joint with fever suggests infection or crystal arthritis and needs
urgent assessment — this is not an osteoarthritis flare. Prolonged morning stiffness, multiple
symmetric small-joint involvement, or systemic symptoms suggest inflammatory arthritis instead.
Sudden joint locking or giving way, or new neurological symptoms with spinal pain, also warrant
prompt assessment.

[9] (condition-influenza)
## What it is

Influenza is a respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses, of which types A and B cause
seasonal epidemics. Influenza A is subtyped by two surface proteins, hemagglutinin and
neuraminidase — the H and N in designations such as H1N1 and H3N2. The virus changes continuously
through small mutations, which is why immunity from one season is incomplete against the next and
why the vaccine is reformulated annually rather than given once.

It is more severe than a common cold in both symptoms and consequences, and it causes substantial
seasonal hospitalization and death, concentrated in older adults, young children, pregnant people
and those with chronic conditions.

## How it is usually recognized

Abrupt onset — people can often name the hour — with fever, chills, muscle aches, headache, marked
fatigue and dry cough. Sore throat and nasal symptoms occur but are less prominent than in a cold.
Fever typically lasts three to five days; cough and fatigue commonly persist two weeks or more.
Gastrointestinal symptoms occur more often in children than adults.

Laboratory confirmation is not required to manage a typical case during a known outbreak, and is
used where the result would change management — in hospital, in high-risk people, or where an
antiviral decision or outbreak control depends on it.

## Complications

Pneumonia is the main one, either from the virus itself or from a secondary bacterial infection.
Secondary bacterial pneumonia classically appears as a deterioration after several days of
improvement, which is a pattern worth recognizing. Other complications include worsening of
underlying asthma, COPD, heart failure or diabetes, and less commonly inflammation of the heart
muscle, brain or muscle tissue. Influenza is also associated with a transient increase in the risk
of myocardial infarction and stroke in the weeks after infection.

## How it is generally managed

Supportive care for most otherwise healthy people: rest, fluids, and symptomatic relief. Antiviral
treatment is targeted rather than universal, and is most effective when started early — the timing
threshold and the groups in whom treatment is recommended are covered by the influenza guideline
note in this corpus. Antibiotics have no effect on the virus and are reserved for a bacterial
complication.

Annual vaccination is the principal preventive measure, alongside staying home while febrile, hand
hygiene and respiratory etiquette.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Difficulty breathing or breathlessness at rest, chest pain, persistent dizziness or confusion,
inability to keep fluids down, seizures, severe muscle pain or weakness, or symptoms that improve
and then return with fever and worse cough — these need urgent assessment. In children, additional
signs include fast or labored breathing, blue lips, no tears when crying, and significantly reduced
wet diapers. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[10] (condition-gerd)
## What it is

Gastroesophageal reflux disease — gastro-oesophageal in British spelling, and abbreviated GERD or
GORD accordingly — is the condition in which stomach contents move back into the esophagus often
enough, or with enough consequence, to cause troublesome symptoms or damage to the esophageal
lining. Some reflux is normal and happens in everyone; what makes it a disease is the symptom burden
or the injury, not the presence of reflux itself.

The usual mechanism is transient relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, the ring of muscle at
the junction between esophagus (oesophagus) and stomach, sometimes with a hiatus hernia that
displaces the junction and weakens the barrier further.

## How it is usually recognized

The typical symptoms are heartburn — a burning discomfort rising behind the breastbone — and
regurgitation of acid or food into the throat, often worse after meals, on bending forward, and when
lying down. The pattern, particularly its relation to meals and position, is more informative than
the severity.

Less typical presentations include chronic cough, hoarseness, throat clearing, a sensation of a lump
in the throat, dental erosion, and non-cardiac chest pain. These are considerably less specific:
many people with them turn out to have another explanation, which is why attributing them to reflux
without considering alternatives is unreliable and why they respond less predictably to acid
suppression.

## What contributes to it

Excess body weight, particularly abdominal; hiatus hernia; pregnancy; smoking; large or late meals;
and alcohol. Several medications can worsen it, including calcium-channel blockers, nitrates and
others that relax the lower esophageal sphincter. Individual food triggers vary and are far less
consistent between people than is usually assumed, which is the argument for identifying a person's
own triggers rather than applying a standard list.

## Why it is treated

Beyond symptom burden, which can be substantial and affects sleep and quality of life, persistent
acid exposure can cause esophagitis, stricture with narrowing and difficulty swallowing, and
Barrett's esophagus — a change in the lining that carries a small increased risk of esophageal
cancer. That risk is the reason long-standing or alarm-feature-associated reflux is investigated
rather than treated indefinitely on assumption.

## How it is generally managed

Weight management where relevant, meal timing and portion changes, elevating the head of the bed for
night-time symptoms, smoking cessation, and acid-suppressing treatment with a defined trial period
and reassessment rather than open-ended use. Alarm features, endoscopy indications and the step-down
approach are covered by the GERD guideline note in this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Chest discomfort must not be assumed to be reflux. Discomfort brought on by exertion, or coming with
breathlessness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to the arm, neck or jaw, or occurring in someone
with cardiovascular risk factors, requires emergency assessment for a cardiac cause first —
heartburn and cardiac pain are not reliably distinguishable by how they feel. Difficulty swallowing,
painful swallowing, vomiting blood, black tarry stools, or unintentional weight loss also require
prompt medical assessment. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

question: I've been meaning to ask about switching my blood pressure tablets. Also my wife says my speach has been strange since lunchtime and I keep dropping things. And can I still drink coffee on them?

[1] (red-flag-stroke-symptoms)
## Call emergency services immediately

Any sudden onset of the following is treated as a stroke until proven otherwise:

- **Face** — drooping on one side, or an uneven smile.
- **Arm** — weakness or numbness in one arm, or one arm drifting downward when both are raised.
- **Speech** — slurred speech, difficulty finding words, or difficulty understanding others.
- **Time** — note the time symptoms began, or the last time the person was known to be well, and
  call emergency services now.

Symptoms beyond the four above that carry the same urgency: sudden numbness or weakness of the leg
or of one whole side; sudden confusion; sudden loss or blurring of vision in one or both eyes;
sudden difficulty walking, dizziness, or loss of balance and coordination; and sudden severe
headache with no known cause.

## Why the time of onset matters so much

Treatments that restore blood flow to the brain — clot-dissolving drugs and mechanical clot removal
— are effective only within a limited window from symptom onset, and their benefit falls steeply
with every passing minute. The single most useful piece of information a caller can provide is when
the person was last known to be well. Where symptoms were present on waking, the relevant time is
when the person was last seen normal, not when they woke.

Brain tissue is lost continuously while an artery is blocked. This is the reason emergency services
are called rather than waiting for a routine appointment or driving to a clinic, and the reason a
stroke is treated as time-critical in the same way as a heart attack.

## Symptoms that resolve are still an emergency

Symptoms that disappear within minutes may indicate a transient ischemic attack. The event itself
has ended, but the risk of a full stroke in the following days is substantially raised, and it is
highest in the first 48 hours. Resolution is not reassurance and does not convert this into a
routine appointment — urgent assessment is what reduces the subsequent risk.

## What not to do

Do not give food, drink, or medication, including aspirin, to someone with suspected stroke:
swallowing may be impaired, and the type of stroke — clot or bleed — determines the treatment and
cannot be established without imaging. Do not wait to see whether symptoms improve. Do not let the
person drive.

## While waiting

Keep the person resting, comfortable and observed, note the time of onset and what was observed, and
gather a list of their medications if it can be done without leaving them unattended. Anticoagulant
use is particularly important for the receiving team to know.

This system does not diagnose. Any presentation matching this note is escalated, and no answer it
produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

[2] (red-flag-sepsis)
## Call emergency services immediately

Sepsis is the body's dysregulated response to infection causing organ dysfunction. In someone with a
known or suspected infection, any of the following warrants emergency assessment:

- Confusion, disorientation, slurred speech, or unusual drowsiness.
- Very fast breathing, or breathlessness.
- A fast heart rate, or dizziness on standing.
- Not passing urine for many hours.
- Skin that is mottled, ashen, very pale or blue; or a rash that does not fade when pressed.
- Shivering, or feeling very cold, or a very high or very low temperature.
- Severe muscle pain, or a feeling of being more unwell than ever before.

In a child, additional signs include fast breathing, a fit or convulsion, mottled or ashen skin, a
rash that does not fade, lethargy or difficulty waking, feeling abnormally cold, not feeding, no
urine for many hours, and repeated vomiting.

## Why the phrase "just say sepsis" exists

Sepsis progresses over hours, and survival falls with every hour of delay in recognition and
treatment. Its early presentation is nonspecific and resembles a bad case of an ordinary infection,
so it is regularly missed at first contact. Guidance encourages the person or family to raise the
possibility explicitly — asking "could this be sepsis?" — because that question reliably prompts a
structured assessment, and because the family's sense that the person is unusually unwell is
diagnostically valuable and often the earliest signal available.

## Where it comes from

Any infection can cause it. Common sources are the lungs, the urinary tract, the abdomen, and skin
or wounds, including surgical wounds and intravenous lines. The original infection may be minor and
may already be treated.

## Who is at higher risk

Infants and adults over 65; pregnancy and the six weeks after; people with diabetes, chronic liver
or kidney disease, or cancer; people on chemotherapy, steroids or other immunosuppressants; people
without a functioning spleen; people with indwelling lines or catheters; and anyone with a recent
operation or invasive procedure. In these groups the threshold for escalation is lower still, and
fever may be absent.

## What not to do

Do not wait to see whether a fever settles overnight in someone with these features. Do not be
reassured by a normal temperature: a low temperature is as concerning as a high one, and older
adults may have neither. Do not delay because antibiotics have already been started — sepsis can
develop despite them, and an infection that was responding can still progress if the source has not
been controlled.

produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

[3] (coding-icd10-chapter-18-symptoms)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 18 of ICD-10-CM covers R00 through R99: symptoms, signs and abnormal clinical and laboratory
findings not elsewhere classified. Every code begins with the letter R. It is the chapter for the
state a record is in before a diagnosis exists, and almost every other chapter has a boundary with
it.

The rule that governs the whole chapter is about when *not* to use it. An R code is assigned when
the documentation records a symptom, a sign or an abnormal result and no more specific diagnosis has
been established. Once a diagnosis is documented, the diagnosis code replaces the symptom code —
with one exception, for a symptom that is not routinely associated with that diagnosis, which is
reported in addition because it carries information the diagnosis does not.

## The blocks, in order

The first blocks follow body systems. Symptoms and signs involving the circulatory and respiratory
systems open the chapter at R00 to R09 and hold some of the most-used codes in it: palpitations, an
elevated blood-pressure reading in someone with no diagnosis of hypertension, cough, breathing
abnormalities including shortness of breath, hemoptysis and chest pain. Digestive and abdominal
symptoms follow at R10 to R19 — abdominal pain by site, nausea and vomiting, heartburn, dysphagia,
flatulence, change in bowel habit and an abdominal mass.

Symptoms involving the skin sit at R20 to R23, and those involving the nervous and musculoskeletal
systems at R25 to R29, covering abnormal involuntary movements, gait and mobility abnormalities,
lack of coordination and other abnormal neurological findings. Genitourinary symptoms occupy R30 to
R39: painful urination, urinary frequency and urgency, hematuria reported as a finding, retention
and incontinence where no diagnosis is recorded.

Symptoms involving cognition, perception, emotional state and behavior follow at R40 to R46. This is
where somnolence, coma, disorientation, memory loss and an abnormal cognitive screening result are
classified, and it is also where suicidal ideation is coded. Speech and voice disturbances sit at
R47 to R49.

General symptoms and signs occupy R50 to R69 — fever, headache, malaise and fatigue, syncope,
convulsions not identified as epilepsy, dizziness, shock, enlarged lymph nodes, volume depletion,
abnormal weight loss and pain not classified elsewhere.

The chapter then turns to results without a diagnosis: abnormal blood findings at R70 to R79,
abnormal urine findings at R80 to R82, abnormal findings in other body fluids and tissues at R83 to
R89, and abnormal diagnostic imaging and function studies at R90 to R94. Elevated glucose levels
including prediabetes sit inside the blood-findings block. Abnormal tumor markers are at R97, and
R99 closes the chapter with ill-defined and unknown cause of mortality.

## Codes from other chapters that symptom questions commonly need

Every diagnostic chapter is the destination for these codes once a diagnosis exists, so the useful
direction of travel is outward: chest pain to the circulatory chapter, cough and breathlessness to
the respiratory chapter, abdominal pain to the digestive chapter, painful urination to the
genitourinary chapter, prediabetes to the endocrine chapter once diabetes is diagnosed. Encounters
for observation or examination where no condition is found are not R codes at all — they belong to
the factors-influencing-health chapter.

## Screening

The screening test is a lipid panel — total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and
triglycerides. A non-fasting sample is acceptable for initial screening in most adults; a fasting
sample is preferred where triglycerides are markedly raised, since the triglyceride value and the
calculated LDL derived from it are the parts most affected by a recent meal.

The usual screening interval is every four to six years for adults aged 20 to 75 who are at low risk
and not on lipid-lowering therapy, and shorter where risk factors are present or where risk is being
reassessed before a treatment decision.

## Risk stratification

The central move in current guidance is that the decision is driven by estimated 10-year
atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk, not by the LDL number alone. Risk is estimated from age, sex,
race, total and HDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, treatment for hypertension, diabetes and
smoking status. The four named risk categories, for adults aged 40 to 75 without established
disease, are:

- **Low** — estimated 10-year risk below 5 percent.
- **Borderline** — 5 percent to below 7.5 percent.
- **Intermediate** — 7.5 percent to below 20 percent.
- **High** — 20 percent or above.

Risk-enhancing features shift a decision within the borderline and intermediate bands rather than
replacing the estimate: family history of premature cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease,
chronic inflammatory conditions, persistently raised triglycerides, metabolic syndrome, conditions
specific to pregnancy such as pre-eclampsia, and, where the decision remains uncertain, a coronary
artery calcium score.

## Groups in which therapy is indicated

- **Established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease** — high-intensity statin therapy as
  secondary prevention.
- **LDL cholesterol at or above 190 mg/dL** — high-intensity statin therapy regardless of the
  calculated risk score, which is not designed for this group.
- **Diabetes, aged 40 to 75** — at least moderate-intensity statin therapy.
- **Intermediate risk** — moderate-intensity statin therapy after a risk discussion.
- **Borderline risk** — guidance describes a risk discussion rather than a default action, with
  therapy favored where risk-enhancing features are present and reasonably deferred where they are
  not.

## Monitoring interval

The lipid panel is repeated four to twelve weeks after starting therapy or changing intensity, which
assesses response and adherence together, then every three to twelve months once stable. Routine
liver enzyme monitoring is not part of ongoing care in the absence of symptoms; a baseline
measurement is usual.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on whether to state numeric LDL targets. United States guidance describes statin
intensity and percentage reduction from baseline; European guidance describes explicit LDL goals
that fall as risk category rises, pursued with combination therapy where a statin alone falls short. Answers should say
which framing they are using rather than blending the two, since "at goal" means different things
under each.

[5] (red-flag-severe-breathing-difficulty)
## Call emergency services immediately

- Breathlessness at rest, or coming on suddenly.
- Inability to speak in full sentences, or having to pause for breath between words.
- Blue or gray discoloration of the lips, tongue, face or fingertips.
- Drowsiness, confusion, agitation or exhaustion in someone struggling to breathe.
- Gasping, or noisy breathing with a high-pitched sound on breathing in.
- Chest pain with breathlessness.
- In an asthma attack: no improvement after reliever treatment, or symptoms returning within a few
  hours, or a chest that has gone quiet.
- In a child: fast breathing, the skin sucking in between or under the ribs, grunting, flaring of
  the nostrils, or a child too breathless to feed or talk.

## The signs that are most often misread

**Drowsiness in someone working hard to breathe is a late and serious sign, not a sign of settling.**
It can reflect rising carbon dioxide or exhaustion of the muscles of breathing, and it frequently
precedes respiratory arrest. Calm in this setting is not improvement.

**A quiet chest during a severe asthma attack is dangerous, not reassuring.** Wheeze is produced by
air moving through narrowed airways; when too little air moves to make the sound, the obstruction
has worsened rather than resolved.

**Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude a serious problem.** Saturation can be maintained until
compensation fails, particularly in younger people, and a home device gives an incomplete picture at
best. Work of breathing and the ability to speak are more informative than a number from a
fingertip device.

## Why the threshold is set low

The causes of acute severe breathlessness include asthma attack, COPD exacerbation, pneumonia,
pulmonary embolism, heart failure with fluid in the lungs, anaphylaxis, pneumothorax, and airway
obstruction. Several are immediately life-threatening, several are treatable if reached in time, and
they are not reliably distinguishable without assessment. That combination is what makes escalation
on the symptom rather than the suspected cause the correct policy.

## While waiting

Keep the person sitting upright, which is usually the easiest position; loosen tight clothing; keep
the room calm, since anxiety increases the work of breathing. Someone with prescribed reliever
inhaler or emergency medication uses it per their own action plan while help is on the way. If
anaphylaxis is possible, the anaphylaxis note in this corpus takes precedence and adrenaline comes
first. Note when the breathlessness began and what preceded it, which helps the receiving team
narrow the cause quickly.

produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

## The dietary pattern with the most evidence

The dietary approach most consistently described for blood pressure emphasizes vegetables, fruit,
whole grains, low-fat dairy, poultry, fish, beans, nuts and vegetable oils, while limiting saturated
fat, full-fat dairy, fatty meat, sweets and sugar-sweetened drinks. It is a whole pattern rather
than a single food, and the trials that established it changed everything on the plate at once —
which is why substituting one "blood pressure food" into an otherwise unchanged diet does not
reproduce the result.

The reduction seen with the pattern alone is meaningful, and combining it with sodium reduction
produces a larger effect than either alone.

## Sodium

Sodium reduction is the single most-studied dietary change for blood pressure. Commonly stated
targets are under 2,300 mg per day, with a further benefit described at 1,500 mg for many adults.
Any reduction helps: the relationship is graded, so moving from very high intake to merely high
intake is worthwhile even if a target is not reached.

The practical point that surprises people: most dietary sodium does not come from the salt shaker.
The large majority is already in packaged and restaurant food — bread, processed meat, cheese,
sauces, soups, snacks and prepared meals. Cooking at home from unprocessed ingredients does more
than removing salt from the table, and reading labels for sodium per serving is more effective than
any single substitution.

Salt substitutes containing potassium chloride are described as reducing blood pressure, but they
are not appropriate for everyone — particularly people with chronic kidney disease or on medication
that raises potassium — and are a matter for the person's own clinician.

## Potassium

Higher dietary potassium is associated with lower blood pressure, and increasing it through food —
vegetables, fruit, beans, dairy — is the described route rather than supplements. The same caution
about kidney disease and potassium-raising medication applies.

## Alcohol

Alcohol raises blood pressure in a dose-related way, and reducing intake lowers it. Commonly stated
limits are up to two drinks per day for men and one for women, with less being better. For someone
drinking well above that, reduction is one of the more reliable non-drug interventions available.

## Weight

Weight reduction lowers blood pressure roughly in proportion to the amount lost, and the effect
begins early rather than requiring a target weight to be reached. A modest, sustained reduction is
described as worthwhile in its own right.

## What is not established

Specific "superfoods", vinegar, garlic supplements and similar single-ingredient remedies do not
have evidence comparable to the whole-pattern approach. Caffeine raises blood pressure acutely but
habitual intake has little sustained effect in most people. The hypertension guideline notes in this
corpus cover thresholds, targets and when drug treatment is added.

[7] (lifestyle-insomnia-sleep)
## What this note is and is not

These are the day-to-day habits that support sleep. They are supportive measures, not a treatment
for chronic insomnia in their own right — the insomnia guideline note in this corpus covers what the
first-line treatment is and why habit change alone does not substitute for it. What follows is the
practical content of the habits themselves.

## The wake time, not the bedtime

The single most useful anchor is a consistent wake time, held seven days a week. Sleep timing is
regulated by a body clock that takes its strongest cue from morning light, and a wake time that
moves by two or three hours at weekends shifts the clock in a way that makes falling asleep on a
weeknight harder. Bedtime is allowed to vary; the wake time is the part that is held.

Going to bed earlier to compensate for a bad night generally backfires, because time in bed spent
awake is what teaches the association between bed and wakefulness.

## Light

Bright light in the first hour or two after waking advances the clock and strengthens the signal
separating day from night. Outdoor light is far stronger than indoor lighting even on an overcast
day, so a short walk in the morning does more than a lamp. In the evening the aim is the reverse:
dimmer light in the last hour or two.

Screens matter less for their light than for what is on them. A device that is emotionally
activating at midnight is a problem whatever its color temperature.

## Caffeine, alcohol and nicotine

Caffeine has a long half-life, and a meaningful fraction of an afternoon dose is still present at
bedtime. People who report that coffee does not affect them are usually reporting that it does not
stop them falling asleep, which is a different thing from it not fragmenting the night. A cut-off in
the early afternoon is the common practical approach.

Alcohol shortens the time to fall asleep and then degrades the second half of the night, producing
lighter, more broken sleep and early waking. It is the most frequently self-prescribed sleep aid and
the one most likely to entrench the problem. Nicotine is a stimulant and withdrawal across the night
contributes to early waking.

## Naps

A short early-afternoon nap is compatible with good night sleep for most people. Long or late naps
reduce the sleep pressure that has been building since waking, and where insomnia is the problem,
protecting that pressure matters more than recovering the lost hour.

## The room, and the clock

Cool, dark and quiet, with the clock turned away. Checking the time during the night converts
wakefulness into arithmetic about how little sleep remains, which raises arousal exactly when the
aim is to lower it. Exercise supports sleep generally; vigorous exercise very close to bedtime
suits some people and not others, and it is worth testing individually rather than assuming.

[8] (lifestyle-type-2-diabetes-adherence)
## Why this has its own note

Diabetes is largely self-managed. Most decisions affecting the outcome are made by the person
between appointments, and adherence to glucose-lowering medication is measurably imperfect in
practice. Treating non-adherence as a character issue misses what the evidence shows: cost,
complexity, side effects, low health literacy, depression, and simply forgetting account for most of
it, and each has a different remedy.

## Diabetes self-management education

Structured education and support is described as a core part of care rather than an optional extra,
with specific points at which it is offered: at diagnosis, annually where treatment targets are not
met, when complicating factors develop, and when transitions in care occur. It improves glucose
control and quality of life, and it is consistently underused.

## Making the regimen easier to follow

- **Simplify where possible.** Fewer daily doses and fixed-dose combinations improve adherence.
  Where a regimen has become more complex than the individualized target requires,
  de-intensification is an appropriate response rather than a concession.
- **Name the cost problem out loud.** Cost-related underuse — skipping doses, splitting tablets, not
  filling prescriptions — is common and is rarely volunteered unless asked about directly.
- **Tie doses to existing routines** rather than to clock times, and use pill organizers, blister
  packs or reminders.
- **Anticipate side effects.** Gastrointestinal effects with metformin and genital mycotic infections
  with SGLT-2 inhibitors are common early reasons for silent discontinuation, and both are usually
  manageable if raised.
- **Screen for depression.** It is more common in diabetes and materially reduces self-care; treating
  it improves both.

## Monitoring that is actually used

Glucose monitoring only helps if the readings change something. Guidance describes agreeing in
advance what the person will do in response to particular readings, rather than recording numbers
that are reviewed only at the next appointment. Where continuous monitoring is available, the same
principle applies to time-in-range.

## The review schedule

Long-term glucose control is measured at least twice yearly when stable and at goal, and quarterly
otherwise. Alongside it, ongoing care includes annual eye screening, kidney function and urine
albumin testing, foot examination, blood pressure and lipid review, dental care, and vaccination.
These are separate from glucose control and are frequently the parts that lapse.

## Sick days and travel

Illness raises glucose and changes requirements, and glucose-lowering medication is not simply
stopped because someone is not eating — that combination is a recognized route into a
hyperglycemic emergency. A sick-day plan agreed in advance with the person's own clinician is the
described approach. This system does not provide one, and does not give dosing instructions.

[9] (condition-hypertension)
## What it is

Hypertension is persistently raised pressure in the arteries, sustained over time rather than on a
single occasion. Blood pressure is written as two numbers: the systolic pressure, generated when the
heart contracts, over the diastolic pressure, present between beats. Both are measured in
millimeters of mercury.

Pressure varies continuously through the day — with activity, stress, pain, caffeine, sleep and time
of day, typically lowest during sleep and rising before waking. That variation is why a diagnosis
rests on repeated measurements rather than one reading, and why a single high reading in a clinic is
not itself a diagnosis.

## How it is usually recognized

Hypertension is typically without symptoms and is most often found on routine measurement rather
than because someone felt unwell. That is the main reason screening for it exists at all. Where
symptoms such as headache, visual disturbance or nosebleed are attributed to raised blood pressure,
they usually reflect either a very high pressure or an unrelated cause — the belief that ordinary
hypertension can be felt leads people to treat by symptom rather than by measurement, which does not
work.

## What contributes to it

Most cases have no single identifiable cause and reflect a combination of age, genetic
predisposition, excess body weight, high dietary sodium, low potassium intake, physical inactivity,
alcohol intake, poor sleep including untreated sleep apnea (apnoea), and chronic stress. Arterial
stiffening with age is why systolic pressure tends to rise across the lifespan while diastolic
pressure often falls after middle age.

A minority of cases have an identifiable secondary cause — kidney disease, renal artery narrowing,
primary aldosteronism, thyroid or adrenal disorders, obstructive sleep apnea, and certain medications
including combined oral contraceptives, decongestants, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and
some stimulants. Investigation for a secondary cause is usually considered when hypertension appears
at a young age, is unusually severe, responds poorly to treatment, or worsens abruptly after a period
of stability.

## Why it is treated

Sustained high pressure damages arteries over years, and the conditions that follow are the reason
for treating a symptomless number: stroke, heart attack, heart failure, chronic kidney disease,
retinal damage, and cognitive decline. The benefit of treatment is measured in reduced rates of those
events, not in how the person feels — which is also why adherence is difficult, since a treatment
that produces no felt improvement and occasional side effects is easy to stop.

## How it is generally managed

Lifestyle measures — dietary sodium reduction, a diet pattern high in vegetables, fruit and whole
grains, regular activity, weight management, limiting alcohol, and stopping smoking — apply to
everyone. Drug treatment is added according to the level of risk. Diagnostic thresholds, treatment
targets, drug classes and follow-up intervals are covered by the hypertension guideline notes in
this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

A very high reading accompanied by chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, visual loss,
confusion, weakness or numbness on one side, or difficulty speaking is an emergency and requires
immediate medical attention rather than a routine appointment. The emergency-symptom notes in this
corpus govern those situations.

[10] (lifestyle-hypertension-activity)
## What is generally recommended

The commonly stated target for adults is 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic
activity, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, or an equivalent combination, plus muscle-strengthening
activity on two or more days. For blood pressure specifically, the aerobic component carries most of
the evidence, and the reduction it produces is comparable in size to what a single
antihypertensive agent achieves in some people.

Moderate intensity means breathing harder and able to talk but not sing — brisk walking, cycling on
the flat, swimming, dancing, gardening that raises the heart rate. Vigorous means being unable to
say more than a few words without pausing.

## The part that matters most

Sessions can be accumulated across the week in whatever blocks fit, and short bouts count. The
older advice that only sustained ten-minute blocks counted has been dropped, and the practical
consequence is that stairs, brisk walks between tasks and short bursts of activity all contribute.

The largest single gain is from moving from doing nothing to doing something. The dose-response
curve is steepest at the low end, so someone currently inactive gains more from the first 60 minutes
a week than an already-active person gains from the last 60.

## Strength training

Resistance training two or more days per week is described as lowering blood pressure independently
of aerobic activity, and the two together are better than either alone. Isometric exercise — such as
sustained handgrip or wall-sit protocols — has attracted attention for a comparatively large effect
on blood pressure in trials, though the evidence base is smaller than for aerobic work and it is
usually described as an adjunct rather than a replacement.

## Reducing sedentary time

Prolonged uninterrupted sitting is associated with worse cardiovascular outcomes partly
independently of how much a person exercises. Breaking up long periods of sitting is described as a
separate target from the weekly activity total, not a substitute for it.

## Building it sustainably

Starting below the target and increasing gradually is more effective than beginning at the target,
because the failure mode is not insufficient ambition but abandonment. Activity that fits an
existing routine, and that the person is willing to keep doing, outperforms a theoretically superior
program that stops after three weeks.

## When medical review comes first

Anyone with chest pain on exertion, breathlessness disproportionate to effort, fainting, palpitations
with exercise, known heart disease, or very high uncontrolled blood pressure should be assessed
before starting vigorous activity. Anyone who develops chest discomfort, severe breathlessness or
faintness during exercise should stop and seek assessment. The emergency-symptom notes in this
corpus govern those situations.

## Call emergency services immediately

Sepsis is the body's dysregulated response to infection causing organ dysfunction. In someone with a
known or suspected infection, any of the following warrants emergency assessment:

- Confusion, disorientation, slurred speech, or unusual drowsiness.
- Very fast breathing, or breathlessness.
- A fast heart rate, or dizziness on standing.
- Not passing urine for many hours.
- Skin that is mottled, ashen, very pale or blue; or a rash that does not fade when pressed.
- Shivering, or feeling very cold, or a very high or very low temperature.
- Severe muscle pain, or a feeling of being more unwell than ever before.

In a child, additional signs include fast breathing, a fit or convulsion, mottled or ashen skin, a
rash that does not fade, lethargy or difficulty waking, feeling abnormally cold, not feeding, no
urine for many hours, and repeated vomiting.

## Why the phrase "just say sepsis" exists

Sepsis progresses over hours, and survival falls with every hour of delay in recognition and
treatment. Its early presentation is nonspecific and resembles a bad case of an ordinary infection,
so it is regularly missed at first contact. Guidance encourages the person or family to raise the
possibility explicitly — asking "could this be sepsis?" — because that question reliably prompts a
structured assessment, and because the family's sense that the person is unusually unwell is
diagnostically valuable and often the earliest signal available.

## Where it comes from

Any infection can cause it. Common sources are the lungs, the urinary tract, the abdomen, and skin
or wounds, including surgical wounds and intravenous lines. The original infection may be minor and
may already be treated.

## Who is at higher risk

Infants and adults over 65; pregnancy and the six weeks after; people with diabetes, chronic liver
or kidney disease, or cancer; people on chemotherapy, steroids or other immunosuppressants; people
without a functioning spleen; people with indwelling lines or catheters; and anyone with a recent
operation or invasive procedure. In these groups the threshold for escalation is lower still, and
fever may be absent.

## What not to do

Do not wait to see whether a fever settles overnight in someone with these features. Do not be
reassured by a normal temperature: a low temperature is as concerning as a high one, and older
adults may have neither. Do not delay because antibiotics have already been started — sepsis can
develop despite them, and an infection that was responding can still progress if the source has not
been controlled.

produces is a substitute for emergency assessment.

## What it is

Influenza is a respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses, of which types A and B cause
seasonal epidemics. Influenza A is subtyped by two surface proteins, hemagglutinin and
neuraminidase — the H and N in designations such as H1N1 and H3N2. The virus changes continuously
through small mutations, which is why immunity from one season is incomplete against the next and
why the vaccine is reformulated annually rather than given once.

It is more severe than a common cold in both symptoms and consequences, and it causes substantial
seasonal hospitalization and death, concentrated in older adults, young children, pregnant people
and those with chronic conditions.

## How it is usually recognized

Abrupt onset — people can often name the hour — with fever, chills, muscle aches, headache, marked
fatigue and dry cough. Sore throat and nasal symptoms occur but are less prominent than in a cold.
Fever typically lasts three to five days; cough and fatigue commonly persist two weeks or more.
Gastrointestinal symptoms occur more often in children than adults.

Laboratory confirmation is not required to manage a typical case during a known outbreak, and is
used where the result would change management — in hospital, in high-risk people, or where an
antiviral decision or outbreak control depends on it.

## Complications

Pneumonia is the main one, either from the virus itself or from a secondary bacterial infection.
Secondary bacterial pneumonia classically appears as a deterioration after several days of
improvement, which is a pattern worth recognizing. Other complications include worsening of
underlying asthma, COPD, heart failure or diabetes, and less commonly inflammation of the heart
muscle, brain or muscle tissue. Influenza is also associated with a transient increase in the risk
of myocardial infarction and stroke in the weeks after infection.

## How it is generally managed

Supportive care for most otherwise healthy people: rest, fluids, and symptomatic relief. Antiviral
treatment is targeted rather than universal, and is most effective when started early — the timing
threshold and the groups in whom treatment is recommended are covered by the influenza guideline
note in this corpus. Antibiotics have no effect on the virus and are reserved for a bacterial
complication.

Annual vaccination is the principal preventive measure, alongside staying home while febrile, hand
hygiene and respiratory etiquette.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Difficulty breathing or breathlessness at rest, chest pain, persistent dizziness or confusion,
inability to keep fluids down, seizures, severe muscle pain or weakness, or symptoms that improve
and then return with fever and worse cough — these need urgent assessment. In children, additional
signs include fast or labored breathing, blue lips, no tears when crying, and significantly reduced
wet diapers. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

## The spiral this is trying to interrupt

Breathlessness on exertion makes activity unpleasant, so activity is avoided; muscles decondition,
so the same task demands more; and the breathlessness arrives sooner than it did before. The lungs
have not changed over that period — the body using them has. Most of the improvement available in
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes from reversing this loop rather than from anything that
acts on the airways, which is why exercise is treated as a therapy here rather than as general
advice.

The COPD guideline note in this corpus covers where pulmonary rehabilitation sits among the
recommended measures. This note is about what the activity consists of and how to keep it going.

## Breathing techniques used during exertion

**Pursed-lip breathing** — breathing in through the nose and out slowly through lightly pursed lips,
with the out-breath longer than the in-breath — keeps a small back-pressure in the airways so they
stay open longer during exhalation. It is used during the effort, not only afterwards, and it is the
technique most people find gives immediate control when breathlessness rises.

**Paced breathing** links breath to movement: breathing out during the effortful part of a task and
in during the recovery, so stairs are climbed on the out-breath and rested on the in-breath.

Leaning forward with the forearms supported on a rail, a table or the thighs puts the breathing
muscles at a mechanical advantage, and it is a recovery position rather than a sign of defeat.

## What the exercise looks like

Walking is the usual foundation, built up by adding a few minutes at a time rather than by pushing
until breathless. Interval work — a few minutes of effort alternating with recovery — is often
better tolerated than continuous effort at the same total volume.

Arm work is disproportionately valuable and disproportionately neglected. Tasks held at or above
shoulder height, such as reaching into a cupboard or hanging washing, are frequently the most
breathless part of a day, because the same muscles help stabilize the chest wall for breathing.
Light resistance work for the shoulders and arms addresses this specifically.

Breathlessness during exercise is expected and is not harmful in itself. The intensity usually
described is effort at which speaking is possible in short phrases but not in full sentences.

## Pacing, and bad days

Energy conservation is about sequencing rather than about doing less: heavier tasks spread across a
day rather than stacked, sitting where a task allows it, and equipment such as a shower stool or a
wheeled trolley used without treating it as a concession.

On a bad day the aim is to reduce rather than to stop, because a few days of nothing costs more than
it saves. Increasing breathlessness over days, a change in sputum color or volume, or fever is a
different situation and a reason for contact rather than for pacing.

## The general target

Diabetes association guidance describes an HbA1c below 7 percent as a reasonable goal for many
non-pregnant adults, on the basis that this level of control reduces the small-vessel complications of diabetes — retinal, kidney and nerve
disease — over the following years. The evidence for large-vessel benefit from tighter glucose
control alone is weaker, which is why the target sits alongside blood pressure and lipid management
rather than above them.

The target is individualized rather than applied uniformly:

- **A more stringent goal**, such as below 6.5 percent, where it can be reached without significant
  low blood sugar or other harm — typically shorter duration of diabetes, longer life expectancy,
  and no significant cardiovascular disease.
- **A less stringent goal**, such as below 8 percent, where there is a history of severe low blood
  sugar, limited life expectancy, advanced complications, extensive other illness, or where the
  target has proved difficult to reach despite appropriate management.

## Monitoring intervals

HbA1c is measured at least twice a year in people meeting their goal on a stable regimen, and
quarterly in people not at goal or whose therapy has recently changed. It reflects average glucose
over roughly the preceding three months, which is why a shorter retest interval adds little: a test
repeated at six weeks is still reporting mostly the old period.

Continuous glucose monitoring and self-monitoring of blood glucose are complementary to HbA1c
rather than alternatives to it. They show the variability and the low readings that an average
conceals — two people with the same HbA1c can have very different exposure to hypoglycemia — and
they matter most for anyone using insulin or an agent that stimulates insulin release.
Time-in-range metrics derived from continuous monitoring are increasingly reported alongside HbA1c.

## Hypoglycemia is a target too

Guidance treats low blood sugar as an outcome to be measured, not only a side effect to be
mentioned. Episodes are classified by severity, with any episode requiring the assistance of another
person counted as severe, and a history of severe hypoglycemia is one of the explicit reasons to
relax the HbA1c goal rather than pursue it.

## Targets other than glucose

Glycemic control is one of several targets and not the most important one for cardiovascular
outcomes. Blood-pressure control, lipid management, smoking cessation, and — where indicated by
other conditions — the choice of glucose-lowering agent with demonstrated cardiovascular or kidney
benefit sit alongside the HbA1c goal.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on how firmly to state a single number. Some guidance describes 7 percent as the
default with individualization around it; other guidance describes the individualized range as
primary and declines to headline a figure at all, on the grounds that a headline number is applied more rigidly in practice
than its authors intend.
